  • borderline-drop: MongoDB CVE-2026-118383, replica-set peer path, crash only reproduced, no exploitation
  • borderline-drop: Report URI scan data on the APT29 watering hole, marginal delta
  • borderline-drop: Kaspersky IT threat evolution Q3 2026, detection counts, no defender takeaway
  • borderline-drop: PowerFolder cloud breach and /wopi/ server flaw, no CVE, no technical detail, no constituency deployment shown
  • borderline-drop: CNIL ten sanctions on French territorial authorities, generic hardening failings, no Swiss obligation change
  • borderline-drop: University of Tuebingen, Gleis D Chur (Cloak), INCERT eTourismus (Zermatt Tourismus), Maileva, Notion/Fireworks AI, Maersk, private or foreign victims without a stated transferable technique or vector (incident floor)

Verification: four iterations. Iteration 1 found 29 findings (16 truth, 6 editorial, 7 advisory), iteration 2 found 19, iteration 3 found 9 (one new upstream fact: Huntress updated its ScreenConnect post with the RMM+ blank-access-key finding), and iteration 4 returned NEEDS_FIXES with truth 2 and editorial 0 and no F1 or F4, so decision rule 5 applied: the five findings were remediated, the gate re-run clean (58 pass, 0 warn, 0 fail), and the fire published on that early exit without a fifth pass. No double-CLEAN was reached; the two residual truth findings are fixed but unverified by a further cold pass, and the audit should give the ScreenConnect and Fortinet entries an independent read.

Operational notes: the jina reader pool is dead (every key HTTP 402), so pages that only the reader could serve were read by WebFetch or reported as unconfirmed. Research workers FU2 left six stray stub files at the filesystem root (/A_chrome_android.md, /A_chrome_android.err, /A_chrome_extended_156.md, /A_chrome_extended_156.err, /A_edge_security.md, /A_edge_security.err); the sandbox safety check denied deleting them and the run did not work around it, so the operator may remove them. They hold fetch scratch output only and are not part of the repo.

Gate note for the audit: check_run.py citation-cve matches an id against a skeleton that joins the id to the digits of the next bug number on Chrome Releases rows, so a clause naming CVE-2026-125346 on the Extended Stable page reads as a miss although the id is on the page; the Chrome entry avoids naming the id there. The three KEV additions the verifier listed for 2026-11-09 and 2026-11-10 without entries (CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks, CVE-2026-102895 GPUStack, CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Webtop) were dispositioned as borderline-drops by the 2026-11-10 and 2026-11-11 fires and are left for the audit sweep. The main analyses of the Publica (1100 words) and eMudhra (895) entries stay above the 550-word bound as before this fire, for the audit to restructure.

Source health: seven records stay UNSOLVED. Fixed this run: ico-uk, safeonweb-be, netzwoche (recipes in sources_changed). Left for a refilled reader pool or a changed host: schneier (blog and atom feed 403 on every free transport), belden-psirt (403 direct), ahnlab-asec (WebFetch reads it; bridge and extract do not), mozilla-ca-compliance-bugzilla (the REST recipe reads, its rows carry no security vocabulary the health check recognises).

  • Essential-coverage: every essential record was attempted. Coverage gaps: connectwise-trust-center (403 on every transport), sygnia (403), Siemens knowledge-base articles (login-gated), news-admin-ch, srf-news and swissinfo-ger (shallow reach through the listing recipes), the NCSC.ch BACS card recipe, ictjournal-ch, and rapid7's RSS (malformed).
  • Watchlist: none configured.

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-11-11
item.description:
• Outlook zero-day CVE-2026-124194 exploited: a crafted message file leaks authentication data; install the Office update. Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook spoofing flaw (CVSS 3.1 6.5) that Microsoft marks as exploited and not publicly disclosed and that CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-10: a user who opens a crafted message file lets Outlook connect to an attacker-controlled location without the usual external-content warning, which can disclose authentication information. The Preview Pane is not an attack vector; BleepingComputer reports that the disclosed credential is the user's NTLMv2 hash, and no source names the actor or the victims. →
  • Chrome zero-day CVE-2026-125350 exploited: update Chrome and relaunch; Edge for Android fixed, Edge desktop pending. Google's Stable-channel update of 2026-11-09 says an exploit for CVE-2026-125350, a high-severity use-after-free in Chromium's XML component, exists in the wild; CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-10 and no source describes the attacks. The fix is in Stable 157.0.8103.50 (Linux) and 157.0.8103.50 or .51 (Windows, macOS) and in Extended Stable 156.0.8078.96, all of 2026-11-09, later Stable and Extended Stable builds of 2026-11-11 include it, and Microsoft's notes list the fix in Edge for Android 157.0.4341.53 while no Edge desktop release names it yet. →
  • Stolen Qubole vendor credentials assumed customers' idle AWS integration roles; a source-IP condition stops it. Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, reports that between 2026-10-14 and 2026-10-26 an actor used IAM credentials from an AWS account associated with the data platform Qubole to assume customers' cross-account integration roles, each call carrying the correct External ID; most roles had otherwise been idle. Inside each account the actor listed resources, read Secrets Manager, Parameter Store and Lambda configuration, tested harvested AWS, Entra ID and Okta credentials with TruffleHog and downloaded S3 data, in some cases whole buckets; no victim is named, the counts range from more than a dozen to dozens, and how the vendor identities were compromised is not known. →

Active threats, incidents & disclosures 4Trending vulnerabilities 8Updates to prior coverage 8Action items 24

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures4 items

NOTABLENATOB2

GhostFrame: Recorded Future's Insikt Group finds an ESXi post-exploitation framework (vmhostd-core implant, VM control panel, VMkatz credential theft) used by TAG-218, whose activity overlaps Settra ransomware and which targeted SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks and Fortinet VPN appliances in the US and Europe

Insikt Group describes GhostFrame, a previously undocumented command-and-control and post-exploitation framework for compromised VMware ESXi hosts, which it saw used by TAG-218, a group "whose operations overlap with Settra ransomware" (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Operators must already hold root on the host: the implant, an ELF named vmhostd-core generated from a web operator panel, does not exploit a vulnerability to gain access (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). It copies itself to /opt/vmhostd-core, edits the ESXi boot script /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh and runs /sbin/auto-backup.sh to keep the change across reboots, masquerades as vmhostd (resembling VMware's vmware-hostd), and about every five seconds disables the ESXi firewall and the execInstalledOnly control that restricts execution of unsigned binaries, so an administrator who re-enables them is undone (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Its command channel opens simultaneous TCP connections to one address on ports 53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443 and 9443, keeps the first that succeeds and retries after a random delay of 5 to 12 seconds, which Insikt notes is a network detection opportunity; the implant is mainly an in-memory shellcode loader with a reverse-shell fallback.

From the hypervisor the panel can list registered VMs, change power state, create or delete snapshots, enable VNC on a guest, run a SOCKS5 proxy for pivoting, intercept ESXi logins, and run the open-source VMkatz against VM memory snapshots, virtual disks or whole datastores to recover NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, SAM and LSA secrets and NTDS.dit data without running anything inside the guest (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Insikt ties TAG-218's victim-facing servers to VPN-appliance targeting across the US and Europe between late August and October 2026, "predominantly SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks, and Fortinet devices", and says four of those organisations later appeared on the Settra leak site; it assesses that other financially motivated actors are highly likely to adopt the framework, which is an assessment, not an observation (Recorded Future, 2026-11-10). Unit 42 independently reports that after CVE-2026-0257 exploitation attackers pivot from the VPN gateway directly to the virtualization layer (Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, 2026-10-20).

Exposure
ESXi hosts whose root credentials, SSH or shell, or vCenter are reachable after an edge compromise; no ESXi vulnerability is involved, so patching ESXi does not address it, and an estate that runs both a SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks or Fortinet VPN appliance and ESXi without isolated hypervisor management is in the pattern Insikt describes.
Detection
In ESXi file-integrity and shell-audit telemetry, changes to local.sh, a process masquerading as the host daemon or an unexpected executable under /opt, and repeated firewall-off and execInstalledOnly resets; in network telemetry, six near-simultaneous SYNs from the hypervisor management address to one destination on those ports, and any outbound command-style traffic from a hypervisor at all; in vCenter and ESXi logs, snapshot creation or deletion, VNC enablement and power-state changes outside change windows; in datastore telemetry, reads of VM memory-snapshot and virtual-disk files by an identity that is not the backup service.

Triage: administrators legitimately edit local.sh, create snapshots and use VNC; the discriminators are a firewall-off and execInstalledOnly loop, a binary under /opt named vmhostd where the genuine daemon is vmware-hostd, and snapshot-file reads by a non-backup account.

Defender takeaway
Treat a VPN-appliance compromise as a possible hypervisor compromise and check the ESXi persistence files and the execInstalledOnly state before declaring the incident closed; restrict ESXi and vCenter management to dedicated administration hosts.

Turla's Cereal toolset turns a compromised on-premises Exchange server into the command channel and mail collector at Kazakh and Romanian government bodies, with no attacker infrastructure and no new transport agent registered (ESET)

ESET found a previously undocumented .NET toolset, Cereal, on a Kazakh government organisation's Exchange server on 2025-11-28 and, after tuning its detections, on a Romanian government organisation's Exchange server compromised from 2025-12-23; in Romania the mail-collection module was configured to identify messages to or from NATO and EU institutional addresses (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). ESET attributes Cereal to Turla with high confidence, on the concurrent use of another component publicly linked to Turla and conceptual similarity to older Turla malware, and could not determine the initial access method, although it considers a vulnerability exploit possible because the servers are reachable from the internet (ESET Research, 2026-11-10).

The command channel is the victim's own Exchange server. CerealNeuron runs on the compromised server and passively waits for requests on web paths made to look like Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync traffic; a correctly encrypted request is treated as a command and a bad one gets a normal-looking Exchange error page, and ESET found no operator-controlled server and could not identify ingress addresses (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). CerealHermit is a network-less variant that reads encrypted command files from disk, and each task runs as a small .NET assembly inside a CerealRunner (mailbox retrieval, Active Directory and WMI queries, LSA secrets extraction, file operations) (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). CerealLoader, the only component written to disk in recognisable .NET form, abuses .NET VTable fixups so native code runs before managed code and is placed where trusted processes load it: the System32 wbem directory (ncobjapi.dll, wbemcomn.dll, loaded by WMI) and the .NET native image cache (ESET Research, 2026-11-10). CerealBox, injected into EdgeTransport.exe, wraps the handlers of transport agents already loaded, so "no new agent appears anywhere in Exchange's configuration"; it keeps messages with .doc, .docx or .pdf attachments that match hard-coded sender, recipient, subject or attachment-name lists and stages them compressed and encrypted on disk for exfiltration through CerealNeuron (ESET Research, 2026-11-10).

Exposure
Any organisation that runs Microsoft Exchange on premises with a role reachable from the internet; ESET names no vulnerable version, so exposure is the deployment model.
Detection
File-integrity telemetry on the Exchange host for DLLs in the System32 wbem directory and .NET native image cache files that do not match the Microsoft originals; module telemetry for non-Microsoft assemblies loaded into EdgeTransport.exe while Get-TransportAgent lists nothing new; web-server logs for requests to the Outlook Web Access, Autodiscover and ActiveSync look-alike paths from clients with no matching mailbox flow, whose encrypted bodies return a generic error page; and Exchange Web Services mailbox retrievals made from the server's own context. With no external C2 and no known entry vector, the check is a compromise assessment of every internet-facing Exchange server.

Triage: third-party anti-spam, data-loss-prevention and archiving products also inject into the transport service, but they are vendor-signed and appear in the transport-agent configuration, which CerealBox does not; the native image cache regenerates legitimately after .NET updates, so a changed timestamp alone is weak, while a file that does not match the Microsoft binary is the signal.

Defender takeaway
Treat internet-facing Exchange servers as top-tier assets with endpoint detection and restricted egress, baseline the wbem directory and the native image cache, and run the compromise assessment now, because network-only detection will not find a channel that rides the victim's own web paths.

CopperDragon: Check Point ties three China-nexus intrusion sets to one Sparrow-framework supplier, among them SilentDelivery watering holes on government, shipping, IT and research sites that show a fake Chrome certificate warning (Czech Republic, Germany and France in its telemetry)

Check Point Research's year-long investigation groups three intrusion sets under one malware-supply entity it calls CopperDragon, a possible "digital quartermaster" for China-nexus actors that use the cross-platform Sparrow framework (FamousSparrow and Earth Estries among them); Check Point itself cautions that the use of the same backdoor or C2 infrastructure "does not necessarily mean" the same actor ran two intrusions, so this is a hypothesis (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10).

SilentDelivery, active since early 2026 against Europe and Asia, is the set nearest the constituency. Compromised government, shipping, IT and research websites, one through cross-site scripting in an unsanitised input field, carry obfuscated JavaScript that fingerprints the visitor and replaces the page with a language-localised fake Google Chrome SSL warning urging a "Certificate Fix" utility; the MSI, served from compromised cloud storage buckets, installs the new SquadC backdoor or a SparrowDoor variant (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10). SquadC can be set to run only while a browser process is alive, persists through a Run key named WindowsUpdateAssist, and offers file operations, command execution and screenshots. A second route is a spear-phishing RAR whose LNK abuses ftp.exe, with the same C2 (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10). Positive Technologies independently documented the same fake-certificate chain, with victims in Taiwan, Germany, Indonesia and the Czech Republic (Positive Technologies, 2026-08-21).

The other two sets show what follows an intrusion. OceanGate in Asia starts from an exploited internet-facing Linux server and moves through trojanised ssh and sshd binaries that log passwords, a Linux backdoor that can load a kernel rootkit, FRP and Chisel tunnels, a hidden local administrator account and an LSA security-package credential interceptor; recent SparrowDoor builds embed the WinDivert driver to share a service port such as 443. DarkWire against Latin American telecom and government bodies uses DLL sideloading of uncommon executables, SoftEther VPN renamed to system-process names, DNS MX tunnelling and WMI lateral movement (Check Point Research, 2026-11-10). No Swiss victim is named.

Exposure
Staff of public bodies, shipping, IT and research organisations who browse peer websites, web teams whose sites accept unsanitised input, and Windows endpoints that let a standard user run an MSI from a browser download.
Detection
In endpoint telemetry, a browser followed by msiexec running an installer named like a certificate repair utility and a new Run key value with an update-themed name; in module-load telemetry, DLL sideloading by rarely abused executables, and the WinDivert driver loaded by a process that is not a VPN or firewall product; in account telemetry, a new local administrator account; on Linux, ssh and sshd binaries that differ from the package-manager copy and frpc or chisel binaries; in DNS, MX-query volume from servers that send no mail.

Triage: WinDivert is legitimate in VPN and firewall products, so the signal is a parent that is a sideloaded DLL or backdoor rather than the vendor's signed service; SoftEther is legitimate software, but not under a system-process name in a non-system path; a genuine Chrome SSL warning is never cleared by installing an MSI.

Defender takeaway
Treat a browser page that offers a "certificate fix" installer as an incident trigger and stop standard users running MSI installers from a browser download; web teams of government and research sites should check for injected third-party script and input-handling flaws, because a compromised site becomes a delivery vehicle for its peers.

Qubole: an attacker used IAM credentials from a vendor-associated AWS account to assume dormant cross-account integration roles in dozens of customer accounts, then harvested secrets and validated Entra ID and Okta client credentials (Wiz and Sentra, 14 to 26 October)

Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, observed a threat actor using IAM credentials from an AWS account associated with Qubole, a big-data platform, between 2026-10-14 and 2026-10-26 (Wiz, 2026-11-09). The actor used two Qubole IAM users to call sts:AssumeRole on the cross-account integration roles that customers had created to trust Qubole's account; "every AssumeRole request we attributed to the threat actor included an External ID, and every one succeeded", most of the roles were otherwise not in use, and the traffic came from a rented hosting server and commercial VPN exits, not the AWS infrastructure where legitimate platform traffic originates (Wiz, 2026-11-09; Sentra, 2026-11-09).

Inside each account the actor enumerated resources, read Lambda function configuration, Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store, ran TruffleHog to test AWS access keys, Entra ID service-principal client secrets and Okta client credentials it found, and then downloaded S3 data opportunistically, in some cases whole buckets in one session (Wiz, 2026-11-09). Wiz found no tie to other reported activity and judges the targeting opportunistic; how the Qubole IAM users were compromised is not stated. Sentra writes that dozens of Qubole customers were impacted, and BleepingComputer could not find a public Qubole announcement (Sentra, 2026-11-09; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10). No Swiss or public-sector victim is named, but the exposure is shared by any account that gave a data or analytics vendor a cross-account role and left it in place.

Exposure
Any AWS account holding an IAM role whose trust policy lets a Qubole account, or any other vendor account, assume it, including roles left from integrations that ended; the roles' trust policies and last-used data show them, and Wiz publishes the vendor account identifier, the two principals and the attacker address ranges for a CloudTrail hunt back to 2026-10-01 (Wiz, 2026-11-09).
Detection
In cloud control-plane audit logs, AssumeRole events into integration roles whose calling identity is the vendor account but whose source address is not AWS infrastructure, and session names with a consistent attacker-chosen prefix; GetCallerIdentity calls from many keys within seconds and Entra ID or Okta sign-ins by service principals or clients right after, as the actor validates credentials; ListSecrets, GetSecretValue, Parameter Store and Lambda configuration reads in bursts. Object reads are absent from CloudTrail management events, so S3 data events or server access logs must be on, and Wiz says missing logs left responders unable to see what was read (Wiz, 2026-11-09).

Triage: legitimate vendor traffic comes from the vendor's own AWS infrastructure; the correct External ID does not discriminate, because it is logged in plaintext and often stored by the vendor, while a vendor role assumed from a consumer VPN or a hosting provider the vendor has never used is the high-signal case.

Defender takeaway
Inventory third-party trust relationships, delete the roles of ended integrations, narrow each trusted principal to the vendor's specific principal and add a source-address or endpoint condition, which Wiz says alone would have blocked every observed assumption; after an incident, revoke the issued role sessions and rotate every secret, parameter, Lambda variable and identity-provider credential the role could read.

CVE-2026-124194, Microsoft Outlook: opening a crafted message file makes Outlook reach an attacker-chosen network location without the usual warning and disclose authentication information; exploited as a zero-day, fixed in the November 2026 updates and listed by CISA (CVSS 3.1 6.5)

Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes CVE-2026-124194, an Outlook spoofing flaw (CWE-356, the product does not warn the user of an unsafe action) scored CVSS 3.1 6.5, which the Security Update Guide marks as exploited and not publicly disclosed (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). Microsoft's FAQ says an unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted message file and convinces the user to open it, whereupon Outlook may connect to an attacker-controlled network location without showing the usual external-content warning, "potentially disclosing authentication information that could be used to impersonate the user"; the Preview Pane is not an attack vector, so the file has to be opened (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-10 (CISA, 2026-11-10), and BleepingComputer counts it as the one actively exploited zero-day of this Patch Tuesday (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10). The affected products are Outlook in Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Office LTSC 2024 (fixed in 16.0.17932.21140) and Office LTSC 2021 (fixed in 16.0.14334.21048); Microsoft 365 Apps take the fix through the Office security-update channel (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-10). BleepingComputer calls it an NTLM credential disclosure flaw: opening the attachment makes Windows connect to an attacker-controlled share and expose the user's NTLMv2 hash, which can be captured and cracked offline (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10). No source names the actor or the victims.

Exposure
Every Outlook desktop below those builds; the build shows under File, Office Account, and the delivery path is mail or a download that carries a message file, which the user must open.
Detection
Outbound connections to non-corporate addresses over SMB (TCP 445), WebDAV or HTTPS from OUTLOOK.EXE or from the user's session shortly after a message-file attachment is opened, authentication events carrying the user's identity toward an external address, and mail-gateway logs for message-file attachments from unknown senders. Because the credential material may already have been captured before the patch, the check also covers the weeks before it. The disclosed material is the user's NTLMv2 hash, which can be cracked offline or used to impersonate the user, so also watch for later logons by the account from unfamiliar hosts.

Triage: Outlook legitimately contacts SharePoint, OneDrive and corporate file servers; the discriminator is an external, non-corporate destination preceded by the opening of a message file.

Defender takeaway
Install the November Office update now rather than in the normal cycle, because the flaw is exploited and a patched machine still leaves earlier captured credentials valid; reset the accounts of users whose Outlook reached an external destination.

A Confluence Data Center instance is vulnerable only if the "Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)" setting is enabled; the setting has been off by default for new installations since Confluence 3.0 and the feature was removed in Confluence 10.0, so 10.x is not affected, nor is Confluence Cloud (Atlassian, 2026-11-09). Atlassian scores the flaw 9.3 (CVSS 4.0, network vector, no privileges, no user interaction), lists Confluence Data Center 1.x to 9.x as affected and 9.2.28 as the fixed version (Atlassian, 2026-11-09). If patching must wait, clearing the Remote API checkbox needs no restart, and a request to the soap-axis1 confluenceservice-v2 servlet path should then answer HTTP 403. Atlassian says it "cannot confirm if your instances have been affected" and asks teams to check affected instances for compromise (Atlassian, 2026-11-09); no source reports exploitation of Confluence, and BSI CERT-Bund's bulletin rates the issue high (BSI CERT-Bund, 2026-11-10). The Apache Axis project says the flaw allows unauthenticated remote class instantiation through a SOAP fault and that it does not expect to release an Axis 1.x fix (Apache Axis project, 2026-11-06), and the same flaw is exploited against on-premises N-able N-central servers (Huntback, 2026-11-12; Previdian, 2026-11-12; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-12).

A Data Center instance on any 9.x or earlier release, with 9.2.28 the only fixed version listed, whose Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP) setting is ticked; the setting sits under General Configuration, Further Configuration.

Web access logs for requests to the soap-axis1 servlet path and the XML-RPC endpoint from unexpected sources, and child processes of the Confluence JVM that the application does not normally start; this is an inference from the attack mechanics, not a source statement.

Switch the Remote API off today and upgrade to 9.2.28, because the flaw is already exploited against another product's embedded Axis; because Atlassian asks for a compromise check, review the access logs of any instance that had the API enabled and was reachable from untrusted networks.

Patch internet-facing Connect servers to the fixed build of their train now, because five flaws need neither credentials nor a user and the bulletin offers nothing but the update.

Microsoft November 2026 Patch Tuesday: seven of the unauthenticated network flaws rated CVSS 9.8, in domain infrastructure and server roles, among them a Kerberos relay to a domain controller (CVE-2026-85844) and zero-click code execution through Exchange attachment indexing (CVE-2026-116928); none exploited or disclosed

Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes seven flaws in domain infrastructure and server roles scored CVSS 3.1 9.8 that need no credentials over the network (the release carries further 9.8 rows, DirectMusic among them, that are not covered here (Microsoft, 2026-11-10)); the only record Microsoft marks as exploited in this release is the Outlook zero-day, which is a separate item, and none of these rows is marked exploited or publicly disclosed (Microsoft, 2026-11-10; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10). Two have mechanics that make the timeline short. CVE-2026-85844 is an authentication bypass in Windows Kerberos: an unauthenticated attacker sends crafted Kerberos authentication traffic and relays the resulting authentication to an affected domain controller, with no user interaction (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). CVE-2026-116928 is an out-of-bounds write in the Windows Search component that Exchange Server uses: an attacker emails a crafted attachment, Exchange indexes it automatically, so "the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment", and the code runs with the permissions of the processing service (Microsoft, 2026-11-10).

The other five are described more thinly: a double free in Windows DNS (CVE-2026-88218) (Microsoft, 2026-11-10), an out-of-bounds read in Windows DHCP Server (CVE-2026-88243) (Microsoft, 2026-11-10) and a release of an invalid pointer in Windows iSCSI (CVE-2026-88234) (Microsoft, 2026-11-10), each reachable by an in-network attacker calling arbitrary endpoints; an out-of-bounds write in the Windows LDAP service that gives code execution in its context through crafted LDAP calls (CVE-2026-119958) (Microsoft, 2026-11-10); and a heap overflow in SQL Server (CVE-2026-116945) that needs an attacker who controls a network endpoint an integration package connects to, with no credentials or user interaction when the package runs automatically (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). The fixes are the November cumulative updates per release, for example KB5131291 (Windows Server 2016), KB5131085 (Server 2019), KB5131090 (Server 2022) and KB5131080 or KB5131077 (Server 2025), and the November SQL Server updates, for example KB5129299 (2025 CU10) and KB5129300 (2022 CU27).

Exposure
Domain controllers (Kerberos, LDAP, DNS), DNS and DHCP servers, Exchange servers that receive mail from the internet, and SQL Server hosts that run Integration Services packages against endpoints an attacker could control; the installed cumulative update shows in the update history of each host.
Detection
No exploitation is reported, so detection is hardening-grade: crashes or restarts of the DNS Server, DHCP Server and LSASS processes on domain controllers, Kerberos or LDAP bursts from workstation networks toward domain controllers, content-indexing or transport worker crashes on Exchange after inbound mail with unusual attachments, and an inventory of which domain controllers and Exchange servers already carry the November update.
Defender takeaway
Put the November update on domain controllers and internet-facing Exchange servers first; Microsoft's records give an unauthenticated attacker a relay to a domain controller and a mail-borne path to code execution on Exchange, and the DNS, DHCP and iSCSI rows are reachable by an in-network attacker, so keep those services off untrusted segments until they are patched.

Vates Xen Orchestra (VSA-2026-062): a crafted empty-object login cookie bypasses authentication and is exploited to take over XCP-ng hosts; fixed in xo-server 5.213.1 and 5.211.2, no CVE assigned yet

Vates published advisory VSA-2026-062 on 2026-11-10, rated Critical, for Xen Orchestra and the Xen Orchestra Appliance (XOA), the web management plane for XCP-ng pools; no CVE id or CVSS score has been assigned (Vates, 2026-11-10; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10). Vates says a threat actor is actively exploiting the flaw, that an adversary can bypass authentication and act with Admin privilege, and that a compromise can lead to arbitrary code execution on managed pools and a full takeover of XCP-ng nodes as root (Vates, 2026-11-10). The mechanism, per Vates: the REST cookie parser turns an authenticationToken cookie of j:%7B%7D into an empty object, the REST authentication path hands that object to the token provider without requiring a string, the token lookup treats it as unfiltered and returns the first token, and the provider authenticates as that token's owner if the token has not expired; the authenticated token-listing route then returns reusable login token ids (Vates, 2026-11-10). The attacker needs network reach to the interface and an unexpired first token in the Xen Orchestra token store, and no credentials or user interaction.

Xen Orchestra before 6.9.2 (stable) and before 6.10.1 (latest) is affected, and the fixes are xo-server 5.211.2 on the stable channel and 5.213.1 on the latest channel; a source install must move to the latest master (Vates, 2026-11-10). BleepingComputer gives different release numbers, so check the installed xo-server version rather than the release label (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-10).

Exposure
Any Xen Orchestra or XOA instance below those versions whose web or REST port is reachable from an untrusted network; Vates' first mitigation is a dedicated management network, never the internet (Vates, 2026-11-10).
Detection
A successful exploit leaves no Xen Orchestra log, so the signal is on the wire or at a reverse proxy: HTTP requests whose authenticationToken cookie is an empty JSON object in the encoded or the literal form, and Vates warns that a rule written as a regular expression can be bypassed with other encodings (Vates, 2026-11-10). On the XCP-ng hosts Vates lists a VM that sends its serial console to a file, a VM with an unexpected name, cron files written by the actor and the dynamic-linker preload file, and says these cover only the known campaign, so their absence does not prove a clean host (Vates, 2026-11-10).
Defender takeaway
Update now and take the interface off any untrusted network; for an instance that was exposed, treat the stack as possibly compromised, rotate every secret it held (backup remotes, the root and pool secrets, user and OTP secrets, mail-server passwords) and reinstall where compromise is confirmed (Vates, 2026-11-10).

SonicWall's informational advisory SNWLID-2026-0021 of 2026-11-10, which has no CVE and no workaround, says SonicOS appliances with Client DPI-SSL enabled continued to trust certificate chains issued by the compromised eMudhra intermediate CAs because the firewall's local certificate store trusted the underlying roots, and that the firewall then re-signed traffic from the impacted servers with its local DPI-SSL CA certificate, preventing client browsers from rejecting connections signed by the untrusted intermediates (SonicWall, 2026-11-10; SonicWall advisory data, 2026-11-10). SonicWall removed the affected root certificates from the SonicOS certificate store and added blocking logic for the compromised chain. Affected are Gen7 hardware firewalls (TZ 270 to TZ 670, NSa 2700 to 6700, NSsp 10700 to 15700) and Gen7 NSv up to 7.3.4-7013, fixed in 7.3.4-7015 and higher, and Gen8 hardware (TZ 80 to TZ 680, NSa 2800 to 5800) and Gen8 NSv up to 8.2.2-8015, fixed in 8.2.3-8015 and higher; a Gen7 firewall that took only 7.3.4-7013 is therefore still affected (SonicWall, 2026-11-10).

Apple revised its support page on 2026-11-10: from macOS 27.2.1 the command-line tools no longer accept the twelve intermediate certificates, and the two roots they chain to, with three more eMudhra roots, leave /etc/ssl/cert.pem; macOS 26.7.3 and 15.8.3 carry the same protection, and after updating the manual removal need not be repeated (Apple, 2026-11-10). The revised page no longer carries the block dates of its 2026-10-30 version, so the 2026-10-22 date of the tracker and BleepingComputer stands for Apple's block.

Microsoft's post carries an update of 2026-11-10: the remaining eMudhra roots leave Microsoft products starting 2026-11-16, the ten remaining roots leave the Windows trusted root list through the automatic certificate-trust update, Edge and WebView2 drop default trust for emSign Root CA - G1, C1, ECC Root CA and Root TLS CA - G1 on the same date, Azure Linux images follow that day, and the .NET container images and the Microsoft Build of OpenJDK follow upstream releases (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). What is new is the wider population: BACS lists butchers and food producers, restaurants and hotels, pharmacies, doctors' practices and laboratories, logistics and warehouses, industry and farms among the users, many of which do not know their cooling plants are reachable from the internet or run by an external provider, and it repeats what the Hub advisory already said, that security updates fixing the known flaws are available for the AK-SM 800A and 8xxA family and that newer firmware activates additional protections and enforces encrypted HTTPS communication (translated from German) (BACS, 2026-11-10). It recommends identifying the controllers, those run by contractors included, installing vendor updates, restricting unsupported systems to trusted networks or a VPN, reaching them remotely only through one centrally managed access point with default passwords replaced, and replacing end-of-life products; it names no attacker, no exploited CVE and no count of Swiss victims.

N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on 2026-11-10 with seven CVE ids, which replaces the entry's statements that no fix, no CVE ids and no affected or fixed builds existed, and reports scanning activity associated with the public proof-of-concept code but no evidence of successful exploitation; on-premises servers must be upgraded and every Agent and Probe upgraded too.

N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2, build 2026.4.1.26, on 2026-11-10 as a critical security update; hosted servers are already upgraded, on-premises customers must upgrade their own servers, and every customer must upgrade Agents first and then Probes (N-able, 2026-11-10). Huntress lists seven CVE ids for the fixed flaws and relays N-able's status-page statement that it observed "scanning activity associated with the published proof-of-concept code" but no evidence that any customer environment was successfully exploited; Huntress has seen no exploitation in its partners' environments, and N-able's guidance is to keep on-premises servers offline until the upgrade is complete (Huntress, 2026-11-10). After the hotfix the built-in remote control is temporarily disabled and Take Control still works (N-able, 2026-11-10).

Update11 Nov 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-11-11T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarycvessourcesevidenceverificationsourcing_noteconfidenceactionsbody

SAP's Patch Day page of 2026-11-10 is published and Onapsis, which found the Web Dispatcher, ICM and Gateway flaws, supplies the fixed kernel patch levels, the Gateway parameter gw/acl_mode_proxy = 1 and the statement that it gave SAP a working unauthenticated exploit for the Web Dispatcher and ICM pair and has seen no attacks, replacing the entry's earlier statement that fixed releases were not public.

SAP's Security Patch Day page of 2026-11-10 lists 35 new notes and four GitHub security advisories and carries the four CVSS 10.0 notes above (SAP, 2026-11-10). Onapsis published threat advisories for the Web Dispatcher and ICM pair, which it names ICM2SHELL, and for the Gateway flaw, which it names ProxyGate, with the fixed kernel patch levels, the Gateway parameter gw/acl_mode_proxy = 1 and the statement that it gave SAP a working unauthenticated exploit for ICM2SHELL and has seen no attacks (Onapsis, 2026-11-10; Onapsis, 2026-11-10). Five further notes on the page are rated Critical at CVSS 9.1 to 9.9, among them an ABAP application server OS command injection for low-privileged users (CVE-2026-76965, note 3792735) and a code injection in NetWeaver Knowledge Management XML Forms (CVE-2026-109803, note 3809153); they are not covered here (SAP, 2026-11-10).

CVE-2026-116606 / CVE-2026-111560, Barracuda Email Security Gateway: an unauthenticated configuration-import bypass chained with a root command injection, with watchTowr's detection tool public since 2026-11-03 and its full chain since 2026-11-05; patches are out, Barracuda reports exploitation against a small number of organizations and CISA lists both flaws as exploited (CVSS 9.3 and 8.6)

Update11 Nov 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-11-11T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

CISA added both Barracuda flaws, CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-10, so the exploitation Barracuda reported without naming a flaw is now tied to both and CVE-2026-111560 moves to exploited; CISA marks both for forensic triage.

CISA added both CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-10 "based on evidence of active exploitation" (CISA, 2026-11-10). The catalog describes the two as chainable, the first letting an unauthenticated remote attacker restore a crafted backup archive and the second letting an authenticated administrator run commands as root through a crafted timezone value, and marks both for forensic triage (CISA, 2026-11-10). The listing makes CVE-2026-111560 exploited as well; Barracuda's own statement of 2026-11-09 still names no flaw, and no source says how many organizations were hit or what the attacker did afterwards.

    FindingCVE-2026-91403 +3→
Verification & coverage notes1 run

2026-11-11T0256Z-intel · Sonnet 5.5 · window 26 h · 12 entries published

Verification & coverage notes

Coverage window: standard, 26 h (gap 24.0 h to 2026-11-10T0255Z-intel). Twelve new entries and eight changelog records; no deep dive, no critical. A heavy Patch Tuesday day (Microsoft, SAP, Adobe, Fortinet, Ivanti, Synology) plus six KEV additions drove most of it.

  • KEV sweep (kev-window.txt): CVE-2026-125350 (Chromium) and CVE-2026-124194 (Outlook) became new entries; CVE-2026-111560 (Barracuda, COVERED-STALE) moved to exploited through an update record on the existing entry; CVE-2026-116606 already covered. borderline-drop: CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks XXE; carrier and UC-supplier product with no stated constituency footprint, fix since 2026-08-19. borderline-drop: CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Webtop Media Transcoder; niche authenticated telecom webmail component, vendor CVSS 4.3, no European public-sector footprint. No RANSOMWARE rows.
  • Microsoft November Patch Tuesday: one entry for seven unauthenticated CVSS 9.8 rows in domain infrastructure and server roles (Kerberos relay to a DC and zero-click Exchange attachment indexing are the two whose mechanics force the timeline). borderline-drop: SharePoint CVE-2026-120002 (9.9, authenticated), Azure DevOps Server, VS Code, ASP.NET Core and the Edge Chromium rows (authenticated or user-driven), and further unauthenticated 9.8 rows in client-side or non-server components (DirectMusic, Media Foundation, Color Management, Xbox Live Networking Service) and cloud services (Entra Device Registration, Azure OpenAI, Azure Managed Grafana), which carry no mechanism beyond an in-network or crafted-packet prerequisite and are not server roles an on-premises estate patches; the entry says they exist.
  • borderline-drop: Roundcube 1.6.21 and 1.7.6 (17 fixes, no CVE ids, scores or exploitation); AXIS Camera Station CVE-2026-13312 (low-privilege prerequisite, no detail); Adobe Experience Manager APSB26-189 (authenticated 9.9); Red Hat Ruby errata and the Metasploit module for GitLab CVE-2026-97229 (no delta on a complete KEV-listed entry); Apple, Siemens WinCC and Cisco 1.11 inventory additions to the Brotli flaw (no exploitation against those products); React Server Components CVE-2026-126187, Rails Active Storage CVE-2026-126082, MongoDB, Arista EOS, rConfig, mailcow, GPUStack, the Polish CMS flaws, OpenSSL (all Low), Apache httpd 2.4.70, Firefox 160, Cisco ISE CVSS 4.3 and Exchange authenticated rows.
  • borderline-drop (S2, S3, S4): Vaud Grand Council interpellation 26_INT_155 (questions only; revisit after the Conseil d'Etat answers); CNIL ten sanctions on local authorities (French enforcement, generic control list); ENISA State of Cybersecurity in the Union 2026 (policy index, Switzerland not covered); Chur medical centre Gleis D and Medi Porta with Cloak's 87 GB claim (private provider, no vector, below the incident floor); Erowa (Büron LU) with Akira's claim (private manufacturer, no vector); UZ Brussel shared patient-record outage (hospital reports no indication of a cyberattack); five Japanese bulk-email SaaS breaches (no Swiss nexus, one secondary compile); Push Security AI-event lures with Kali365 and VoidProxy (delta on covered device-code themes, vendor pitch); iVerify Advanced Mobile Threat Report 2026 and Kaspersky Q3 statistics (vendor population statistics, no new technique); NoName057(16) doxing bounty portal (no Swiss nexus); iOS worse_query sandbox escape (no CVE, sideload precondition, no exploitation).
  • Backlog state/coverage_backlog.md: the single open row (ChimeraZ claim against the Belgian rescue zone Hainaut-Est) stays held, unchanged: S2 searched in French and English again and found no zone statement, Belgian press report or CCB notice; expiry 2026-11-17 stands.
  • Single-source items: Xen Orchestra VSA-2026-062 (Vates, first-hand for its own product; BleepingComputer is a restatement), Adobe Connect APSB26-191 (vendor bulletin), Ivanti EPM and Cloud Services Application (CNA records only, confidence medium), Turla Cereal (ESET) and GhostFrame (Insikt Group) as telemetry holders. Included with reduced confidence: Ivanti, because Ivanti's advisory pages are a script-built application that no transport read and the jina pool is empty; the entry says so.
  • Contradiction: BleepingComputer names Xen Orchestra releases 6.9.1 and 6.10.0 where Vates names 6.9.2 and 6.10.1; the entry uses Vates' numbers and the xo-server package numbers, which agree.
  • Registry: Check Point lists UAT-9244 as an actor separate from FamousSparrow while the registry carries it as an alias of actor:famoussparrow, and ESET's SparroWocky is Check Point's CopperDoor; no alias was merged or added, left for the audit. CopperDragon, SquadC and SilentDelivery are registered, SparrowDoor, SparrowShell and Melofee are not.
  • Candidate sources added: vates-security-advisories, vrt-nws, watson-ch-digital (each with its reason in sources_changed); S3's Cofense and Positive Technologies leads are not added (Positive Technologies publishes on Medium, vendor-site home to be found), and S1's Onapsis lead already exists as onapsis. Promoted to active: censys-advisories, cert-fr-cti (three contributing runs each).
  • Audit lead (S2): the ENISA Threat Landscape 2026 of 2026-09-22 has no matching entry in the store.
  • Essential-coverage: all 21 essential records were attempted. Coverage gaps: connectwise-trust-center (403 on every transport), sygnia (403), ico-uk (403, ninth fire in a row), Ivanti and N-able advisory pages (script-built, read through ENISA EUVD and N-able's status release notes), Fortinet's RSS is capped at 50 items so more 2026-11-10 advisories may exist.
  • Mid-run stop-hook nudges to commit were acknowledged and ignored per the prompt: nothing was committed before Phase 6.
  • Verification loop: six independent cold passes (iteration 1 full ledger, 2 to 6 post-fix passes), findings falling from 32 (16 truth, 13 editorial) to 4 (0 truth, 1 editorial, 3 advisory); the loop ended on rule 5 (final truth + editorial ≤ 2 without F1 or F4), so the final NEEDS_FIXES verdict is an early exit, not a confirmed CLEAN, and its one editorial finding (an uncited console clause on the Adobe Connect entry) was fixed after the pass. Every finding and its remediation is in verification.iterations[]; per-iteration deltas are in work/<run-id>/deltas.iter*.md.
  • Follow-up research (iteration 1, F10): a scoped cti-research sub-agent (F10, 325 s) resolved the Cisco lead: the SD-WAN Controller and Secure Email Gateway advisories are revisions of advisories existing entries cover, and the Meraki advisory (first published 2026-10-07, revised 2026-11-09) is below the bar; no entry, findings in work/<run-id>/findings.F10.yaml. Recipe note for the audit: Cisco PSIRT's feed date is the last-updated date, so revisions of old advisories surface as new rows; read "First Published" on the advisory page.
  • Declined verifier suggestions, each with its reason in the iteration findings: priority high for the Vates and SAP entries (no CVE record and unconfirmed constituency exposure; unexploited), dropping the Confluence, Adobe Connect and Patch Tuesday entries, product keys on the Vates and Chrome entries (they would overlap other entries and raise the dedup warning), and removal of vendor-published implant, registry and file names from mechanism prose (Detection lines and actions describe behaviour).
  • Corrections made through verification: the Outlook entry now states the NTLMv2 hash disclosure; the Patch Tuesday entry scopes its seven rows to domain infrastructure and server roles and names the further 9.8 rows; eight updated entries were corrected in place with their records re-declared, among them eMudhra (Apple macOS 27.2.1 / 26.7.3 / 15.8.3, Microsoft's 2026-11-16 root removal, Cisco 1.9), the Linux kernel entry (Ubuntu fixed builds, scoped to the generic kernels) and Fortinet (FG-IR-26-265, CVE-2026-126251, added).

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-11-10
item.description:
• N-central: 4EverAble2Shell exploited on 21+ servers, Agent2Shell adds SYSTEM on agents; disable Legacy API. An independent researcher published proof-of-concept code on 2026-11-08 and 2026-11-09 for what Huntress counts as 33 critical flaws in N-able's N-central remote monitoring and management appliance, and N-able released 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on 2026-11-10 with seven CVE ids; on-premises customers must upgrade their servers, then Agents and Probes. On 2026-11-12 the researcher published a second chain, 4EverAble2Shell, that pairs an Apache Axis 1.x flaw (CVE-2026-90436) with a separate root escalation and works against Hotfix 2 when the Legacy API is turned on and reachable: Huntback reports at least 21 production servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2, running a cryptominer, Previdian's honeypot recorded attempts at the chain, and Huntress's latest guidance is that a Hotfix 2 server with the Legacy API disabled is not exposed to it. The same disclosure includes Agent2Shell, whose chains give an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the server SYSTEM commands on managed Windows endpoints and which N-able confirms also needs the Legacy API; N-able has published indicators of compromise for customers that have not disabled it, has no fix for the new claims and plans a follow-up hotfix; the Legacy API is off by default and keeping it disabled is the stated protection. →
  • BluePhishing: consent to a rogue Entra agent blueprint gives tenant access, and default users can soon create blueprints. Proofpoint describes BluePhishing, a research proof of concept that extends OAuth consent phishing to Microsoft Entra Agent ID: a victim who consents to an attacker's multi-tenant agent blueprint gets a blueprint principal with an agent-creation permission that Proofpoint says cannot be revoked, and the attacker then creates agent identities, up to 250 per blueprint, that inherit the consented permissions, which Microsoft's documentation says neither the Entra portal nor Microsoft Graph shows. Proofpoint has identified no in-the-wild activity, and Microsoft 365 message MC1506733 says default Entra users will be able to create agent blueprints from November 2026. →
  • CISA lists IBM Aspera Faspex 5 admin takeover as exploited; patch to 5.0.19 PL1, IBM names no workaround. IBM's bulletin of 2026-11-07 fixes CVE-2026-123218 in Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 through 5.0.19, an incorrect-authorization flaw that lets a user craft a specific message to bypass authorization and gain full administrative privileges (CVSS 3.1 9.8); the fix is 5.0.19 PL1 on Linux, applied by patching the container images, and IBM lists no workaround. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09 on evidence of active exploitation that it does not describe; IBM's bulletin does not mention exploitation. →

Proofpoint describes BluePhishing, a research proof of concept that extends OAuth consent phishing to Microsoft Entra Agent ID: a victim who consents to an attacker's multi-tenant agent blueprint gets a blueprint principal with an agent-creation permission that Proofpoint says cannot be revoked, and the attacker then creates agent identities, up to 250 per blueprint, that inherit the consented permissions, which Microsoft's documentation says neither the Entra portal nor Microsoft Graph shows. N-able N-central: a researcher published exploits for 33 alleged flaws and N-able shipped 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) with seven CVE ids, but a second disclosure adds 4EverAble2Shell, a chain through Apache Axis (CVE-2026-90436) and a root escalation that works against Hotfix 2 when the Legacy API is on and is exploited on at least 21 production servers, and Agent2Shell, SYSTEM commands on managed Windows agents, with no fix yet for either

An independent researcher published what Huntress counts as 33 critical flaws in the N-central appliance, chaining into four exploits, and N-able took its hosted environments offline on 2026-11-09 (Huntress, 2026-11-09); the chain BleepingComputer calls most critical abuses an unauthenticated XML external entity flaw to steal a trusted local session and run commands as the service user (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-09).

On 2026-11-10 N-able released N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2, build 2026.4.1.26, "a critical security update", for which Huntress lists seven CVE ids (N-able, 2026-11-10; Huntress, 2026-11-10; N-able CNA record, 2026-11-10; N-able CNA record, 2026-11-10). N-able reported scanning for that set but no successful exploitation (Huntress, 2026-11-10), and none of the seven is in CISA's catalog (Tenable, 2026-11-12).

On 2026-11-12 the researcher published a second set. 4EverAble2Shell is unauthenticated command execution as root that requires the Legacy API to be enabled, per BleepingComputer; it chains CVE-2026-90436, an Apache Axis 1.x deserialization flaw for which Apache does not expect a fix, with a root escalation in N-central's maintenance helper (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-12; Apache Axis project, 2026-11-06; Huntback, 2026-11-12). Huntback counts at least 21 servers, 19 of them on Hotfix 2, in North America, South Africa and Europe but not Switzerland, and Previdian's honeypot recorded attempts at the chain (Huntback, 2026-11-12; Previdian, 2026-11-12). Agent2Shell is a set of more than ten issues in how the server talks to Windows Agents and Probes, two chains of which let an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the server run commands as SYSTEM on managed endpoints; N-able confirmed it also requires the non-default Legacy API (The Hacker News, 2026-11-12; Huntress, 2026-11-13). N-able has published indicators of compromise for customers that have not disabled the Legacy API, has no fix for the new claims and plans a follow-up hotfix (Huntress, 2026-11-13; Tenable, 2026-11-12).

Exposure
An on-premises N-central server, yours or an IT provider's: below build 2026.4.1.26 for the first set, and any build up to Hotfix 2 for the second when the Legacy API, off by default, is on and reachable (Huntress, 2026-11-13). A compromised server reaches the systems N-central manages (Field Effect, 2026-11-09).
Detection
In N-central's authentication and audit logs from 2026-11-08 onward, unexpected logins, new administrator accounts and changes to stored credentials or API integrations; on managed endpoints, unscheduled software deployments, scripts and remote-control sessions (Huntress, 2026-11-09; Field Effect, 2026-11-09). For 4EverAble2Shell, Huntback names POST requests to the Axis endpoint /dms/services/ServerUI, a symlink at the N-central flag file path, a systemd unit or cron entry relaunching a miner and a hidden miner directory under /tmp or /var/tmp (Huntback, 2026-11-12). Huntress's Agent2Shell indicators come from static analysis of the proof of concept, not attacks seen: SYSTEM PowerShell with an encoded command spawned by the Agent, where PowerShell as an Agent child is common and the command is what matters (Huntress, 2026-11-13).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade on-premises servers to Hotfix 2, then Agents and Probes, and confirm the Legacy API is disabled and not internet-reachable, because Hotfix 2 does not fix 4EverAble2Shell and 19 of the 21 compromised servers already ran it (Huntback, 2026-11-12); treat a hit as a full compromise, ask each IT provider managing your endpoints through N-central whether it runs a server on premises and has upgraded it, and rotate the administrator, service and integration credentials the platform holds where activity looks unauthorised (Field Effect, 2026-11-09).

CVE-2026-123218, IBM Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 to 5.0.19: a crafted message bypasses authorization and gives full administrative rights, fixed in 5.0.19 PL1 with no workaround; CISA lists it as exploited two days after IBM's bulletin (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

IBM's bulletin of 2026-11-07 says Aspera Faspex 5.0.0 through 5.0.19 contains CVE-2026-123218, an incorrect-authorization flaw (CWE-863) in which an authorized user can craft a specific message to bypass user authorization and gain full administrative privileges; IBM scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8 with a vector that needs no privileges and no user interaction (IBM, 2026-11-07). The description speaks of an authorized user while the vector requires no privileges, and the bulletin does not resolve the difference. The fix is Faspex 5.0.19 PL1 on Linux, applied by patching the container images and checking that the faspex-core container image is 5.0.19 (1ce4b13, Fix Pack 1); IBM lists no workaround or mitigation (IBM, 2026-11-07). CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09, two days after IBM's bulletin, "based on evidence of active exploitation" that it does not describe (CISA, 2026-11-09). IBM's bulletin does not mention exploitation, and neither it nor CISA's listing gives an actor, a victim or the mechanism of the crafted message.

Exposure
An IBM Aspera Faspex 5 server at 5.0.19 or earlier (IBM lists the fix for Linux), above all one whose portal is reachable from the internet; the tag of the faspex-core container image shows the build (IBM, 2026-11-07).
Detection
Neither source names an indicator or describes the message, so the signal is the outcome: a non-administrator account that acquires administrator rights, new administrator accounts and API keys, and shares or packages created by accounts that did not previously have that access, in Faspex application and web logs. The fix does not undo a takeover that already happened, so the same review applies after patching.
Defender takeaway
Patch Faspex 5 on Linux to 5.0.19 PL1 by patching the container images now, because CISA lists the flaw as exploited and IBM offers no workaround (IBM, 2026-11-07; CISA, 2026-11-09); then review administrator accounts, API keys and shares created since the server was reachable.

CVE-2026-120017, CVE-2026-89126, CVE-2026-76964 and CVE-2026-89103, SAP NetWeaver AS ABAP, Web Dispatcher and Gateway: four unauthenticated network flaws rated CVSS 10.0 and fixed on SAP's November 2026 Patch Day; Onapsis, which found three of them, says a working exploit exists and has seen no attacks

SAP's November Patch Day of 2026-11-10 fixes four flaws that SAP scores CVSS 3.1 10.0, each reachable over the network without privileges or user interaction and with changed scope. In the SAML2 service provider of NetWeaver AS ABAP and the ABAP Platform, an unauthenticated attacker could submit crafted data, under certain configurations, to bypass authentication and impersonate arbitrary users, privileged accounts included (CVE-2026-120017, note 3849308) (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-10). SAP Web Dispatcher and the Internet Communication Manager of NetWeaver AS ABAP share a memory corruption that could allow arbitrary code execution (CVE-2026-89126, note 3778556; CVE-2026-76964, note 3778530) (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-10; ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-10), and SAP Gateway activates its default access control list with high privileges, so an external attacker is treated as an internal application server (CVE-2026-89103, note 3798345) (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-10).

Onapsis, which found and reported the Web Dispatcher, ICM and Gateway flaws, names the first pair ICM2SHELL: a memory corruption in the shared kernel code that reassembles fragmented WebSocket messages, reachable on the HTTP or HTTPS port with no credentials, and "WebSocket support is enabled by default, whether or not it is used" (Onapsis, 2026-11-10). Onapsis provided SAP a working unauthenticated code-execution exploit that runs commands as the system's <sid>adm user, a single connection crashes the process on every kernel it tested, and it has not observed attacks; NCSC Switzerland lists the exploitation status as unknown (Onapsis, 2026-11-10; NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-10). It affects ABAP systems on kernel 7.40 or higher and every Web Dispatcher, the one in SAP HANA XS included; AS Java alone and kernel 7.22 are not affected, and kernels out of maintenance may get no fix. The fixed patch levels are 7.53 PL 1616 or 1617, 7.54 PL 710, 7.77 PL 914, 7.93 PL 401 or 420, 9.16 PL 111, 9.18 PL 37 and 9.20 PL 11 or 13 (Onapsis, 2026-11-10).

ProxyGate lets an unauthenticated attacker with network access run operating system commands as <sid>adm on the Gateway, and its exploitability depends on the proxy access list: a permissive prxyinfo file, or none with gw/acl_mode_proxy at its default of 0, leaves the system exposed, so "neither a version check nor patching alone tells you whether you are safe"; on most releases SAP's fix combines the kernel patch with gw/acl_mode_proxy = 1, and Onapsis lists the minimum patch level for each kernel release, for example 7.53 PL 1625 and 7.54 PL 718 (Onapsis, 2026-11-10).

Exposure
A system that runs one of the components and lets an untrusted network reach its Web Dispatcher, Internet Communication Manager, Gateway or SAML2 endpoint; the SAML2 flaw applies under certain configurations of the SAML 2.0 service provider (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-10).
Detection
Onapsis expects every exploitation attempt against ICM2SHELL to crash the ICM or Web Dispatcher at least once, so unexpected restarts of either process outside maintenance deserve investigation; requests with status 101 in the ICM or Web Dispatcher HTTP log show whether WebSocket is in use before anyone considers disabling it (Onapsis, 2026-11-10). The sources name no indicator for the SAML2 flaw or the Gateway.
Defender takeaway
Patch internet-facing Web Dispatchers and Internet Communication Managers first and every application server and Web Dispatcher after them, set gw/acl_mode_proxy to 1 on every Gateway, and apply note 3849308 where the SAML2 service provider runs; Onapsis calls the notes the only complete fix.

BluePhishing: Proofpoint's proof of concept turns a consent link for a third-party Entra agent blueprint into tenant initial access, with an agent-creation permission that Proofpoint says cannot be revoked

Proofpoint presents BluePhishing, a proof of concept that extends OAuth consent phishing to Microsoft Entra Agent ID. The attacker builds an agent blueprint, the agent analogue of an app registration, in their own tenant with a client secret and permissions set to be inherited, sets its sign-in audience to work across tenants (a setting the Entra portal does not expose, so it takes Microsoft Graph, PowerShell or a manifest edit), and sends the victim a one-time consent link (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09). When a victim consents, a blueprint principal appears in the victim tenant with the AgentIdentity.CreateAsManager permission, which Proofpoint says cannot be revoked from the principal; the attacker then obtains an app-only Graph token for the victim tenant and creates agent identities, up to 250 per blueprint, that inherit the consented permissions (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09). Creating one needs the victim's tenant ID and the object ID of a sponsor user, both obtainable through documented unauthenticated lookups, and Proofpoint's tests used the Graph permissions User.Read.All and Group.Read.All (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09). Proofpoint, citing Microsoft's documentation, says inherited permissions are not visible in the Entra portal or in Microsoft Graph, which limits auditing what an agent identity can do; in its tests silent inheritance appeared only for delegated permissions, those granted through user consent (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09).

Proofpoint has identified no in-the-wild activity and says agent consent controls are less mature and less widely deployed than app consent controls; it adds that Microsoft 365 Message Center item MC1506733 says default Entra users will be able to create agent blueprints from November 2026 (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09).

Exposure
A Microsoft Entra tenant whose users or administrators can be led to approve a consent link; Proofpoint says the user consent settings that limit third-party app consent also extend to agent blueprints and their agent identities (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09).
Detection
Proofpoint says agent and blueprint events surface in the Entra audit log as app consent operations do, the creation of an agent identity blueprint as "Add application" and the creation of an agent identity as "Add service principal", and that the blueprint ID is the same in every tenant that consents to it, so a known malicious blueprint can be searched for across tenants (Proofpoint, 2026-11-09).
Defender takeaway
Review the tenant's user consent settings and permission classifications before the November 2026 default lets default Entra users create agent blueprints, and look in the audit log for blueprint and agent-identity creations that nobody in IT made; no attacks have been reported, so this is a hardening decision, not an incident response.

First published 2026-10-10 · open finding →

Update10 Nov 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-inteltechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Huntress's follow-up on servers exploited between 8 and 11 October, before the hotfixes, describes five webshell families, a second miner and a host-bound Python implant, plus Veeam credential theft on a neighbouring server; it advises a full re-image from a trusted backup and rotation of the credentials the server held or could reach.

Huntress's follow-up covers an organisation whose AhsayCBS servers were exploited between 8 and 11 October 2026, before Ahsay's hotfixes; Huntress verified that 10.3.4.45 blocks the entry point it saw and ties the intrusion to the first campaign by webshell location, an exploit source address and matching files (Huntress, 2026-11-09). The operator planted five JSP webshell families under the console's web application directories (Huntress, 2026-11-09); Huntress reads the Linux-style copies, in directories such as /opt, /usr/local and /home, as showing that the exploit simply tried every likely location (Huntress, 2026-11-09). One family hides an AES-encrypted Java class in the least-significant bits of an uploaded PNG's pixels and runs it in memory, so no command parameter appears in access logs; another is a signed-API shell with command execution and chunked upload and download of up to 4 GB per file, a ready exfiltration channel on a backup host; a third can delete itself and any path it is given, so a missing file does not prove it was never there (Huntress, 2026-11-09).

Huntress also found a second XMRig miner kept alive by a SYSTEM scheduled task with a backdated start time that runs every minute, an embedded Python distribution under the SYSTEM profile started from a Run key whose wrapper only runs if a marker file named for the SHA-256 of the host's MachineGuid exists and which then loads a DLL whose strings are consistent with DNS-over-HTTPS lookups, the tunnelling tools gost and chisel, the remote access tools AnyDesk, Atera and Splashtop, a rogue local account, a Mimikatz package and Microsoft Defender exclusions that include the AhsayCBS service process (Huntress, 2026-11-09). On a Veeam server in the same environment it saw a command consistent with NetExec's Veeam credential-theft module, a PowerShell script launched through WMI that queried the VeeamBackup database for stored credentials and decrypted them; it cannot say how many credentials were retrieved, has not identified the implant family and cannot say what, if anything, was taken through the webshell's download action (Huntress, 2026-11-09). For any server exposed before the hotfix, Huntress recommends a full re-image from a trusted backup and rotating the credentials stored on or reachable from the server, including those saved in AhsayCBS and in any backup software on the same network (Huntress, 2026-11-09).

Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controllers compromised in France, six more European countries and Switzerland, with France blaming the IRGC unit Shahid Kaveh for the October campaign; Midnight Blue reports six unpatched pre-authentication flaws in AK-SM 800A firmware up to 5.3.2

Update10 Nov 2026 03:42 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagsentitiestechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

France's foreign ministry and the C4 crisis cell attributed the 11 to 12 October refrigeration-controller campaign to Iran on 2026-11-09, naming the Revolutionary Guard unit Shahid Kaveh, and the Paris prosecutor requested arrest warrants against its leader and two deputies; the French documents cover that campaign only, and the later waves and the Swiss cases are not attributed in them.

France's foreign ministry said on 2026-11-09 that, following the investigation, France is able to attribute the destructive actions of the night of 11 to 12 October to Iran, carried out by the cyber-offensive unit Shahid Kaveh, affiliated with the electronic and cyber centre of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and calls it the first cyber-offensive campaign run purely for sabotage on French soil (translated from French) (French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs, 2026-11-09). The report of the C4 crisis cell, which CERT-FR published, words the case as a bundle of indicators that names the Revolutionary Guard as sponsor and Shahid Kaveh as executing unit (translated from French) (CERT-FR, 2026-11-09). The indicators it lists are attack infrastructure also used in the same period to reconnoitre Schneider Electric equipment, use of the FOFA scan tool, which it says the unit habitually uses, relay of the attack on the unit's CyberbanNews outlet from 13 October, and traces of Farsi in the attack infrastructure (CERT-FR, 2026-11-09).

The same report says the unit is known mainly through hacktivist personas, CyberAveng3rs among them, and the CyberbanNews outlet, and that it has held scripts since at least June 2024 to scan, access and control Schneider Electric, Siemens and Rockwell industrial equipment; in April 2026 it was seen using Modbus on TCP port 502 for mass reconnaissance of Schneider Electric systems, including in France (CERT-FR, 2026-11-09). The C4 links to the same attack the concurrent targeting of Schneider Electric equipment at small hydroelectric installations in France, with moderate effects on the targeted equipment (CERT-FR, 2026-11-09). Industrial controllers of that class, reachable on Modbus, belong in the same internet-exposure check as the refrigeration controllers.

The attribution covers the French campaign of 11 to 12 October. Sekoia's honeypots recorded unauthenticated requests to the controllers' xml.cgi endpoint from 26 addresses, password spraying of the Supervisor and admin accounts and, on 2026-11-01, an attempt to use a non-public flaw that renames an account by its numerical identifier; Sekoia says the evidence shows similarities between the October and November waves that suggest they may share an actor, and that it assesses the NoName057(16) and Z-Pentest Alliance claim with doubts (Sekoia, 2026-11-10). Reuters reports that the Paris prosecutor's office said it had requested international arrest warrants against the leader of Shahid Kaveh and his two deputies, and that it could not establish exactly how the French made their determination (Reuters via NBC News, 2026-11-09). NCSC Switzerland's advisory still says the public information does not establish a common attack method across the incidents (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13).

Sources: CERT-FR (alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012) · AFP (via Khaleej Times) · BFMTV · Infosecurity Magazine · BleepingComputer · CERT-FR (alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012, revised version) · NCSC Switzerland (Security Hub advisory 13054) · Cooling Post · Blick · Censys · CERT-FR (alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012, third version) · Dixell France (Copeland) · Le Monde · SecurityWeek · Cybersecurity Dive · Public Sénat · Le Monde Informatique · Forescout Research (Vedere Labs) · Reuters (republished by Internazionale) · Nextgov · The Guardian · Euronews · Tagesschau (ARD) · CyberInsider · 20 Minuten · heise online · WDR · SentinelLABS · Le Canard enchaîné · Établissement français du sang (press release, in French) · Coolworld International (statement) · ENISA (joint statement) · BleepingComputer (blood-storage refrigeration) · heise online (blood-bank cooling) · SRF · franceinfo · CSIRT Italia (bulletin BL02/261104/CSIRT-ITA) · CSIRT Italia (bulletin BL01/261013/CSIRT-ITA, version of 2026-11-04) · Keystone-SDA via swissinfo.ch (Köniz butcher) · Keystone-SDA via swissinfo.ch (BACS statement) · CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA and DOT (joint fact sheet) · Ransom-ISAC · Unit 42 (Palo Alto Networks) · French Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs (attribution statement) · CERT-FR (CERTFR-2026-CTI-009, report of the C4 crisis cell) · Sekoia · Reuters (via NBC News) · BACS / NCSC.ch (public warning on cold-chain controllers) · Midnight Blue · BSI (IT-Sicherheitshinweis BITS-H 2026-306525-10e2) · CCB (Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium) · heise · Danfoss (security advisories page, as read) · Danfoss (AK-SM 800A software readme, as read)

CVE-2026-19868, SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN: valid credentials for an alternate authentication method bypass SAML and the MFA it enforces; SonicWall investigated a report of exploitation and CISA lists it as exploited (CVSS 3.1 7.1)

First published 2026-11-07 · open finding →

Update10 Nov 2026 03:39 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-intelsummarycvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

SonicWall revised advisory SNWLID-2026-0014 on 2026-11-09 to add an interim workaround for SAML deployments that cannot upgrade: disable or delete every active LDAP, RADIUS and TACACS+ authentication server. The upgrade stays the primary action.

SonicWall revised advisory SNWLID-2026-0014 on 2026-11-09 and added a workaround for CVE-2026-19868: if SAML authentication is in use and upgrading the firmware is not possible, disable or delete any active LDAP, RADIUS and TACACS+ authentication server configured on the firewall, through Device, Users, Settings, Authentication and the Configure page of each of the three methods (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-09). The advisory's first version named no workaround (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-06). It still urges upgrading; the workaround removes the alternate authentication methods through which the bypass works, which means any administrator or VPN login that relies on those servers stops working until SAML is the only method (an inference from the mechanism, not a SonicWall statement).

Sources: SonicWall PSIRT (SNWLID-2026-0014) · CISA · BleepingComputer · SonicWall PSIRT (SNWLID-2026-0014, revision of 2026-11-09)

CVE-2026-123158, OpenSSH Portable before 10.6p2 (*sshole): on Linux with musl libc and no PAM, a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes logs in to accounts whose password field is *; NCSC Switzerland issued an advisory (CVSS 3.1 8.1)

First published 2026-11-06 · open finding →

Update10 Nov 2026 03:36 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-intelheadlinesummarytagstechniquescvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

CISA added CVE-2026-123158 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09, and GreyNoise records hands-on logins on its gridpoints from 2026-11-07, including key planting and a dropped Python agent; BleepingComputer relays watchTowr's observation of botnet and cryptomining use. Still no source reports a compromised production host.

CISA added CVE-2026-123158 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09 on evidence of active exploitation, without describing a victim or the behavior (CISA, 2026-11-09); the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security repeats the listing (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-11-09). NCSC Switzerland's advisory, last edited on 2026-11-06, still rates the exploitation status unknown (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05). GreyNoise, which holds the telemetry, says its first successful exploitation came on 2026-11-07 at 00:46 UTC against one of its vulnerable gridpoints, and the sessions it records there show reconnaissance, attempts to read root's SSH keys and /etc/shadow through doas, a new key written into authorized_keys, and in some sessions a Python runtime installed with apk and an init-script service for a Python agent that polls an HTTPS server every 150 seconds; on the host it describes, the agent never enrolled and never received a task (GreyNoise, 2026-11-10). GreyNoise's confirmed successes are on its own gridpoints, and no source reports a compromised production host.

Sources: NCSC Switzerland (Security Hub advisory 13155) · OpenSSH project (Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes) · OX Security · heise online · Previdian · The Hacker News · Alpine Linux · SANS Internet Storm Center · GreyNoise (SSHole event tracker) · CISA · Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (AV26-1130, Update 1) · BleepingComputer

Update10 Nov 2026 03:35 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Barracuda's advisory now says it has identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations without naming the flaw, and the Canadian Cyber Centre says open-source reporting indicates CVE-2026-116606 is exploited in the wild, so the earlier statement that no source reports attacks no longer holds.

Barracuda added on 2026-11-09 to its advisory that it has identified exploitation activity affecting a small number of organizations; the advisory does not say which flaw, how many organizations, since when or what the attacker did afterwards (Barracuda, 2026-11-09). The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security's update of the same day says open-source reporting indicates that CVE-2026-116606 is exploited in the wild, without naming the reporting (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-11-09). Barracuda's lever is unchanged: organizations whose administrative interfaces are not publicly accessible from the internet are less exposed to this attack path (Barracuda, 2026-11-09), so an appliance whose interface was reachable before patching should also be checked for a restore nobody made and a timezone value that is not a timezone name.
