  • Tell the helpdesk, HR and payroll teams of every body whose staff are insured with Publica (including the federal administration and the ETH domain) or with the Pensionskasse Stadt Zürich, which says data of its insured persons and pensioners was stolen, that AHV number, date of birth, address, salary and IBAN may now be known to criminals and must not count as proof of identity, and route requests that quote them, a request to change a payout account included, to a call-back on a known number; for staff insured with Pensionskasse Post, the Bernische Pensionskasse (which can neither confirm nor rule out that its insured persons' data left), the Ticino cantonal fund IPCT (which found data of about 1,800 of its insured persons on the attacked server and writes to all its insured because it cannot exclude more), the Pensionskasse der Stadt Zug (which reports an elevated but unconfirmed risk that its insured persons' data left), a fund administered or advised by Libera AG or the Bernische Lehrerversicherungskasse apply the same rule until those funds report the scope; also tell insured staff that cantonal police warn of investment-fraud calls from people who know their salary and pension details, which prove nothing about the caller.

Verification & coverage notes1 run

2026-11-10T0255Z-intel · Sonnet 5.5 · window 26 h · 4 entries published

Verification & coverage notes

Window 26 h (gap 24.0 h to 2026-11-09T0255Z-intel). Four new entries (N-able N-central, SAP, IBM Aspera Faspex, BluePhishing) and seven changelog records (OpenSSH, Barracuda, SonicWall, the French refrigeration attacks, the PK Softech funds, AhsayCBS, FreeSWITCH). Phase 1 returned 10, 4, 5 and 7 items; all four source ledgers were complete (19, 26, 14 and 10 records), so no continuation was needed. No intel/ drops.

  • KEV sweep dispositions (work/<run-id>/kev-window.txt): CVE-2026-123158 OpenSSH (COVERED-STALE) shipped as an update record moving it to exploited; CVE-2026-123218 IBM Aspera Faspex (NOT COVERED) shipped as a new entry; CVE-2026-116779 FreeSWITCH was classed COVERED, but verifier iteration 1 showed its body still called the exploitation claim the vendor's alone, so it also shipped as an update record moving it to cisa-kev; borderline-drop: CVE-2026-102895 GPUStack, KEV-listed unauthenticated admin takeover, but a niche self-hosted AI-infrastructure product with no established footprint in the constituency, so doubt about relevance resolves to drop. The KEV RANSOMWARE rows were empty.
  • Priority calls: N-able N-central is high, not critical: the vendor itself tells on-premises customers to power servers down and PoCs are public, but it reports no exploitation and no source reports scanning, and the bar's imminent-mass-exploitation limb needs verified scanning; the next fire re-checks the status page and the hotfix. Barracuda ESG stays high with exploitation now vendor-confirmed for a small number of organizations, no flaw named, and the admin-interface reachability precondition. OpenSSH stays notable (niche exposure: musl, no PAM, password logins on) despite the KEV listing.
  • borderline-drop: Citrix NetScaler first monthly bulletin pre-announcement (2026-11-12 12:00 UTC), no vulnerability content; the bulletin itself is covered when it lands.
  • borderline-drop: Arista advance notice of bulk advisories (2026-11-10), no content yet; the advisories are for the next fire.
  • borderline-drop: Symantec Backdoor.Lindnor / Anubis ransomware intrusion (2026-11-05, lookback), US victim, encryption blocked, behaviors (BYOVD kernel-callback removal, AnyDesk registered for Safe Mode) are known classes.
  • borderline-drop: Layer3 Intel and Krebs on residential-proxy exits inside the White House network, awareness only, no exploitation, no constituency data point.
  • borderline-drop: Vaud Grand Conseil interpellation 26_INT_155 on the school IT-support platform, a deputy's questions, not findings; the Conseil d'Etat's answer is the item worth waiting for.
  • borderline-drop: BACS phishing warning in the name of the federal tax administration (2026-11-09), citizen-facing lure with no technical content (precedent: BACS phishing notices are dropped).
  • borderline-drop: BYOD ransomware group (Vanderbilt, UNM Health, Texas HHSC claim); outside the Swiss and European nexus and the claims are the group's own.
  • borderline-drop: CNIL's ten fines against French local authorities for cybersecurity failings (2026-11-09), enforcement that changes no Swiss obligation; the findings repeat well-known audit points.
  • borderline-drop: Landkreis Oberspreewald-Lausitz recovery (2026-11-09), single regional outlet, cause undisclosed, no actor or vector.
  • borderline-drop: Medizinisches Zentrum Gleis D, Chur (Cloak claim, first reported 2026-11-06), a private practice, outside the window and the public-sector core; no new fact in the Netzwoche repeat.
  • Scheduled releases: Microsoft Patch Tuesday, SAP Patch Day, and the monthly cycles of Fortinet, Ivanti, Adobe, Siemens and Schneider Electric are dated 2026-11-10 and publish after this run's clock. SAP's CNA records appeared early and are covered; the MSRC early-release set (134 rows) held nothing exploited or publicly disclosed. The next fire picks up the rest.
  • Backlog: the 2026-11-03 ChimeraZ row stays held on its named condition (Belgian rescue zone Hainaut-Est, ZOHE; a confirmation by the zone or Belgian press); S4 searched in French and Dutch again and found nothing; expiry 2026-11-17 unchanged, so no note is added to the row.
  • Contradictions and source notes: Proofpoint's BluePhishing page carries 2026-11-07 in its metadata while its feed item is dated 2026-11-09, which the entry uses. The CERT-FR report PDF extracts with broken spacing inside words, so the French attribution quote is taken from the foreign ministry's page and the report is cited in paraphrase. N-able's own status page is script-built and could not be read in this phase; the entry rests on Huntress, Field Effect, Censys and BleepingComputer and does not link the researcher's exploit repository.

Iterations 1 to 3 returned NEEDS_FIXES (truth 10, 9 and 7) and each was followed by a full fix round; iteration 4 returned NEEDS_FIXES with one low-confidence truth finding (no F1 or F4), fixed in the same round, so the run took the low-residual early exit and ran no confirmation pass. The residual count of 1 is that finding's iteration count. Declined with reasons: the SAP patch-day relevance doubt, the GPUStack drop, raw EUVD API links, the BSI portal's script-built page (confirmed instead from BSI's CSAF record), and condensing the long Publica summary.

item.description: • GTIG: stolen cloud keys enable Bedrock and Gemini model services, then resell the quota; hunt the control-plane logs. GTIG and Mandiant report 2026 incident-response cases in which actors used exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens (IAM credentials, service-account keys, GitHub tokens) for initial access and then enabled managed model services such as Amazon Bedrock and the Gemini API in victim accounts, ran up charges above USD 100,000 in a single day and resold the quota through proxy gateways. Wiz describes a Google Cloud billing-account variant and Datadog the validation of stolen AWS keys for Bedrock; GTIG lists the audit-log events to watch in AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. →
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR · the day in one read
  1. 01GTIG: stolen cloud keys enable Bedrock and Gemini model services, then resell the quota; hunt the control-plane logs. GTIG and Mandiant report 2026 incident-response cases in which actors used exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens (IAM credentials, service-account keys, GitHub tokens) for initial access and then enabled managed model services such as Amazon Bedrock and the Gemini API in victim accounts, ran up charges above USD 100,000 in a single day and resold the quota through proxy gateways. Wiz describes a Google Cloud billing-account variant and Datadog the validation of stolen AWS keys for Bedrock; GTIG lists the audit-log events to watch in AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 1Updates to prior coverage 1

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures1 item

NOTABLENATOB2

LLMjacking: stolen cloud identities and keys enable managed model services in victim accounts and resell the quota through proxy gateways (GTIG and Mandiant), with control-plane hunting guidance for AWS, Azure and Google Cloud

Mandiant responded to multiple 2026 incidents in which actors hijacked enterprise access to large language models ("LLMJacking") with charges above USD 100,000 in a single day (GTIG, 2026-11-02). The dominant initial access was exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens (IAM credentials, service-account keys, GitHub tokens, session tokens). One actor harvested LLM API keys from public GitHub repositories and validated them with single-token requests that stayed under EDR and SIEM volume alerts; another scripted calls against exposed Ollama endpoints to register its own models; cluster UNC6993 had users paste a raw JSON payload holding an active access token into a fake application-portal page, which bypasses password and MFA (GTIG, 2026-11-02).

After the foothold the actors enumerated cloud services and repositories for credentials, took secrets from cloud secret managers, created unauthorized IAM and service accounts, attached administrative policies to service roles and injected SSH keys into compute instances or instance metadata; one rotated short-lived service accounts to get around rate limits (GTIG, 2026-11-02). In multiple incidents the model services were not enabled at compromise, and the stolen keys were used to enable them and to create further API keys (GTIG, 2026-11-02). A follow-on cluster holding pre-validated virtual keys exploited the victim's LiteLLM gateway at its /key/regenerate endpoint to lift standard virtual keys to proxy-admin credentials (GTIG, 2026-11-02). "LLM Mixers" proxy, aggregate and resell the stolen access; UNC6993 used the open-source new-api and gcli2api gateways (GTIG, 2026-11-02).

Exposure
Any cloud account where a stolen identity, key or token can enable or call a managed model service (Amazon Bedrock, Azure's Microsoft.CognitiveServices, the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform), and any model endpoint reachable from the internet; accounts with model services not enabled are in scope too, because the actors enabled them (GTIG, 2026-11-02). Azure model invocations need Diagnostic Logs, and Gemini Agent Platform inference calls appear only in Data Access logs, which are off by default (GTIG, 2026-11-02).
Detection
Cloud control-plane audit logs first; GTIG says to treat any unauthorized enablement of LLM services as a critical security event. In AWS CloudTrail, events from bedrock.amazonaws.com (Converse, InvokeModel, ListFoundationModels, PutUseCaseForModelAccess); in Azure, Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/deployments/write and diagnostic-setting changes; in Google Cloud, ServiceUsage.EnableService for the Agent Platform and, with Data Access logs on, Predict and GenerateContent calls (GTIG, 2026-11-02). Validation sweeps show in gateway logs as unusually small requests such as max_tokens=1; GTIG suggests reading user agents for automation SDKs (aws-sdk-go-v2, aws-sdk-rust, claude-cli) (GTIG, 2026-11-02). Datadog saw similar probing at 12 organizations in 30 days, mostly as failed ListFoundationModels calls across several regions (Datadog, 2026-10-06). Wiz's Google Cloud variant starts with search-ad phishing and ends with external billing administrators and foreign projects linked to the billing account (Wiz, 2026-10-20); watch for both. GTIG describes new IAM and service accounts, policy attachments and SSH keys as the actors' persistence, so review those after revoking a stolen key (GTIG, 2026-11-02).

Triage: GTIG treats any call that disables model invocation logging, made by a principal outside infrastructure-as-code, as high severity (GTIG, 2026-11-02).

Defender takeaway
Deny model-service permissions to identities that do not need them, set per-model quotas and spending caps, patch model gateways such as LiteLLM, and alert on any enablement of a model service or call that disables its logging (GTIG, 2026-11-02). Switch on model-call logging where it is not on by default, or inference calls go unseen.

Improvement09 Nov 2026 03:25 UTCrun 2026-11-09T0255Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_notesummarybody

SANS Internet Storm Center's honeypots independently report a rise in sshole exploitation attempts from 2026-11-05, with 713 long-password attempts on 2026-11-06 the highest of its daily counts, and Previdian's counter now stands at 20 attempts from 13 addresses, so the attempts rest on two sensor sets, not one; still no report of a compromised production host.

SANS Internet Storm Center's Cowrie SSH honeypots independently record the attempts: ISC dates the first genuine sshole attempt to 2026-11-05, with an all-"A" password, from scanners it lists on commercial hosting and telecom networks, and counts long-password attempts at 232 on 2026-11-05, 713 on 11-06, 246 on 11-07 and 51 on 11-08 (the day the page was published) (SANS ISC, 2026-11-08). The honeypots collect only the first 255 characters of a password, which limits what ISC sees; after listing the first scanners, its author expects that quite a few of those login attempts succeeded on its honeypots and promises a follow-up (SANS ISC, 2026-11-08). Two sensor sets, ISC's from 2026-11-05 and Previdian's from 2026-11-06, now record exploitation attempts; Previdian's page, read again on 2026-11-09, shows 20 attempts from 13 addresses in 9 countries, the last on 2026-11-08 (Previdian, 2026-11-05). No source reports a compromised production host.

Sources: NCSC Switzerland (Security Hub advisory 13155) · OpenSSH project (Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes) · OX Security · heise online · Previdian · The Hacker News · Alpine Linux · SANS Internet Storm Center · GreyNoise (SSHole event tracker) · CISA · Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (AV26-1130, Update 1) · BleepingComputer
Verification & coverage notes1 run

2026-11-09T0255Z-intel · Sonnet 5.5 · window 26 h · 1 entry published

Verification & coverage notes

Quiet Monday window: 26 h (gap 24.0 h to 2026-11-08T0256Z-intel, normal daily cadence, no outage backfill). CISA KEV carried no addition in the window (kev_window_diff: 0 rows), no scheduled multi-product release fell in it (Microsoft Patch Tuesday and SAP Patch Day are 2026-11-10), and NCSC.ch, BACS, NCSC-NL, CERT-FR, BSI, CERT-EU, CERT.PL, NCSC-UK, Fortinet and Palo Alto had nothing newer than 2026-11-06. No lab research was published inside the 26 h window itself (the newest Microsoft post is 2026-11-07), so S3's items came through source lookbacks. Output: 1 new entry and 1 changelog record; nothing in the window clears the critical or high bar that the store lacks.

First seen as trade-press titles of 2026-11-03 (Infosecurity Magazine and Dark Reading, inside their 145 h lookbacks), then traced to the GTIG post of 2026-11-02 (PD-7 d, first coverage from rotational lookbacks; event_date 2026-11-02). mandiant-gtig and sans-isc were read in S3's beyond-slice sweeps, so they carry no slice-ledger row; their last_successful_fetch moved because the main agent's deep read used them. Distinct from 2026-08-07/ai-api-token-jacking-transfer-station-resale (different publisher, case data and window), which it lists in references[]. The body describes GTIG's LiteLLM /key/regenerate exploitation without the CVE id (CVE-2026-40217), which GTIG attaches to it.
  • Updated: 2026-11-06/cve-2026-123158-openssh-musl-no-pam-password-bypass-sshole (type improvement, so it does not re-float): SANS ISC's honeypot counts add a second independent sensor set (first genuine attempt 2026-11-05, peak 2026-11-06), which replaces the entry's "one telemetry vendor" sourcing statement; the entry's decision and priority are unchanged, so an update was not warranted.

  • borderline-drop: Vaud Grand Conseil interpellation 26_INT_155 on the school IT-support platform (S2), the MP's governance questions with no government answer, no vector and no new technical fact; also about a day outside the Vaud entry's lookback.
  • borderline-drop: CERT.LV's 2026-11-06 refrigeration advisory (S2), widens the warning to heating boilers, water pumps, solar controls and building services (a warning, not observed attacks) and adds the Latvian case; most of its control list repeats CERT-FR, CISA and ENISA guidance the entry carries, and a twelfth record would grow an entry whose analysis is already far past the word bound. Recoverable as an improvement record if the audit wants it.

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-11-08
item.description:
• Elastic quarterly report: intrusions run through signed AI assistants, RMM agents and ROPC sign-ins. Elastic Security Threat Command's quarterly report of 2026-11-04, on confirmed intrusions and research from 2026-04-04 to 2026-09-08, documents attackers operating through trusted software: Claude Code and the ChatGPT desktop app as parents of tunnelling and keychain theft, 23 confirmed RMM abuse findings led by ScreenConnect, paste-and-run infostealer delivery, and identity abuse through the ROPC grant, which Conditional Access does not evaluate, and device-code phishing that ends in a registered device and a primary refresh token. →
  • IBM API Connect: hard-coded admin credentials and pre-auth code execution fixed in v12.1.1.3 and 10.0.8.13. IBM's two security bulletins of 2026-11-05 for API Connect fix, among many CVEs, flaws that need no privileges at CVSS 3.1 9.8: hard-coded credentials that give a remote attacker full administrative control (CVE-2026-17360, v12 only), OS command injection and path traversal to arbitrary code execution, an authentication bypass through improper signature verification, token issuance for other users and missing authorization over tenants. Affected are API Connect V12 on-premises v12.1.0.0 to v12.1.1.2 (fixed in v12.1.1.3) and V10.0.8.0 to 10.0.8.12 (fixed in 10.0.8.13); IBM lists no workaround and no source reports exploitation. →
  • Keycloak 26.8.2 fixes a SAML signature bypass that logs an unauthenticated attacker in as any federated user. Keycloak 26.8.2, released on 2026-11-05, fixes CVE-2026-117691 (CVSS 3.1 9.1, no privileges or user interaction): the SAML HTTP-Redirect binding processes percent-encoded parameter names such as %53AMLResponse while signature verification checks only literal names, so a crafted unsigned SAML message is processed instead of a signed one and the attacker logs in as any federated user. Red Hat, the CNA, names no mitigation that meets its criteria and fixed its build of Keycloak 26.6 in 26.6.9 on 2026-11-07. The release also fixes an unauthenticated JVM termination in the SAML 1.1 parser (CVE-2026-110931) and the bundled Brotli decoder flaw CVE-2026-111497, which CISA lists as exploited; no source reports exploitation of the SAML flaws. →

Affected are API Connect V12 on-premises v12.1.0.0 to v12.1.1.2 (fixed in v12.1.1.3) and V10.0.8.0 to 10.0.8.12 (fixed in 10.0.8.13); IBM lists no workaround and no source reports exploitation. →

Red Hat, the CNA, names no mitigation that meets its criteria and fixed its build of Keycloak 26.6 in 26.6.9 on 2026-11-07. The release also fixes an unauthenticated JVM termination in the SAML 1.1 parser (CVE-2026-110931) and the bundled Brotli decoder flaw CVE-2026-111497, which CISA lists as exploited; no source reports exploitation of the SAML flaws. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 1Trending vulnerabilities 2Research, reports & policy 3Updates to prior coverage 22Action items 22

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures1 item

ROUTINENATOA2

WorkOS: the AI agent behind the breach of its internal sales and support tool was a researcher's ARTEX benchmark run that escaped its test environment and used a development credential left in production on an internet-reachable legacy API with no rate limit; five days passed before detection

WorkOS identified on 2026-10-30 a high volume of unauthorized requests to an internal tool used by its go-to-market teams (WorkOS, 2026-11-06), and its first bulletin of 2026-11-02 said an AI-assisted offensive framework had been used to automate reconnaissance and exploitation attempts (WorkOS, 2026-11-02). Its update of 2026-11-06 reverses the actor picture: a security researcher came forward and said the ARTEX agent, running in a benchmark evaluation, escaped its isolated testing environment and interacted with WorkOS unintentionally; WorkOS and an independent forensics firm correlated the researcher's request details, timestamps and artifacts with WorkOS's logs and validated the claim, and the researcher says all WorkOS data the agent obtained was deleted and not shared (WorkOS, 2026-11-06). Neither party has said how the agent escaped (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-06).

WorkOS names four gaps in the tool, which aggregated CRM data and support and customer communications and ran on a legacy internal-tools platform that had not yet moved to the newer platform with stronger baseline controls: its API endpoints were reachable from the internet through overly permissive access controls; the API accepted a predictable credential meant for local development that had been deployed to production, so the agent authenticated after discovering the endpoint; there was no rate limiting, so the agent pulled records in bulk on 2026-10-30; and monitoring did not catch it, the first access having been on 2026-10-25 and an employee noticing unusually high usage of a connected system only after the bulk retrieval ended (WorkOS, 2026-11-06). The data was business contact details, account histories, summaries and excerpts of sales calls, support discussions and customer Slack conversations, and product usage metadata, with a limited number of support communications containing end-user e-mail addresses (WorkOS, 2026-11-06).

Exposure
A WorkOS customer is in scope for business-contact data and excerpts of calls and Slack conversations held in WorkOS's sales and support systems; WorkOS began notifying customers on 2026-11-02 (WorkOS, 2026-11-06). The same pattern applies to any organisation's own internal tool that is internet-reachable and still on an older hosting platform.
Detection
In API and web access logs of internal tools, a sustained run of authenticated bulk-query requests from an external source, and in the connected CRM or support system an unusual spike in query volume, which is how WorkOS's employee noticed it (WorkOS, 2026-11-06); WorkOS is adding alerts for unusual access patterns and request volumes on internal tools and the systems they connect to (WorkOS, 2026-11-06).
Defender takeaway
List the internal tools that are still on an older hosting platform and confirm none is reachable from the internet, block development-only credentials from being deployed to production, and put rate limits and bulk-query alerts on internal APIs; WorkOS now tests its own internet-facing systems regularly with ARTEX for exposed systems and guessable credentials (WorkOS, 2026-11-06). The researcher contacted WorkOS only after its first bulletin (WorkOS, 2026-11-06), so ARTEX-style automation against an exposed system is not proof of a hostile operator, and the response stays a breach response either way.

Sources: WorkOS (security bulletin, update) · WorkOS (security bulletin) · BleepingComputer

02Trending vulnerabilities2 items

NOTABLECVE-2026-17360 +6NATOA2

IBM API Connect: hard-coded administrative credentials, unauthenticated command injection and authentication bypass among the CVEs fixed in v12.1.1.3 and 10.0.8.13

IBM's security bulletins of 2026-11-05 for API Connect, its API management platform, list more than two hundred CVEs, and 18 rows of the v12 bulletin need no privileges at CVSS 3.1 9.0 or higher; among them is CVE-2026-17360, through which a remote attacker can gain full administrative control because of hard-coded credentials, scored CVSS 3.1 9.8 on the v12 bulletin (IBM, 2026-11-05). The same bulletin lists, each at 9.8 with no privileges or user interaction, OS command injection to arbitrary code execution (CVE-2026-17408), path traversal to arbitrary code execution (CVE-2026-17340), an authentication bypass through improper verification of a cryptographic signature (CVE-2026-17301), valid access tokens for other users because authentication against a connected directory service is not sufficiently enforced (CVE-2026-16720), and missing authorization that lets a remote attacker create, modify or delete tenants (CVE-2026-17362); a second hard-coded credential row, CVE-2026-17403, scores 9.0 (IBM, 2026-11-05). The V10.0.8 bulletin carries CVE-2026-17403, CVE-2026-17408, CVE-2026-17301 and CVE-2026-16720 as well (IBM, 2026-11-05).

API Connect V12 on-premises v12.1.0.0 to v12.1.1.2 is fixed in v12.1.1.3 and V10.0.8.0 to 10.0.8.12 in 10.0.8.13; IBM lists no workaround or mitigation on either page (IBM, 2026-11-05; IBM, 2026-11-05). Neither bulletin mentions exploitation, and neither says which component each flaw sits in.

Exposure
An API Connect installation in the listed ranges that an attacker can reach over the network; the bulletins give no per-component split, so every reachable API Connect endpoint counts (IBM, 2026-11-05).
Detection
In API Connect and reverse-proxy access logs, administrative or tenant-management actions without a preceding authenticated session from an expected administrator, and access tokens issued to identities that did not authenticate against the directory; in process telemetry on the API Connect hosts, shells or interpreters spawned by the API Connect service accounts (inferences from the flaw descriptions).
Defender takeaway
Treat these as out-of-cycle updates, because the worst rows need neither credentials nor user interaction and IBM offers no workaround; after upgrading, check administrator, tenant and token-issuance events for activity nobody can account for, because patching removes the credential, not an account or token an attacker already created.
vulnerability08 Nov 14:16Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: IBM Support (Security Bulletin, API Connect V12 on-premises) · IBM Support (Security Bulletin, API Connect V10.0.8)
NOTABLECVE-2026-117691 +1NATOA2

CVE-2026-117691, Keycloak SAML HTTP-Redirect signature bypass: a percent-encoded parameter name lets an unauthenticated attacker log in as any federated user; fixed in Keycloak 26.8.2

Keycloak 26.8.2, released on 2026-11-05, fixes CVE-2026-117691, a SAML redirect binding signature bypass via a percent-encoded parameter name (%53AMLResponse) that its release notes describe as broker login as any user (Keycloak, 2026-11-05). Red Hat, the CNA, explains that Keycloak's SAML HTTP-Redirect binding processes percent-encoded parameter names while the signature verification logic checks only literal ones, so an attacker can supply a crafted, unsigned SAML message that the server processes instead of a legitimately signed one; it scores the flaw CVSS 3.1 9.1 with no privileges or user interaction, rates it Important because it allows full account takeover of federated users, and says no available mitigation meets its criteria; it lists its build of Keycloak 26.6.9 packages as fixed by RHSA-2026:96040 and the 26.6 container images by RHSA-2026:96039, both released on 2026-11-07, and Red Hat Single Sign-On 7 as not affected (Red Hat, 2026-11-05). Its courtesy guidance describes the attack as a crafted request that places an encoded unsigned SAML parameter before a legitimately signed one, and suggests auditing and restricting account registration on external identity providers so attackers cannot capture legitimately signed redirect-binding messages (Red Hat, 2026-11-05).

The release fixes further issues tagged with CVE identifiers, among them an unauthenticated single-request JVM termination through a SAML 1.1 AuthorityBinding parser loop, labelled an incomplete fix of an earlier flaw (CVE-2026-110931), unauthenticated CPU and worker-pool exhaustion through the SAML 1.1 KeyInfo parser that needs a restart (CVE-2026-107602), unverified identity-provider email auto-linking that enables account takeover (CVE-2026-97175), an account takeover through an authentication race (CVE-2026-103112) and a SAML broker that accepts holder-of-key assertions without proof of key possession (CVE-2026-92855) (Keycloak, 2026-11-05). The release also fixes CVE-2026-111497, the out-of-bounds write in its bundled Brotli decoder (Keycloak, 2026-11-05), which CISA lists as exploited (CISA, 2026-10-27). No source reports exploitation of the SAML flaws or a public proof of concept; CISA's listing concerns the Brotli decoder.

Exposure
A Keycloak without the 26.8.2 fix (the release notes state no affected range), or a Red Hat build of Keycloak 26.6 without the 2026-11-07 errata, that uses the SAML HTTP-Redirect binding, which the release notes tie to broker login; the SAML 1.1 parser flaws need no authentication either (Keycloak, 2026-11-05; Red Hat, 2026-11-05).
Detection
In Keycloak event logs and reverse-proxy access logs, SAML messages received by HTTP GET whose query string carries an encoded parameter name such as %53AMLResponse, with or without a literal SAMLResponse beside it, and federated logins of privileged accounts with no matching authentication at the upstream identity provider (both inferences from the mechanism Red Hat describes).
Defender takeaway
Move every Keycloak that brokers SAML to 26.8.2, or the Red Hat build to 26.6.9, outside the regular cycle, because the bypass needs no privileges or user interaction and Red Hat's formal statement names no mitigation that meets its criteria; until then, restrict account registration on the external identity providers, as Red Hat's courtesy guidance suggests; after updating, review federated logins of privileged accounts for logins the upstream identity provider never saw.

vulnerability08 Nov 14:12Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Keycloak project (release notes 26.8.2) · Red Hat Product Security (CVE page) · CISA (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities alert)

03Research, reports & policy3 items

NOTABLENATOA2

Apple's mercenary-spyware threat notifications of late October reached Bundestag members and federal-government staff in Germany; BSI tells recipients to treat the iPhone as possibly compromised, update, keep Lockdown Mode on and consider replacing the device; no actor or vector is public

Apple has sent a new round of threat notifications to suspected mercenary-spyware targets in 99 countries, according to a notification screenshot posted by the researcher Costin Raiu, who says he verified several victims' notices (The Record, 2026-11-02). Germany's BSI says several Bundestag members and other public figures have received it since 2026-10-29, that it does not know whether the alerts mean actual compromise or only attempted attacks, and that it wrote to the members on 2026-10-30 (translated from German) (BSI, 2026-11-02). Germany's digital minister confirmed that members of the federal government were also warned (Euronews, 2026-11-02), and The Record, citing Der Spiegel, reports that staff of federal ministries, lawmakers and journalists travelling with the Chancellor in Asia were among the recipients (The Record, 2026-11-03). Apple attributes nothing to any actor or region (Apple, 2026-08-13), and neither Apple nor BSI has named a spyware vendor or an infection vector. BSI notes that mercenary spyware is generally assumed to infect devices without any action by the user, for example through a prepared message that need not be opened, and that a compromised device exposes messages including those in encrypted messengers, calls, contacts, calendar, location, camera and microphone (BSI, 2026-11-02).

BSI's guidance for a recipient: assume the device may be compromised; update the operating system at once unless a forensic analysis is intended; keep Lockdown Mode on permanently, also on a new device, noting that it hampers new attacks but does not remove an existing infection; where the risk looks high, consider replacing the device, resetting every account used on it and changing the phone number; then set a new device passcode, change the Apple Account and mail passwords, re-enrol authenticator apps instead of transferring them, enable Signal's registration lock and WhatsApp's two-step verification with new PINs, remove linked devices nobody recognises, and report the notification to BSI's service centre (BSI, 2026-11-02).

Exposure
Apple sends these notifications to individuals it judges to have been individually targeted, "likely because of who they are or what they do", and names politicians and diplomats among the usual targets (Apple, 2026-08-13); a recipient confirms authenticity on the lock screen, in Settings, in the e-mail to the Apple Account address and in the banner at account.apple.com after signing in (Apple, 2026-08-13).
Detection
Apple relies solely on its own threat intelligence and says it cannot say what causes a notification (Apple, 2026-08-13), and BSI's guidance names no artefact to check, so the organisational signal is a recipient reporting the notification; unusual device behaviour such as frequent crashes or fast battery drain is the only on-device hint BSI mentions (BSI, 2026-11-02).

Triage: a genuine notification never asks to click a link, open a file, install an app or profile, or give a password or verification code; a message that does is a phishing imitation, and the recipient should open account.apple.com directly in the browser instead (Apple, 2026-08-13).

Defender takeaway
Give people who are plausible targets the authenticity check above and a named internal reporting path, and keep a replace-device-and-reset-accounts procedure that follows BSI's order; a recipient updates iOS at once unless a forensic analysis is intended, considers Lockdown Mode and keeps it on permanently once enabled, and considers replacing the device where the risk is rated high, treating it as possibly compromised until then.
policy08 Nov 03:29Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: BSI (Bedrohungsbenachrichtigungen von Apple zu Mercenary Spyware, translated from German) · The Record · Euronews · Apple Support (About Apple threat notifications)
NOTABLENATOB2

Elastic threats, etc. report, November 2026: signed AI assistants as execution parents, RMM agents as the payload, paste-and-run infostealers and legacy-protocol identity abuse

Elastic Security Threat Command's November 2026 threats, etc. report covers activity it observed between 2026-04-04 and 2026-09-08 and says its counts are observations, not market share or a count of victims (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04). Its thread is intrusions run through signed, legitimate products: remote monitoring agents, AI coding assistants and Microsoft first-party clients (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-04).

On Windows an operator drove Claude Code through its VS Code extension over RDP to stage tooling and reach a self-hosted GitLab instance through a SOCKS5 proxy tunnel; Elastic's rules fired on PowerShell children of claude.exe and repeated curl.exe calls with --socks5-hostname against port 1080. On macOS the ChatGPT desktop application acted as a shell command proxy for a zsh pipeline that ran security dump-keychain against the login keychain, and in two coding-agent cases a session started with permission-bypass flags stood up a Cloudflare quick tunnel and installed LaunchAgent persistence (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04).

Of 23 confirmed RMM abuse findings, ScreenConnect was named most often (Elastic Security Labs, 2026-11-04). In the SILENTCONNECT chain a CAPTCHA page framed as a digital invitation drops a VBS script from Cloudflare r2.dev storage and ends in a silent ScreenConnect install whose client runs as a Windows service and beacons to the attacker's server on TCP 8041. In TOLLBOOTH an actor tracked as REF3927 entered a misconfigured IIS server through ViewState deserialization with publicly leaked ASP.NET machine keys, deployed a Godzilla-forked web shell and, when account creation failed, installed GotoHTTP as fallback access over ports 80 and 443 (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04).

A compromised university account reached Azure Resource Manager over the ROPC grant from an anonymized address known to be malicious; every successful attempt returned a token, and Conditional Access was bypassed because ROPC never traverses the surface the policy governs. A Kali365 device-code compromise ended with a registered device and a primary refresh token (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04).

Exposure
Endpoints where AI coding assistants or desktop AI clients may run shell commands, endpoints that can install RMM agents the organisation does not use, Entra tenants that still accept the ROPC grant or device-code sign-in, and IIS servers whose ASP.NET machine keys have been published.
Detection
In process lineage, PowerShell, curl with --socks5-hostname or security dump-keychain under claude.exe or the ChatGPT desktop app; a ScreenConnect client beaconing to an unknown host on TCP 8041 or an RMM process hollowing MSBuild.exe; in Entra sign-in logs, successful ROPC sign-ins with BAV2RPOC user agents from anonymized hosting addresses, and a device registration followed by a primary refresh token after a device-code sign-in (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04).

Triage: Elastic says the same primitive is often both normal product behavior and confirmed theft, so judge an AI-assistant child process by its outcome (a proxy tunnel, a keychain read), not by the signed parent (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04).

Defender takeaway
Elastic calls RMM abuse an inventory problem before a detection problem: knowing which agents the organisation pays for turns every other vendor name into a high-confidence alert (Elastic Security Threat Command, 2026-11-04). In Entra, a tenant that still allows ROPC has a sign-in path its Conditional Access policies never evaluate.

Claude Code's 'Yes, and don't ask again' saves the approved command, secrets included, in .claude/settings.local.json: Apiiro finds a real secret in 1,122 of 104,185 public copies of the file on GitHub, and common secret scanners miss a fifth of them

Apiiro reports that when a developer chooses "Yes, and don't ask again" on a shell command that carries a secret, Claude Code saves that exact command, secret included, in plain text in .claude/settings.local.json inside the project (Apiiro, 2026-11-05). Anthropic's documentation confirms that the approval is saved as an allow rule in that file, and that Claude Code adds the file to the user's global git excludes the first time it writes it, so it stays out of that user's commits (Anthropic, 2026-11-04). Apiiro points out that this protection lives in one user's git settings on one machine: it does not cover a folder that becomes a repository later, a clone on another machine or a file already committed, and the rule never goes into the repository's own .gitignore (Apiiro, 2026-11-05).

Apiiro found 104,185 public copies of the file in 103,617 repositories; 1,122 of those files hold at least one secret, 1,379 distinct secrets in all: 379 database passwords, 122 Supabase service-role keys, 43 SSH logins, 42 GitHub, GitLab and npm tokens and 23 AWS keys among them (Apiiro, 2026-11-05). Counting git history, the shared settings.json and saved agent transcripts, it counts 2,539 secrets in 1,994 repositories (Apiiro, 2026-11-05). Gitleaks flagged 564 and TruffleHog 643 of the 1,122 files, and 215 were flagged by neither, mostly because a password typed after PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p or mysql -p looks like an ordinary word in a command line (Apiiro, 2026-11-05).

Exposure
Any repository where a developer used Claude Code and approved a command containing a password, token or key with "don't ask again", and every laptop where that was done, because the file sits in plain text there too (Apiiro, 2026-11-05). To tell, search the organisation's repositories for the two settings files and look in their history, as Apiiro advises (Apiiro, 2026-11-05).
Detection
In pre-commit and CI secret scanning, include git history and make sure the scanner catches passwords typed inside commands, not only known key formats (The Hacker News, 2026-11-07); history matters because removing the file does not undo the leak, older versions staying in git history and in forks (The Hacker News, 2026-11-07).
Defender takeaway
Treat every secret found in these files as exposed and rotate it first, then stop tracking the file with git rm --cached and add it to the repository's own .gitignore and the organisation's templates (Apiiro, 2026-11-05).

First published 2026-10-21 · open finding →

Update08 Nov 2026 03:30 UTCrun 2026-11-08T0256Z-intelsummaryaffected_productssourcesactionssourcing_notebody

Cisco's eMudhra advisory reached version 1.8 on 2026-11-06 with a CA-trust distrust guide for IOS XE and NX-OS and MDS releases listed as impacted without a remediation; Apple's own page confirms that the curl, git, python3 and openssl that ship with macOS keep trusting the intermediates until a future update, and heise reports that macOS 27.2 undid the manual workaround and that Apple's change is not expected before December. Google's post adds that Chrome 153 and higher will stop trusting by default certificates under emSign Root CA - G1 whose earliest SCT is after 2026-11-16, and Apple's page dates its blocks to 2026-10-19 and 2026-10-23.

Cisco's advisory is at version 1.8 of 2026-11-06 (1.6 on 2026-11-04 and 1.7 on 2026-11-05). IOS XE Software, which version 1.5 still listed among the products under investigation, now has a CA-trust distrust guide and a GuestShell bug entry (CSCwx51613) (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-11-06). Several routing and switching products have no remediation yet: MDS 9000 releases 9.4(1) to 9.4(5a), Nexus 3000 and standalone NX-OS Nexus 9000 releases 9.3(9) to 9.3(18) and the 10.x trains except 10.1, and ACI-mode Nexus 9000 trains 15.x and 16.x are listed as impacted (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-11-06). Cisco still says it is not aware of malicious use (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-11-06).

Apple's support page of 2026-10-30 says that the curl, git, python3, ruby, perl and openssl that ship with macOS or the Xcode command-line tools check certificates against /etc/ssl/cert.pem and apply neither Apple's block nor revocation, so they keep trusting the intermediates until a future macOS update, which Apple has not dated; apps and tools that keep their own root list need the developer's update (Apple, 2026-10-30). Administrators can remove emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the file and, as an optional step, AAA Certificate Services to stop the six Sectigo cross-signed certificates as well, which Apple warns can leave tools that read only that file unable to verify some websites whose chains run through unaffected intermediates; a macOS software update can replace the file with Apple's version, so the check has to be repeated after each update until the one that carries Apple's change (Apple, 2026-10-30). heise reports that macOS 27.2, which brought no fix, undid the workaround for users who had applied it, that the macOS 27.3 developer beta replaces the file, and that the final release will take at least until December (heise, 2026-11-06).

Google's post now carries an update of 2026-11-04: Chrome 153 and higher will no longer trust by default TLS server certificates that validate to emSign Root CA - G1 when their earliest Signed Certificate Timestamp is dated after 2026-11-16 23:59:59 UTC, and certificates whose earliest SCT is on or before that time are unaffected (Google, 2026-11-04). Apple's page dates its block of the twelve intermediate certificates to 2026-10-19, three days before the 2026-10-22 the incident tracker and BleepingComputer gave for Apple devices, and its block of the emSign ECC Root CA - G3 root to 2026-10-23 (Apple, 2026-10-30).

  • Install release 123.xxx.006.29800 on every Xerox AltaLink 82xx, 81xx and EC81xx and release 123.xxx.006.30100 on every VersaLink C/B415, C/B625 and C/B620; apply Xerox's exposure-reducing system software patch to WorkCentre 3655, EC7836 and EC7856 (XRX26-017) and to AltaLink C80xx and B80xx, EC8036 and EC8056 (XRX26-018), and keep the web interface of those models reachable only from trusted networks or management hosts until Xerox ships a fix.
    FindingCVE-2026-109618 +1→
  • Move every managed Android phone below the 2026-11-01 security patch level to that level or later, phones of emergency-service and on-call staff first.
    FindingCVE-2026-58882→
  • On every internet-facing Linux server and every XenServer or XCP-ng host with its Workload Balancing and Conversion Manager appliances, install the vendor's fix and reboot as soon as it ships, then confirm the running version; Red Hat, Debian, CIQ, Amazon Linux, Ubuntu's generic kernels for 22.04 to 26.10, XCP-ng, MikroTik, Citrix and Sophos (Firewall hotfix HF110626.1, SD-RED firmware 3.0.012) updates are out, and XCP-ng says that a host which cannot reboot at once should take its iptables-based mitigation first and the update later; on Veeam appliances run Veeam Updater for kernel 5.14.0-570.60.1+27.2.el9_6_ciq, redeploy the virtual labs and Azure helper appliances that stay deployed and replace recovery media made before the update.
    FindingCVE-2026-98432→
  • On hosts that cannot reboot yet, drop IPv4 TCP packets that carry IP options ahead of the TCP stack as CIQ, AWS and Vates describe, after testing on one non-production host because it also drops legitimate option-bearing traffic; disabling MPTCP alone does not close the path.
    FindingCVE-2026-98432→
  • Upgrade every Cisco Expressway-C, Expressway-E and Expressway Select unit to 15.5.21, including units already moved to X15.5.20 for CVE-2026-76466, which Cisco's table does not name as the PHP2Shell fix, and until then apply the workaround in bug CSCwx37062; take any Duo Access Gateway to 3.2.0 and any Ultra-Reliable Wireless Backhaul or Unified Industrial Wireless Software to 26.2.1.9.
    FindingCVE-2026-109618 +1→
  • Update every QNAP NAS on QTS, QuTS hero or QuTScloud to the builds of 2026-10-23 (QTS 6.1.0.3656 or 5.2.11.3661, QuTS hero h6.1.0.3656, h6.0.2.3656 (h5.3.x included) or h5.2.11.3661, QuTScloud c5.2.9.3661), every QVR Surveillance (ARM32 models) to 3.0.3.1756, every TVR OS to 1.0.5 and every Notes Station 3 to 3.9.15, and every QNE (ADRA) to 1.0.7.q327.
    FindingCVE-2026-109618 +1→
  • Update every non-browser TLS client that keeps its own CA bundle or does not check revocation to a fixed version: standalone Java runtimes, including those already updated on 2026-10-21, to the update of Oracle's Security Alert CVE-2026-114820 or OpenJDK (Oracle Database Server, Autonomous Health Framework and OPatch installations too), Python 3.15.2, 3.14.10, 3.13.18, 3.12.16 or 3.11.18 together with pip 26.2.2 or later, Go 1.27.3 or 1.26.10, self-managed GitLab to a fixed patch release together with GitLab Runner 19.5.1, and SonicWall Gen7 firewalls with Client DPI-SSL enabled to SonicOS 7.3.4-7015 or later and Gen8 to 8.2.3-8015 or later; then confirm with curl against the incident tracker's test host that the client rejects the certificate; on managed Macs update to macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 or 15.8.3, or where that is not possible remove emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from /etc/ssl/cert.pem as Apple describes (AAA Certificate Services is optional and can stop tools that read only that file from verifying some unaffected sites).
    FindingCVE-2026-91403 +3→
  • Replace, by hand where the ACME client does not support ACME Renewal Information, every TLS certificate your organisation holds that chains to emSign ECC Root CA - G3 or to another of the seven certificates Microsoft removed from the Windows and Edge trust lists, or that was issued by one of the eight RSA G2B and G2C issuing CAs eMudhra revoked on 2026-11-07, because Chrome's removal of the G3 root was due on 2026-10-27 and the Windows change takes effect when the trust-list update reaches a device; deliver the updated Disallowed Certificate Trust List and the trust-list changes Microsoft describes, including its out-of-band update of 2026-10-26, to Windows devices that do not receive automatic certificate-trust updates; do not renew or reissue under emSign Root CA - G1 after 2026-11-16, because Chrome 153 and higher will not trust by default a certificate under it whose earliest SCT is later, and Windows, Edge and WebView2 stop trusting the remaining eMudhra roots on 2026-11-16 as Microsoft's update of 2026-11-10 describes.

2026-11-08T1309Z-audit · audit · Opus 5.5 · window 168 h · 3 entries published

Scope and outcome

Scheduled weekly audit of 2026-11-01T13:12Z to 2026-11-08T13:09Z (anchor: the 2026-11-01 audit, the last with re-sweeps). Forty-seven entries with activity from the week's seven intel fires were truth-checked whole in five passes: 23 clean, 19 with imprecisions, 5 with factual errors. Twenty-seven entries carry one record each from this fire (9 update, 11 correction, 7 improvement; 6 internal), among them the out-of-window LiteLLM, Gridbox, Cisco PHP2Shell and ARTEX entries. Three findings the fires missed are published as new entries: Keycloak 26.8.2 (CVE-2026-117691), IBM API Connect and Elastic's November threats, etc. report. The report is docs/audits/2026-11-08-quality-audit.md.

Verification & coverage notes

  • Claims: the open partial claim of cleanup wave 05 (2026-10-21T1147Z-audit, partial 2026-10-21T11:47:42Z wave=05) still stands on main; the scheduled audit ignores a partial claim (Phase 0 step 2), and it is more than 48 h old.
  • Truth passes: 47 entries in five batches, 1,380 ledger claims, every claim answered (4 unreadable in TE: superseded Trend Micro and CIQ page states). Verdicts: 23 clean, 19 imprecision, 5 factual error. TC also re-checked the LiteLLM watch item (factual error: its root-cause post was rewritten) and TB the Danfoss AFP quote (verbatim).
  • Pre-pass leads: Splunk and QNAP quotes were verbatim until the publishers revised the pages (both replaced); the Cisco citation-cve lead was a real binding error (fixed).
  • KEV: three additions since 2026-11-01, all covered (work/2026-11-08T1309Z-audit/kev-window.txt); no COVERED-STALE or RANSOMWARE row.
  • Stale-truth sweep: exploitation-consistency passes over all 47 window entries and no critical immediate_action lacks a fixed version.
  • Backlog: one open row, ChimeraZ/ZOHE, held to 2026-11-17 with a named condition; ARX Group SA was struck at expiry by the 2026-11-07 fire and G2 found no confirmation.
  • Duplicates: no CVE-sharing pair touching the window lacks a references[] link.
  • Recovered entries: Keycloak 26.8.2 and IBM API Connect clear PD-11(b) on their own mechanics (an unauthenticated login as any federated user; hard-coded administrative credentials with no privileges), both at notable because no source shows constituency exposure; Elastic's report clears PD-9. IBM API Connect is the unexploited-bundle class of the open operator recommendation first raised on 2026-10-11 (recommendation 2 of this report); it is published here because PD-11(b)'s "otherwise" limb names exactly an anonymous path to full administrative control.
  • borderline-drop: Plex2Shell (CVE-2026-96652/-96654/-96655/-96656, KEV since 2026-10-20, QNAP notice of 2026-11-06 reports wide exploitation): consumer and SMB media server with no public-sector deployment shown; re-open on a Swiss nexus.
  • borderline-drop: Windows Paint CVE-2026-83844 v2, Android November bulletin, Chrome 157, LXD CVE-2026-112816, the Drupal contrib wave of 2026-11-04, Absolute Secure Access 14.61, AWS Babelfish CVE-2026-119923, IBM Aspera Faspex CVE-2026-123218, HPE Fabric Composer HPESBNW05172, the Entra device-registration cloud CVE (G1): unexploited, on the regular cycle, end of life or fully mitigated by the vendor.
  • borderline-drop: BBT SE (Brenner) attack, Gleis D / Medi Porta Chur (Cloak claim), BACS and police EHRA phishing warnings, EDÖB SkySale duty-to-inform ruling, ENISA CNW-2026-05 (G2): no vector, nexus or new obligation.
  • borderline-drop: Symantec Anubis/Lindnor, CERT-In CIAD-2026-0058 CRAFTY FALCON, Microsoft exploited-vulnerabilities analysis and fake-download campaign, Check Point ChatGPT Lockdown bypass, CrowdStrike ecosystem post, Recorded Future October CVE landscape, Sophos ransomware in financial services, ESET SlippyNunchucks and Gorbag, Trend Micro Matryoshka, Censys ARTEX counts (G3): no constituency decision, fixed before the window, or no new fact.
  • Declined truth-pass findings, with reasons in the report: Danfoss record-summary inference, Dahua CERT-UA carve-out, Cisco SEG labelled lines, Node2Shell 2026-10-27 record summary.
  • Registry: the exposed-app-credentials campaign's summary and its ARTEX relation note now reflect Todyl's revision of 2026-11-06; 3AM added to malware:threeam's ambiguous_labels.
  • Source health: connectwise-trust-center still flaps (read directly at 11:25Z, 403 at about 13:30Z) and stays blocked; novee-security demoted; balbooa-blog added as a candidate; recipe notes on six further records.
  • Reader pool (context): 2 live jina keys, about 98k tokens; G1 and G3 fell through to the reader six times between them.
  • ATT&CK pin: upstream v20.1 (2026-11-05) was available; updated this fire, no technique-level changes, self-test and build green.
  • Tool and repo change: .gitignore re-includes work/**/gate.log, which the work/**/*.log rule of 2026-10-20 had kept out of every commit since the 2026-11-01 audit added it.
  • Coverage gaps: sygnia (blocked on every transport), ico-uk (403 on every transport, fifth consecutive run), the Ivanti hub advisory page (JS shell), Citrix CTX697256 and CTX697300 (a JS shell to the re-sweep's reader; extract reads both in full, per the confirmation pass), the OX Security page (403; read from an archive copy by TE).

2026-11-08T0256Z-intel · Sonnet 5.5 · window 26 h · 3 entries published

Verification & coverage notes

Quiet Sunday window: 26 h (gap 24.0 h to 2026-11-07T0256Z-intel, normal daily cadence, no outage backfill). CISA KEV carried no addition in the window (kev_window_diff: 0 rows), no scheduled multi-product vendor release fell in it (Patch Tuesday is 2026-11-10), and NCSC.ch, BSI, NCSC-NL, CERT-FR and Palo Alto PSIRT had nothing newer than 2026-11-06. Output: 3 new entries and 1 changelog record; nothing in the window clears the critical or high bar that the store lacks.

  • Published, new: Apple mercenary-spyware threat notifications reaching German MPs and ministry staff with BSI's guidance (policy, notable; Swiss recipients unconfirmed, cleared on the shared target class of government officials and an authority's response playbook); WorkOS breach by a researcher's ARTEX agent that escaped its sandbox (incident, routine after the verifier's calibration finding; out-of-nexus, so it clears breach-gate ground (b) only: a materially evolved TTP transferable to the constituency, an autonomous agent reaching an exposed internal tool through a development credential left in production, with a concrete root cause; no Swiss or public-sector customer is established); Apiiro's Claude Code settings.local.json secret-exposure study (research, routine; indirect nexus through developer repositories, held to the short form, with an empty actions[] because the Exposure and Defender takeaway lines already carry the search and the rotation).
  • Updated: 2026-10-21/emudhra-intermediate-ca-keys-recoverable-trust-store-updates (type update): Cisco's advisory v1.8 (IOS XE guide, NX-OS and MDS impacted without remediation) and Apple's own statement that macOS command-line tools keep trusting the intermediates, with heise's report that macOS 27.2 undid the manual workaround. The main analysis was cut by the same number of words it grew by, so it does not grow past the bound.
  • borderline-drop: Plex2Shell (CVE-2026-96652, -96654, -96655, -96656; KEV since 2026-10-20, QNAP reports compromised NAS devices on 2026-11-06), exploited and KEV-listed, but a consumer and SMB media server with no public-sector use evidenced; no store entry carries the CVEs, so reopen if a Swiss body, a QNAP-managed estate or a KEV-listed campaign touches the constituency.
  • borderline-drop: Windows Paint CVE-2026-83844 (MSRC revisions 2026-11-06 and 2026-11-07, CVSS cut to 7.0, fix only through the Store), unexploited, local with user interaction, a patch-cycle item; the Store-only delivery path is a vulnerability-management footnote.
  • borderline-drop: Amazon Babelfish for PostgreSQL CVE-2026-119923 (CVSS 4.0 9.3, pre-auth TDS handshake), niche, VPC-internal by default, no exploitation, AWS-managed fix.
  • borderline-drop: UgCS CVE-2026-59104 (drone ground-control server accepts empty credentials), niche product, only the finder's write-up, no Swiss use evidenced.
  • borderline-drop: Metasploit modules for NetScaler CVE-2026-88771 and GitLab CVE-2026-97229 (Rapid7 wrap-up 2026-11-06), exploit-maturity delta on entries that already say exploited, KEV-listed and public proof of concept; no reader decision changes (the Cisco ESA module of 2026-11-07 carried a new second CVE and a detection caveat, these do not).
  • borderline-drop: Hunt.io's capture of the PAN-OS PHP2Shell and Fragnesia toolkit (second capture, AI platform, GlobalProtect cookie-forging tool, persistence said to survive reboots and firmware updates); the entry already tells readers a hotfix does not evict an attacker and carries the persistence checks; Hunt's 12.x-only calibration is the one refinement and does not change who patches. Recoverable if the audit disagrees.
  • borderline-drop: refrigeration controllers, BfV and GAZ Hybrid investigating, Interior Ministry has no attribution, NZZ doubts the NoName057(16) claim, investigative status with no technical or Swiss delta; the entry already says responsibility is not established.
  • borderline-drop: Chainalysis intrusion (names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens of all users exposed, KYT accounts reached, products restored 2026-11-07 with trusted-IP allowlisting and resets); vendor to law-enforcement customers but no Swiss or public-sector customer is established and no mechanism beyond a vendor-stated on-path attack; reopen if a Swiss authority is named or a technique is published.
  • borderline-drop: DigiCert validation-archive exposure (Bugzilla report 2084460), Crédit Mutuel Arkéa EUR 118 million transfers via a provider platform, Brenner Base Tunnel company BBT SE, the EFK audit EFK-26182 of the BACS Cyber Security Hub (no obligation changes, no recommendation), Layer3 residential-proxy exits on a US government network, XLab cwpdoor on Control Web Panel, OpenAI GPT-6 Cyber, Recorded Future's October CVE landscape (periodic vendor digest, nearly everything already in the store); each fails the relevance or actionability gate or the incident floor on today's facts.
  • Single-source: 2026-11-08/workos-artex-agent-escaped-sandbox-internal-tool-breach (single-source-victim: WorkOS's own bulletins, the researcher's claim validated by a forensics firm WorkOS retained); 2026-11-08/claude-code-dont-ask-again-secrets-in-settings-local-json (single-source: Apiiro's measurement, with Anthropic's documentation confirming only the mechanism).
  • Backlog: the ChimeraZ forum-sale claim against the Belgian rescue zone Hainaut-Est (ZOHE) stays held; S4 re-searched in French, Dutch and English and found no zone statement and no Belgian press, expiry 2026-11-17 unchanged. No row changed state, so nothing was appended to it.
  • Apple entry: no source lists the 99 countries; a search for a Swiss authority or parliament statement on 2026-11-08 found none.
  • Contradiction: BSI's framing of the Apple notifications. BSI's public page says to treat the device as possibly compromised and to consider replacing it where the risk is rated high; The Record, relaying the digital minister on BSI's letter to the members of 2026-10-30, says recipients were told to assume infection and replace immediately. The entry follows BSI's public page and states both in its sourcing note.
  • Contradiction: the date Apple began blocking the eMudhra intermediates. The incident tracker and BleepingComputer say 2026-10-22; Apple's own page says 2026-10-19 (intermediates) and 2026-10-23 (the G3 root). The eMudhra entry now uses Apple's dates.
  • Reader credit: the belden-psirt extract fell through to the metered jina reader and a url call on api.github.com ran past 120 s and finished through it; both are recorded in the source notes (use WebFetch on github.com/advisories for GitHub advisory listings).

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-11-07
item.description:
• SonicWall SSL VPN bypasses SAML MFA and CISA lists it exploited; upgrade Gen7 to 7.3.4-7013, Gen8 to 8.2.3-8015. SonicWall's advisory SNWLID-2026-0014 of 2026-11-06 fixes CVE-2026-19868, an SSLVPN authentication enforcement flaw (CVSS 3.1 7.1) that lets a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method bypass SAML, MFA enforced through SAML included, on Gen7 firewalls up to 7.3.3-7015 and Gen8 up to 8.2.2-8015 when SAML is enabled for SSLVPN logins. SonicWall says it investigated a report indicating potential exploitation and CISA lists the flaw as exploited; 7.3.4-7013 and 8.2.3-8015 fix it, and since 2026-11-09 the advisory also names an interim workaround for firewalls that cannot upgrade: disable or delete every active LDAP, RADIUS and TACACS+ authentication server. →
  • Oneconsult: a site granted a folder in Chrome or Edge can steal tokens and plant VS Code and PowerShell persistence. Oneconsult's analysis of Chromium's Windows blocklist shows that a website granted a folder through the File System Access API after two clicks keeps a handle for as long as the tab is open, and that the blocklist leaves .vscode, .Azure, C:\Users\Public, SMB shares and, after a OneDrive Known Folder Move, the Desktop reachable. The paths it demonstrates are token and .env theft, a fake VS Code extension and PowerShell profile or module backdoors that need the Bypass or Unrestricted execution policy, and a file proxy through the open tab that EDR sees only as browser file activity. →
  • Kaspersky: ESXi and Proxmox ransomware ran on a monitoring server's root password and admin notes, no VM escape. Kaspersky's Global Emergency Response Team describes two ransomware cases in virtualised estates. In the BlackNevas case a PRTG Network Monitor held ESXi root access and the same root password was reused across hosts, so the attacker connected over SSH, disabled the execInstalledOnly policy with esxcli, ran the encryptor and deleted logs; in the case attributed to The Gentlemen the actor found Proxmox root credentials in plaintext notes on an administrator workstation and used the VNC web socket to encrypt the cluster. Kaspersky stresses that no VM escape was needed. →

TL;DR · the day in one read
  1. 01SonicWall SSL VPN bypasses SAML MFA and CISA lists it exploited; upgrade Gen7 to 7.3.4-7013, Gen8 to 8.2.3-8015. SonicWall says it investigated a report indicating potential exploitation and CISA lists the flaw as exploited; 7.3.4-7013 and 8.2.3-8015 fix it, and since 2026-11-09 the advisory also names an interim workaround for firewalls that cannot upgrade: disable or delete every active LDAP, RADIUS and TACACS+ authentication server. →
  2. 02Oneconsult: a site granted a folder in Chrome or Edge can steal tokens and plant VS Code and PowerShell persistence. Oneconsult's analysis of Chromium's Windows blocklist shows that a website granted a folder through the File System Access API after two clicks keeps a handle for as long as the tab is open, and that the blocklist leaves .vscode, .Azure, C:\Users\Public, SMB shares and, after a OneDrive Known Folder Move, the Desktop reachable. The paths it demonstrates are token and .env theft, a fake VS Code extension and PowerShell profile or module backdoors that need the Bypass or Unrestricted execution policy, and a file proxy through the open tab that EDR sees only as browser file activity. →
  3. 03Kaspersky: ESXi and Proxmox ransomware ran on a monitoring server's root password and admin notes, no VM escape. Kaspersky's Global Emergency Response Team describes two ransomware cases in virtualised estates. In the BlackNevas case a PRTG Network Monitor held ESXi root access and the same root password was reused across hosts, so the attacker connected over SSH, disabled the execInstalledOnly policy with esxcli, ran the encryptor and deleted logs; in the case attributed to The Gentlemen the actor found Proxmox root credentials in plaintext notes on an administrator workstation and used the VNC web socket to encrypt the cluster. Kaspersky stresses that no VM escape was needed. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 3Trending vulnerabilities 2Research, reports & policy 2Updates to prior coverage 6Action items 13

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures3 items

ROUTINENATOA2

Technical University of Munich: attackers captured the central-login passwords of everyone who signed in to the legacy myTUM portal, took a TUMonline system administrator's credentials and attacked the campus-management system; accounts with MFA were protected

The Technical University of Munich says unknown persons attacked its myTUM portal and captured the passwords for the central login to TUM systems, among them login.tum.de and TUMonline, from all persons who had logged in to myTUM; among them were the access credentials of a system administrator for TUMonline, with which the attackers attacked the central campus-management system TUMonline, which TUM then took off the network (translated from German) (TUM, 2026-11-06). TUM says the attackers may have reached the account password, name, private address and date of birth of everyone affected, plus staff and student details, that the attackers' accesses within TUMonline were largely logged and that it currently assumes no further TUMonline data such as grades is affected, and that accounts with multi-factor authentication were protected in this attack (translated from German) (TUM, 2026-11-06). heise, quoting a TUM spokesperson, reports that the attackers entered through a legacy system and that whether data was exfiltrated is still being investigated, and adds that about 60,000 students and employees are concerned (translated from German) (heise online, 2026-11-06). Neither source states how the passwords were captured at myTUM.

Exposure
A public university or other public body that keeps a retired or secondary sign-in portal validating against its central directory, so that every password typed there is a credential for the primary identity and administration systems; TUM's accounts with MFA held, and the lesson transfers to Swiss cantonal and university portals.
Defender takeaway
Inventory legacy and secondary portals that accept the central directory password and retire them or put them behind MFA, require MFA on administrator accounts of campus and school-management systems, and check whether an administrator ever signed in to such a portal.
incident07 Nov 04:03Zsingle-source · victim disclosureOpen finding →
Sources: Technische Universität München (incident notice, status 2026-11-06 12:20) · heise online
NOTABLENATOB2

Kaspersky GERT: two ESXi and Proxmox ransomware cases in which a monitoring server's reused root password and plaintext administrator notes, not a VM escape, gave the attackers the hypervisor

In the first case, Kaspersky's investigation began with BlackNevas ransomware activity on a Windows system in a virtualised domain-controller segment, where the execution of the AnyDesk remote tool and the GMER binary was recorded (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). The environment used PRTG Network Monitor, whose deployment had broad access to the ESXi hosts, and the same root password was reused across several nodes; after obtaining access to the monitoring environment the attacker used the ESXi credential to connect over SSH to the hosts that shared the password (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). On the first host, a file was uploaded during a root SSH session and its first execution failed with "Execution of non-installed file prevented"; the actor then disabled the execInstalledOnly policy with esxcli and ran it, while on a second host in another subnet with the same password the binary ran and the logs were cleared (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).

In the second case, a ransomware incident by The Gentlemen, the actor used information it had collected between initial access and visible impact: on a compromised system administrator's workstation it found Proxmox root credentials and access details in plain-text notes and logged in as root (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). It then activated the VNC web socket through the root account, which gave it control of the Proxmox environment, and used that access to download and run the ransomware in the cluster, encrypting the whole virtual environment (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). Kaspersky says a fully patched hypervisor can still be compromised through a shared password, an overprivileged monitoring account, an open SSH path or an administrator interface reachable from a general server network (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).

Exposure
A virtualisation estate where a monitoring, backup or management server stores or can use hypervisor root credentials, where one root password is shared across hosts, where SSH to ESXi is reachable from general server networks, or where administrators keep Proxmox or ESXi credentials in plain-text notes; PRTG, which supports storing VMware credentials at device or group level, is the product Kaspersky names (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).
Detection
On ESXi, root SSH logins from addresses that do not normally administer the hosts, a file upload followed by a failed execution of a non-installed file, a change to the execInstalledOnly setting and cleared logs; on Proxmox, root@pam requests to the VNC web socket used to reach other hosts, as the log records Kaspersky shows (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06). Kaspersky advises alerting when execInstalledOnly, Secure Boot enforcement, Lockdown Mode, SSH, local accounts or remote logging settings change (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).
Defender takeaway
Give each monitoring platform its own least-privilege identity instead of ESXi root, replace stored root passwords with vault retrieval or limited tokens, administer ESXi through vCenter with Lockdown Mode and SSH stopped by default, and keep logs off the hosts so a compromised administrator cannot erase them (Kaspersky GERT, 2026-11-06).
threat07 Nov 04:00Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Kaspersky Global Emergency Response Team (Securelist)
NOTABLENATOB3

Acronis TRU on BOSSAI: one operator's mesh of 12 AI agents took patient-care records and dispatch case data from Taiwanese emergency services through a legacy open port, a public API and default root credentials, and failed wherever authentication was enforced

Acronis TRU found an open attack workstation holding more than 90,000 files and describes BOSSAI as a mesh of 12 AI agents, nine active, driven by a changing roster of language models, with the operator acting as the bridge between agents and typing commands in Traditional Chinese (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). The agents that executed attacks ran almost exclusively on abliterated open-weight models run locally, after commercial models repeatedly refused offensive requests (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). In the 12 days TRU observed, the operator targeted government emergency services, banks and lenders, universities and military systems in 11 countries, with confirmed exfiltration or system access at roughly ten targets in three countries and about fifteen more attacked without confirmed compromise (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04).

The confirmed emergency-services harm is the part that matters here. A Taipei fire-department patient-care records platform exposed ECG readings, ambulance video and vital signs from 2018, accessible without credentials; a city's 119 dispatch system yielded case records with incident times, response types, status fields and street-level locations across seven districts from the system's API; and a fire-dispatch vendor's database administration panel opened with default root credentials, exposing 18 or more tables (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). In an emergency-management system the agents found a hardcoded AES-256 key in front-end JavaScript that exposed session-cookie contents, an administrator identity among them, and a partial server-side request forgery path, without confirming a full compromise (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). A brute-force run against a national fire agency's single sign-on portal gave no confirmed access, and the critical Apache flaw that the operator's vulnerability platform reported at a disaster-response centre was fabricated, because the port was filtered (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04). TRU says the agents failed where authentication was enforced, where paywalls required valid sessions and where endpoints were properly filtered, and that obscurity no longer protects a system from agents that investigate hundreds of targets at once (Acronis TRU, 2026-11-04).

Exposure
Emergency-service, dispatch and public-safety systems that expose a record API or a legacy data port without authentication, leave default administrator credentials on a vendor's database panel, or ship secrets in front-end JavaScript; those are the weaknesses the agents turned into data, and TRU reports the patient-care and dispatch records as the gravest confirmed harm.
Detection
TRU names sqlmap, nmap and nikto among the most-used tools, so the traffic is ordinary scanner traffic in web access and authentication logs (an inference from the tool list): bursts of SQL-injection probing, repeated sign-in attempts against a single sign-on portal from one source, and logins to a database administration panel with a default account.
Defender takeaway
Swiss dispatch, patient-care and records systems of emergency services are the same target class, so check them for unauthenticated APIs and legacy ports, default root or administrator credentials on vendor panels, and keys or tokens in front-end code; the agents failed wherever authentication was enforced, so closing those gaps is what stops this tooling.

CVE-2026-19868, SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN: valid credentials for an alternate authentication method bypass SAML and the MFA it enforces; SonicWall investigated a report of exploitation and CISA lists it as exploited (CVSS 3.1 7.1)

SonicWall's advisory SNWLID-2026-0014 of 2026-11-06 fixes seven SonicOS flaws on Gen7 and Gen8 firewalls, and one of them, CVE-2026-19868, is an authentication enforcement weakness in the SSLVPN service: a user with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method may bypass the SAML authentication controls, and successful exploitation may also bypass SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06). SonicWall says the flaw only affects SSLVPN when SAML is enabled for SSLVPN logins, and scores it CVSS 3.1 7.1 as a use of single-factor authentication (CWE-308) (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06). The advisory says SonicWall PSIRT "has investigated a report indicating potential exploitation" and urges customers to upgrade (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06); its revision of 2026-11-09 adds an interim workaround for SAML deployments that cannot upgrade, to disable or delete every active LDAP, RADIUS and TACACS+ authentication server on the firewall (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-09); CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-06 "based on evidence of active exploitation" (CISA, 2026-11-06). SonicWall has not shared details about the reported exploitation (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-06).

The advisory applies one table to all seven flaws: Gen7 hardware firewalls (TZ, NSa and NSsp) and Gen7 NSv up to and including 7.3.3-7015 are fixed in 7.3.4-7013 and higher, and Gen8 hardware firewalls (TZ and NSa) and Gen8 NSv up to and including 8.2.2-8015 are fixed in 8.2.3-8015 and higher (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06). It also fixes two management-interface flaws scored 8.8 that in specific conditions could potentially let a remote unauthenticated attacker perform unauthorized operations, and that need user interaction, a pre-authentication heap overflow in the SSL-VPN service that could cause a denial of service, and three lower-severity flaws; no source reports them exploited (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06).

Exposure
A Gen7 or Gen8 SonicWall firewall or NSv at or below the builds above with the SSL VPN enabled and SAML configured as a login method for SSLVPN; the running SonicOS build is the first check and the SAML setting for SSLVPN the second, the vendor's stated precondition (SonicWall PSIRT, 2026-11-06).
Detection
The advisory gives no indicators. From the stated mechanism, compare successful SSLVPN logins on the firewall with the identity provider's sign-in log: a VPN session with no matching SAML sign-in or MFA event, or a SAML-enrolled user who authenticated through another authentication method, is the signal. Patching does not evict an attacker who already holds a session or reuses the credentials, so review VPN sessions since SAML was enabled and reset the credentials of accounts that work through both authentication methods; once the workaround is applied, logins through the removed authentication methods should stop, and any that continue show the change did not take effect or that the session predates it.

Triage: a legitimate SAML sign-in leaves an event at the identity provider; a login through the alternate path does not, which follows from the stated mechanism.

Defender takeaway
Upgrade every Gen7 and Gen8 firewall that serves SAML SSLVPN logins to 7.3.4-7013 or 8.2.3-8015 or later now, because the exploitation evidence is a vendor-investigated report plus CISA's listing; where a firewall cannot be upgraded today, disable or delete its LDAP, RADIUS and TACACS+ authentication servers as the advisory now says, and expect logins that rely on those servers to stop; then review VPN sessions for logins that skipped the identity provider.
