NOTABLENATOB2

Oneconsult on the File System Access API: after two clicks a website holds read and write access to folders such as .vscode, .Azure, the public desktop and SMB shares in Chrome and Edge, enough for token theft and persistence without a process on the host

Oneconsult analyses, from the Chromium source and tests on Windows 11 with Chrome and Edge 150.0.7871.101, what a website can reach through the File System Access API once a user selects a folder and grants permission: the handle stays valid as long as the tab is open and is obtained after just two user clicks (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02). Chrome rejects blocklisted paths, but a path that is not in its table and not an ancestor of a blocked path is allowed, and the kDontBlockChildren rule leaves the subfolders of listed directories selectable; Oneconsult confirmed .vscode, the Azure token cache, C:\Users\Public and SMB shares as accessible (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02).

Oneconsult demonstrates these paths. A site can search a granted folder and take files such as cached Azure tokens and .env files. It can drop a fake VS Code extension into .vscode/extensions, which runs inside the normal code.exe process and is unaffected by Mark of the Web because Node.js does not check the Zone.Identifier stream. It can plant PowerShell profile and module backdoors, which work only with the Bypass or Unrestricted execution policy because the API stamps every written file with ZoneId=3 and RemoteSigned refuses such files. It can drop files on the public desktop, where they appear for all users and trigger a warning that a certain percentage of users acknowledge. And it can run an interactive file proxy through the still-open tab, where EDR sees only the browser reading and writing files (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02). A OneDrive Known Folder Move enabled while Chrome is running leaves a stale blocklist, so the redirected Desktop was writable; Oneconsult notes that the bypass has been reported to Google, which made the issue public, and that Google classed reading a single dragged file from a blocked folder as "not a security issue" (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02).

Daniel Oz's July write-up of the same technique has a website edit a file the user already holds. He says the user-gesture requirement does not prevent phishing, only automatic picker invocation, and that signed or complex files may fail, be blocked or break in a way that prevents execution (Oz, 2026-07-05).

Exposure
Windows users of Chrome or Edge, above all developer workstations with VS Code, cached Azure tokens or PowerShell on the Bypass or Unrestricted execution policy, and estates that enable OneDrive Known Folder Move; the attack needs a user to choose a folder and confirm a second prompt (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02).
Detection
File-write telemetry for PowerShell profile paths, PowerShell module folders and .vscode\extensions, and changes to the Zone.Identifier stream there, whose ReferrerUrl and HostUrl fields keep the origin of the page that wrote the file (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02). Oz says editing a file does not automatically reclassify it as downloaded, so the stream is a possible marker, not a guaranteed one (Oz, 2026-07-05).

Triage: browsers legitimately read and write files for web editors such as Google Docs and VS Code for Web, as Oneconsult notes; the signal is a browser process writing into a persistence location, not the file activity itself.

Defender takeaway
Restrict file system read and write access with the Chrome Enterprise policies Oneconsult names, FileSystemReadAskForUrls, FileSystemWriteAskForUrls and the respective AskForUrls policies, alert on writes to PowerShell profiles and VS Code extension folders, and treat a website's request to choose a local folder as a social-engineering step (Oneconsult, 2026-11-02).

Alpine's advisory adds that updating the package does not restart a running sshd, so sshd must be restarted, and that on exposed machines the administrator should review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys, treating the machine as compromised if a login cannot be ruled out (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-05). No vendor or authority source reports attacks on production systems.

WordPress core 4.7 to 7.1.3: an unauthenticated race in the core update process can lead to remote code execution, fixed in 7.1.4 and backported to every supported branch, listed by CISA as exploited; Wordfence assigned CVE-2026-119977

First published 2026-10-30 · open finding →

Update07 Nov 2026 03:51 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-intelheadlinesummaryactionssourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

The discoverer, Umut Bayram of Picus Security, shows that the update installing WordPress 7.1.4 still unpacks with the site's old code, so the staging folder under wp-content/upgrade can be reachable at a predictable path during that update, while a partial package exposes the installer only if it contains the installer files; he advises denying web access to the folder and confirming it answers 403 before updating.

Umut Bayram of Picus Security, who found the flaw, shows that the update which installs the fix still unpacks its files with the site's old, unpatched code (Picus Security, 2026-11-05; The Hacker News, 2026-11-06). Picus says the new code's skip of wp-config.php already works in that first update but the randomised folder name does not, so the temporary installer sits at a predictable path on sites running 5.9 or later and, on 4.4 to 5.8, behind a random suffix that hides it unless the site leaks the path; an attacker who reaches it can no longer replace the live configuration but can still set up the temporary copy, log in to it, run PHP and from there read or write files in the live directory (Picus Security, 2026-11-05). Bayram told The Hacker News the deciding factor "isn’t partial versus complete. It’s whether the updater already installed on the site has been fixed", and that a partial package exposes the installer only if it contains the installer files; The Hacker News found WordPress.org offering an in-branch move such as 7.1.3 to 7.1.4 as a partial package, automatic updates included, so whether such an update is exposed depends on what that package contains, and only once 7.1.4 or the branch fix is installed do later updates use a random folder (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06). WordPress 4.6 and earlier get no fix (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06).

The order matters: Picus advises denying web access to wp-content/upgrade/ in the web server configuration first, confirming that the path answers 403, and only then updating; this does not break updates, because WordPress reaches the folder through the filesystem (Picus Security, 2026-11-05). An .htaccess file placed inside the folder does not work, because the old updater deletes the folder's contents before unpacking, and WP-CLI's wp core update is no substitute because it uses the same updater and folder (Picus Security, 2026-11-05). For sites that stayed on an affected version, Wordfence suggests looking for unexpected requests to PHP files under wp-content/upgrade, administrator accounts no one recognises, plugins no one installed and PHP files in wp-content/upgrade that no one put there (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06).

Code that its authors describe as an exploit has appeared in public GitHub repositories since earlier this week, and whether it works has not been established; WordPress's own advisory rates the flaw low, against Wordfence's CVSS 8.1 and CISA's listing as exploited (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06). None of these sources reports a compromise through the update that installs the fix; CISA's listing and Wordfence's probing telemetry above are unchanged.

Sources: WordPress.org · Wordfence · Patchstack · Wordfence Intelligence (CVE-2026-119977) · CISA · Canadian Centre for Cyber Security · Picus Security · The Hacker News

ARTEX: Microsoft reports Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, running an open-source multi-agent LLM penetration-testing framework against hundreds of organizations, with privileged cloud access in under three hours in some cases, and Expel sees the same infrastructure abuse Okta self-service registration

First published 2026-10-22 · open finding →

Update07 Nov 2026 03:50 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-intelsummaryentitiestechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_note

Microsoft reports that Storm-3358, a Cambodia-based, financially motivated cluster, has used ARTEX since October 2026 against financial organisations, pairing it with conventional scanners and installing the open-source remote access tools WISP, vshell and AdaptixC2; Check Point Research reads ten exposed operator consoles showing campaigns that run almost autonomously once a goal is set, and Microsoft says honeypots, decoys, tarpits and fake wins helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence reports that Storm-3358, a Cambodia-based intrusion cluster that primarily targets financial organisations in Southeast Asia and a smaller number of large financial organisations globally, began using ARTEX against the financial sector in October 2026 (Microsoft, 2026-11-06). Microsoft says the cluster combines ARTEX with conventional automated tools to scan internet-facing systems, exploit flaws including anonymous file upload and server-side request forgery, and install the open-source remote access tools WISP, vshell and AdaptixC2, which ARTEX agents download with netcat and curl (Microsoft, 2026-11-06). Microsoft's tell for an agent on a scanned system is "a wide variety of requests in a brief time", retries of variations on one technique and a move to next-stage actions at machine speed; ARTEX by default drives Nmap, curl, wget, Python HTTP clients and headless Chromium through Playwright, and blocking their default traits will not stop an agent, which "will quickly change them" (Microsoft, 2026-11-06). In Microsoft's testing, honeypots, decoys, tarpits and fake wins helped reduce the attack traffic reaching real assets, with no figures given (Microsoft, 2026-11-06).

Check Point Research counts 2,557 systems that host or hosted ARTEX panels, 1,608 of them live and public, and ten that exposed the full database; in those ten consoles the operators set a goal and then "barely interacted with their agent fleets" (Check Point, 2026-11-05). The campaigns it reads are opportunistic crime, not espionage: iOS signing certificates from grey-market shops, a cryptocurrency-service campaign and game-account credentials. In the signing-shop campaign the agents got in through hardcoded administrator passwords in JavaScript bundles, missing API authentication, command injection, insecure direct object references, weak administrative credentials and template injection (Check Point, 2026-11-05). Check Point does not name Storm-3358.

Rapid7's Metasploit framework now carries public modules for two unauthenticated SQL injections on Cisco Secure Email Gateway that end in root command execution: one merged on 2026-11-05 for the injection its author matches, at medium confidence, to the exploited CVE-2026-76461 and which needs URL Filtering and URL Retrospective Service enabled, and one for the non-default S/MIME public-key harvesting feature that Rapid7 believes is CVE-2026-76443. Rapid7's Metasploit framework now carries public exploit modules for two unauthenticated SQL injections on Cisco Secure Email Gateway that end in command execution as root. The first, merged on 2026-11-05, targets an injection in the Email Cloud Scanner URL-retrospective message database and its documentation says "URL Filtering and URL Retrospective Service must both be enabled" (Rapid7 Metasploit module documentation, 2026-10-16), which sits against Cisco's statement that the flaw affects the gateway "regardless of device configuration" (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-09-14); its author says it can only be assessed with medium confidence that this is CVE-2026-76461, the flaw CISA lists, and that of the injections reproduced from the patch diff it was the only one that left the pattern COPY.*TO PROGRAM in mail_logs, the check Cisco's own advisory names (Rapid7 Metasploit pull request 22024, 2026-10-16). The second targets an injection in the S/MIME public-key harvesting feature, "we have reason to believe this maps to CVE-2026-76443" according to Rapid7's wrap-up of 2026-11-06 (Rapid7, 2026-11-06). The S/MIME module was merged on 2026-10-28; its author tested a gateway on AsyncOS 15.5.1-055 with the S/MIME Public Key Harvesting feature enabled for inbound mail, and the module sends one signed S/MIME email carrying 500 certificate addresses to the gateway's SMTP listener (Rapid7 Metasploit pull request 22018, 2026-10-15). Its documentation says "Public-key harvesting must be enabled on the inbound mail flow policy for the target to be exploitable" (Rapid7 Metasploit module documentation, 2026-10-15), and the author of the first module calls that feature "a different non-default feature" (Rapid7 Metasploit pull request 22024, 2026-10-16).

Cisco's hardening advisory lists CVE-2026-76443 with the other grouped CVEs and its fixed-release table gives 15.5.5-014 for 15.5 and earlier, 16.5.0-780 for 16.5 and "Migrate to a fixed release." for 16.0 (Cisco PSIRT, hardening-release advisory, 2026-09-14). A 16.0 appliance on 16.0.4-302 therefore has no named fix for the flaw the S/MIME module most likely uses; moving to 16.5.0-780 closes it. Rapid7 does not report exploitation of the S/MIME module's flaw, and Cisco does not say whether the injection it lists as exploited is the one in either module.

  • Notes for the next audit: the Danfoss refrigeration entry (13 records) and the ARTEX entry have main analyses well over the word bound (this fire only appended sections, none grew either analysis); the Plex2Shell chain was dropped a fourth time and the audit may want to confirm that call against the QNAP notice of 2026-11-06.

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-11-06
item.description:
• Entra app-credential abuse: agents hunt GitHub for secrets, an operator reaches MSP clients, government among them. Microsoft reports that since August threat actors have used the agentic framework ARTEX to query public GitHub for OAuth application secrets and cloud keys, and that from 2026-10-28 valid application credentials were used for service-principal sign-ins across dozens of applications in several tenants, a vendor-owned multitenant application among them. Todyl's telemetry shows one operator since 2026-11-01 targeting about 45 application registrations at MSPs, more than 33 of which authenticated, and reaching 27 organisations, government clients among them; Microsoft says a similar campaign involving the same addresses was reported by Todyl, and Todyl's update of 2026-11-06 now assesses its operator as an automated agentic credential crawler, likely fed by secrets exposed in public repositories or web apps. →
  • Qilin's October build spreads through vCenter and ESXi, reboots into Safe Mode and prints notes on office printers. Seqrite compares a March 2026 and an October 2026 Qilin (Agenda) sample and reports that the newer build embeds a PowerShell engine that logs in to vCenter, disables HA and DRS and pushes Linux payloads to ESXi hosts over SSH, shuts down the processes that lock files through the Windows Restart Manager instead of brute-force termination, sets a Safe Mode reboot so EDR drivers do not load, and sends ransom notes to TCP 9100 on local subnets. It is a vendor analysis of two samples with no incident confirmation. →
  • Microsoft Q3 email report: overrides let authentication-failing spoofed mail through; SVG CAPTCHA phishing returns. Microsoft's Q3 2026 email-threat report finds that many malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of business services were delivered despite failing authentication because tenant- or user-level overrides applied, 63% of the messages with a recorded security outcome in September. It also reports SVG attachments leading CAPTCHA-gated phishing at quarter end, Teams impersonators shifting from help-desk display names to ordinary personal names, and an August device-code phishing campaign that used a QR code in a Word document against legal organisations. →
item.content:encoded:
TL;DR · the day in one read
  1. 01Entra app-credential abuse: agents hunt GitHub for secrets, an operator reaches MSP clients, government among them. Microsoft reports that since August threat actors have used the agentic framework ARTEX to query public GitHub for OAuth application secrets and cloud keys, and that from 2026-10-28 valid application credentials were used for service-principal sign-ins across dozens of applications in several tenants, a vendor-owned multitenant application among them. Todyl's telemetry shows one operator since 2026-11-01 targeting about 45 application registrations at MSPs, more than 33 of which authenticated, and reaching 27 organisations, government clients among them; Microsoft says a similar campaign involving the same addresses was reported by Todyl, and Todyl's update of 2026-11-06 now assesses its operator as an automated agentic credential crawler, likely fed by secrets exposed in public repositories or web apps. →
  2. 02Qilin's October build spreads through vCenter and ESXi, reboots into Safe Mode and prints notes on office printers. Seqrite compares a March 2026 and an October 2026 Qilin (Agenda) sample and reports that the newer build embeds a PowerShell engine that logs in to vCenter, disables HA and DRS and pushes Linux payloads to ESXi hosts over SSH, shuts down the processes that lock files through the Windows Restart Manager instead of brute-force termination, sets a Safe Mode reboot so EDR drivers do not load, and sends ransom notes to TCP 9100 on local subnets. It is a vendor analysis of two samples with no incident confirmation. →
  3. 03Microsoft Q3 email report: overrides let authentication-failing spoofed mail through; SVG CAPTCHA phishing returns. Microsoft's Q3 2026 email-threat report finds that many malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of business services were delivered despite failing authentication because tenant- or user-level overrides applied, 63% of the messages with a recorded security outcome in September. It also reports SVG attachments leading CAPTCHA-gated phishing at quarter end, Teams impersonators shifting from help-desk display names to ordinary personal names, and an August device-code phishing campaign that used a QR code in a Word document against legal organisations. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 3Trending vulnerabilities 2Research, reports & policy 1Updates to prior coverage 2Action items 6

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures3 items

HIGHupdatedNATOB2

Exposed application credentials: Microsoft sees an agentic framework search GitHub for OAuth and cloud application secrets and then sign in as the applications from 2026-10-28, and Todyl sees an operator use MSP applications to reach 27 organisations, government clients among them

Microsoft reports that since August 2026 threat actors have used the agentic offensive framework ARTEX to submit large volumes of queries to public GitHub for secrets (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). As early as 2026-10-28 it saw successful service-principal sign-ins from two IP addresses, one a Tor exit node that may carry unrelated activity, across dozens of applications in several tenants, including a vendor-owned multitenant application whose credential was compromised at the source and used to reach multiple downstream tenants (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). Microsoft states that a similar campaign involving the same addresses was also reported by Todyl (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Todyl, from its managed-detection telemetry, describes one operator who since 2026-11-01 has signed in to MSPs' Microsoft 365 and Azure environments as their own applications with stolen credentials that are still valid: about 45 app registrations at roughly 18 organisations were targeted, more than 33 authenticated, and 27 organisations were reached, among them the MSPs' downstream clients in government (Todyl, 2026-11-03). For nearly every credential the operator requests an Azure Resource Manager token, then a Key Vault token, and within minutes applications that had never been used start authenticating; MSP multitenant and delegated-admin apps and Partner Center tokens reach client tenants, one app sweeping 15 client tenants in about 10-second loops (Todyl, 2026-11-03). Todyl says no Microsoft vulnerability is involved and that it saw no persistence (Todyl, 2026-11-03). Its update of 2026-11-06 assesses the operator as an automated agentic credential crawler and the likely credential source as public repositories or web apps, citing credential scanning from the actor's address before the first sign-in, no sign of earlier compromise and custom-built affected apps (Todyl, 2026-11-03). After its detections fired on 2026-11-03 the operator switched to spoofed browser user agents and replayed users' refresh tokens, all blocked by Conditional Access (Todyl, 2026-11-03).

Exposure
Any Entra tenant, an MSP's or a customer's, that holds app registrations with client secrets, above all multitenant, delegated-admin and Partner Center applications and Azure DevOps service connections, security-tool integration apps among those abused (Todyl, 2026-11-03); Conditional Access for workload identities needs the Workload ID Premium licence and covers only single-tenant apps (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).
Detection
In Entra service-principal and non-interactive sign-in logs, an invalid-secret or expired-secret error for an application followed by a success, one address authenticating as service principals in several unrelated tenants within 24 hours, an Azure Resource Manager token followed at once by a Key Vault token and then by previously unused apps authenticating, and failed service-principal sign-ins from hosting space that never succeed, which success-only logic misses (Todyl, 2026-11-03). In Azure DevOps auditing, personal access token creation and first use, federated service connections and pipeline edits (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Triage: the invalid-secret and expired-secret errors alone only show that someone holds an old or wrong credential for the app; Microsoft treats a failure followed by a success as the urgent case (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Defender takeaway
Inventory the client secrets on app registrations and hunt the sign-in pattern above in every tenant you run or manage, MSP-managed communal tenants included; on an affected app remove every client secret, certificate and federated credential, including those the actor added, and rotate what any Key Vault it could read holds, because tokens already issued stay valid until expiry (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).
Update08 Nov 2026 13:59 UTCrun 2026-11-08T1309Z-auditbodyevidencesourcing_notesummary

Todyl updated its post on 2026-11-06 after Microsoft's research of 2026-11-05: it says Microsoft's findings match its assessment that the activity is an automated, agentic credential crawler, and it now names public repositories or web apps as the likely source of the stolen secrets, citing credential scanning from the actor's address before the first sign-in, no sign of earlier compromise and custom-built affected apps (Todyl, 2026-11-03). It quotes Microsoft for the GitHub access path and the ARTEX name, and adds that the operator replays harvested material within minutes, in one case signing in as a connector's app about 2.5 minutes after downloading its archive (Todyl, 2026-11-03). Todyl says AI agents using or posting credentials in cleartext on the command line have been the largest contributor to the exposed credentials it has observed, and advises hunting service-principal and non-interactive sign-in logs back to at least 2026-10-28 (Todyl, 2026-11-03).

Builds on: 2026-10-22/artex-storm-0940-agentic-llm-pentest-spraying-oauth-abuse · 2026-10-18/connectwise-cloud-backup-skykick-m365-app-credential-abuse · 2026-10-30/vapor-panda-artex-agentic-campaign-foreign-ministries · 2026-10-23/m365-token-spray-replay-rogue-entra-devices-mfa-wipe · 2026-10-26/jpcert-nict-app-to-backend-api-attacks-ai-scanning-japan

threat06 Nov 03:46Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Microsoft Threat Intelligence · Todyl
NOTABLENATOB3

Seqrite: reverse engineering of two Qilin builds shows the October 2026 variant adding a vCenter and ESXi spreading engine, Restart Manager lock release, a Safe Mode reboot loop and ransom notes printed to office printers

Seqrite's reverse engineering of a March 2026 and an October 2026 Qilin (Agenda) sample finds that the Rust code was reworked into a modular workspace of 22 internal crates, that the command line grew from 6 to 42 switches, and that the October build carries subsystems the baseline lacked (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03). It uses the Windows Restart Manager API to shut down the processes that lock SQL Server, Exchange and virtual-machine disk files, instead of the brute-force process termination of the March sample, so that the files can be encrypted (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03). An embedded PowerShell engine, started with --spread-vcenter, authenticates to vCenter, disables HA and DRS, extracts the ESXi host addresses, opens SSH and SCP sessions, uploads Linux ransomware payloads to /tmp on the hosts and runs esxcli to power off virtual machines and encrypt .vmdk volumes (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03).

The build also installs the RSAT Active Directory module itself with DISM before enumerating computers, embeds 32-bit and 64-bit PsExec to spread over the ADMIN$ and C$ shares with harvested credentials, and sets a Safe Mode boot with bcdedit plus an AutoAdminLogon registry value so that it reboots into Safe Mode, where EDR drivers do not load (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03). A raw-printing module scans local subnets for TCP port 9100 and sends cleartext ransom notes to office printers, and the October binary masquerades as resmon.exe with a forged Microsoft code-signing overlay (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03). Seqrite lists healthcare, manufacturing, education and technology as the victim sectors in its telemetry (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03).

Exposure
Windows estates with a vCenter and ESXi hosts that a domain-joined host can reach over the network and SSH, since the spreading engine needs a vCenter login and SSH to the hosts; Seqrite names no initial-access route.
Detection
In vCenter audit events, HA or DRS being disabled on a cluster followed by SSH sessions to ESXi hosts and esxcli activity; in process-creation and registry telemetry, bcdedit setting a Safe Mode boot and a Winlogon AutoAdminLogon change outside a change window, DISM installing the RSAT Active Directory component on a host that never had it, and rstrtmgr.dll loaded by a process that is not an installer; in network telemetry, one host sending to TCP 9100 on many hosts of a subnet; and an executable named resmon.exe outside System32 (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03).

Triage: the Restart Manager and a DISM-installed RSAT component are normal in patching and administration, so each is weak alone; the combination with the print fan-out, the Safe Mode change and the vCenter actions is the signal.

Defender takeaway
Treat HA or DRS being turned off in vCenter, followed by SSH sessions to ESXi hosts, as an incident, and alert on a Safe Mode boot configured by bcdedit outside change windows, which Seqrite names as a detection point (Seqrite Labs, 2026-11-03).

Builds on: 2026-09-21/qilin-ai-generated-wiper-locker-scripts-forensic-markers

threat06 Nov 03:50Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Seqrite Labs
NOTABLENATOB2

Kaspersky reconstructs an intrusion through SharePoint ToolShell, attributed to Storm-2603 with moderate confidence, whose implant lived only inside w3wp.exe: an ASP.NET VirtualPathProvider memory shell with a suo5 tunnel, then Velociraptor, several tunnelling mechanisms and Warlock's AV killer

Kaspersky's retrospective analysis of a December intrusion at a customer's on-premises SharePoint server found activity consistent with Storm-2603, with the access and control layer held entirely inside the IIS worker process w3wp.exe and nothing written to disk (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). On December 20 a single request to a SharePoint administrative endpoint tied to the ToolPane component fingerprinted the host for ToolShell (CVE-2025-53770); the full exploit chain ran on December 24 against the same endpoint, and the gap kept the probe from being correlated with it (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). The payload was loaded into the ASP.NET runtime and lost when the application pool recycled or IIS restarted (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

The memory shell registers a custom VirtualPathProvider through a non-public method of the ASP.NET HostingEnvironment class, subverts trust controls so that the registration works even in a precompiled application, intercepts requests at the GetCacheKey() hook and stays dormant unless a specific User-Agent header arrives (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). It speaks a custom XOR-obfuscated binary protocol, and the open-source suo5 tool proxies traffic so connections from the command server reach arbitrary hosts inside the network through the SharePoint server (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). It reaches SYSTEM by named-pipe token impersonation adapted from EfsPotato and creates administrative accounts through native SAM RPC calls (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

Shortly after the injection w3wp.exe started msiexec.exe to install a remote MSI that was Velociraptor 0.73.4.0, vulnerable to CVE-2025-6264, which the actor used for persistence, discovery, data collection and payload execution and to deploy Zoho Assist unattended access, a VS Code CLI tunnel, Cloudflare Tunnel and a reverse proxy, so access no longer depended on the IIS process (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). The actor then uploaded a vulnerable driver that is used to terminate EDR products and sideloaded a DLL that Kaspersky identified as Warlock ransomware's AV killer, possibly meant to use that driver; Kaspersky's endpoint product blocked the ransomware process (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

Exposure
An internet-reachable on-premises SharePoint Server on which ToolShell (CVE-2025-53770 and CVE-2025-53771) is exploitable (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).
Detection
In CLR loader telemetry, a dynamically compiled App_Web_toolpane assembly and a Microsoft.GeneratedCode assembly loading in the same application domain after a ToolPane request; in the IIS-Configuration ETW provider, events 25 and 47 for a path without the file-change-monitor events 17, 18, 19 and 21 that a real file produces, checked against an allow-list of legitimate VirtualPathProvider implementations; and memory inspection of w3wp.exe (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

Triage: App_Web_* assemblies come from ordinary ASP.NET page compilation and Microsoft.GeneratedCode from legitimate XmlSerializer use, so neither is a signal alone; the signal is the pair in one application domain right after a ToolPane request, and any VirtualPathProvider that is not on the application's inventory (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). The December 20 probe came from infrastructure associated with ONYPHE, an attack-surface discovery platform whose vulnerability checks use non-intrusive probes, so a probe alone looks like a benign scanner; Kaspersky's retrospective analysis established the probe as the initial phase of the intrusion that followed on the same endpoint (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05).

Defender takeaway
On a SharePoint host that shows a code-execution exploit, contain the host, hunt the persistence that was installed afterwards, and rotate credentials and the exposed ASP.NET MachineKey; removing the initial shell or known indicators is not enough (Kaspersky, 2026-11-05). Hunt for VirtualPathProvider implants with the ETW pattern above on SharePoint farms that were exposed to ToolShell.

Builds on: 2026-10-03/warlock-longlegs-sharepoint-machinekey-sysvol-ransomware

threat06 Nov 03:44Zsingle-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: Kaspersky (Securelist)

02Trending vulnerabilities2 items

NOTABLECVE-2026-116779exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-116779, FreeSWITCH 1.11.2 and earlier: one inbound SIP MESSAGE can select the api chat proto and run FreeSWITCH API commands, the vendor says exploitation has been observed, CISA lists it as exploited, and 1.11.3 fixes it (CVSS 3.1 9.8)

SignalWire's advisory GHSA-mg63-h38w-8p9p describes CVE-2026-116779: FreeSWITCH's sofia_presence_handle_sip_i_message() splits the To user of an inbound SIP MESSAGE on + and treats the left half as a chat proto name, the mod_dptools module registers an api chat interface that hands its address to switch_api_execute(), and a peer that can deliver a MESSAGE to a profile therefore selects which FreeSWITCH API command the server runs (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). The impact is command execution with the privileges of the FreeSWITCH process, including arbitrary operating-system commands, disclosure of configuration and credentials and full call control, and where mod_lua is loaded, as the stock configuration does, inline Lua is a second route (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). The advisory scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8, lists 1.11.2 and earlier as affected and 1.11.3 as patched, and states that exploitation of this path has been observed in the wild without naming an actor or a victim (SignalWire, 2026-10-28); CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09 (CISA, 2026-11-09). BSI CERT-Bund rated its advisory on the flaw critical and lists versions before 1.11.3 as affected (BSI CERT-Bund, 2026-11-04).

The default posture is exposed: chat handling is on unless a profile sets enable-chat=false, the stock vanilla configuration leaves it on for the internal and external profiles, and the inbound ACL does not cover MESSAGE; where MESSAGE authentication is enforced (the default from 1.10.7) any one account on the profile is enough, and installations that still carry the sample directory user default, which has no password, need no account of their own (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). The fix is a per-profile enable-chat-api-proto parameter that is off unless set, so the route is closed by default and a MESSAGE that selects the proto is answered with 403 and logged with the source and the requested command (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). auth-messages alone does not close the path, and disable_system_api_commands=true removes the system API but leaves the route to every other registered API, module loading and call origination included (SignalWire, 2026-10-28).

Exposure
A FreeSWITCH of version 1.11.2 or earlier with a SIP profile that accepts inbound MESSAGE from a peer that can reach it, which is the default configuration (SignalWire, 2026-10-28).
Detection
SIP signalling logs, or packet capture at the session border controller, for MESSAGE requests whose To user carries a + with api as the left half, in any letter case; after the upgrade the 403 and the log line with the source and the requested command mark attempts (SignalWire, 2026-10-28). The mechanism also implies child processes such as a shell or a downloader started by the FreeSWITCH process, and, where an instance was reachable before the fix, changes to its Lua scripts, dialplan or loaded modules.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade to 1.11.3, or until then set enable-chat=false on every profile that does not need inbound SIP chat and remove directory users that have no password; on an instance that was reachable by SIP peers, treat its configuration and the credentials it holds as disclosed, because the vendor says exploitation has been observed and CISA lists the flaw as exploited (SignalWire, 2026-10-28; CISA, 2026-11-09).
Improvement08 Nov 2026 14:09 UTCrun 2026-11-08T1309Z-auditsources

The release notes of FreeSWITCH 1.11.3 add the enable-chat-api-proto parameter that gates the api chat proto to mod_verto as well as to mod_sofia (SignalWire, 2026-08-28). SignalWire's advisory describes only the inbound SIP MESSAGE path and does not say whether Verto endpoints reach the same command selector (SignalWire, 2026-10-28), so a deployment that exposes Verto to untrusted clients has a second surface the SIP-profile setting does not cover.

Update10 Nov 2026 04:25 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-intelsummarytagscvessourcesevidenceverificationsourcing_noteactionsbodytitleheadline

CISA added CVE-2026-116779 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09 "based on evidence of active exploitation" that it does not describe (CISA, 2026-11-09). Until then SignalWire's advisory was the only source of the exploitation claim; the listing adds an authority's assessment, still without a victim, an actor or a count of affected systems. The compromise check in the Defender takeaway applies to any instance that SIP peers could reach before it was upgraded.

vulnerability06 Nov 03:42Zmulti-sourceOpen finding →
Sources: SignalWire / FreeSWITCH (GitHub security advisory GHSA-mg63-h38w-8p9p) · BSI CERT-Bund (WID-SEC-2026-4364) · SignalWire (FreeSWITCH v1.11.3 release notes) · CISA
NOTABLECVE-2026-123158exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-123158, OpenSSH Portable before 10.6p2 (*sshole): on Linux with musl libc and no PAM, a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes logs in to accounts whose password field is *; NCSC Switzerland issued an advisory (CVSS 3.1 8.1)

Portable OpenSSH 10.6p2 carries what its release notes call a critical security workaround for Linux systems that use the musl libc with PAM disabled (OpenSSH, 2026-11-05). OX Security explains the mechanism: musl's crypt() refuses inputs over 256 bytes and returns the string *, * is also what /etc/shadow holds for an account with no valid password, and OpenSSH reads the two matching values as a successful login; the conditions are sshd on musl without PAM, password logins enabled, an account whose password field is * and at least one other account with a real password, and OX scores the flaw CVSS 3.1 8.1 (OX Security, 2026-11-05). On Alpine's tiny-cloud images the passwordless alpine user can run doas without a password, so the bypass chains to root (OX Security, 2026-11-05), but Alpine says those images are safe on first boot and become exploitable as soon as any $6$ hash exists on the machine (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-05).

CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09 on evidence of active exploitation, and describes no victim or behavior (CISA, 2026-11-09). GreyNoise says its first successful exploitation came on 2026-11-07 against one of its vulnerable gridpoints and calls the flaw trivial to exploit (GreyNoise, 2026-11-10). Alpine pushed the fix to every branch back to 3.16 (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-05), and NCSC Switzerland adds that other software using similar authentication paths may also be affected (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05). watchTowr saw botnet and cryptomining use, and GreyNoise says its 16 successful chains are not representative of the broader activity (BleepingComputer, 2026-11-09).

Exposure
Sshd on a musl-based Linux system built without PAM, such as Alpine, OpenWrt and the other musl distributions NCSC Switzerland lists, with password logins enabled (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05) and, per OX Security, an account whose /etc/shadow password field is * (OX Security, 2026-11-05). Containers that do not run an OpenSSH server are not affected (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-05).
Detection
Alpine advises looking in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password (alpine, root or any key-only user) and treating the machine as compromised if a login cannot be ruled out (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-05). GreyNoise's gridpoint sessions show what follows a successful login: sshd-session spawning sh -c that runs id, uname and reads /etc/os-release, requests to the AWS, Azure and Alibaba Cloud metadata services, attempts to read root's SSH keys and /etc/shadow through doas, a new key written into the default alpine user's authorized_keys (GreyNoise, 2026-11-10).

Triage: an accepted password login is normal for an account with a real hash; the same event for an account whose password field is * has no benign explanation, because such an account cannot match any password.

Defender takeaway
Install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or the distribution's fixed package on every musl-based host that runs sshd and restart sshd, because updating the package alone does not replace the SSH server that is already running, and rebuild container and cloud images from a fixed base (OX Security, 2026-11-05); until then set PasswordAuthentication no and restart sshd, as NCSC Switzerland advises (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05). Patching does not remove a key or service planted before it, so review the accepted password logins, the authorized_keys files of root and the default user and the init services on every musl host that allowed password logins before patching.
Update07 Nov 2026 03:52 UTCrun 2026-11-07T0256Z-intelsummarytagscvesevidencesourcessourcing_notebody

Previdian's page for CVE-2026-123158, as read on 2026-11-07, says its sensors observed 15 exploitation attempts from 10 addresses in 8 countries, first on 2026-11-06 and last on 2026-11-07, a live counter, and that these observations do not show that a target was vulnerable or that an attempt succeeded, and its timeline lists public proof-of-concept code from 2026-11-05 17:30 UTC (Previdian, 2026-11-05). The Hacker News, quoting a statement from Previdian's chief executive, reports that Previdian confirmed successful root access on a honeypot running Alpine Linux and OpenSSH, where the attacker used oversized passwords to bypass authentication and ran the reconnaissance commands id, uname and hostname in non-interactive SSH sessions, and that the first attempt came less than nine hours after the CVE was published (The Hacker News, 2026-11-06); the honeypot detail is not on Previdian's page, and the article's own total, eight attempts from one address geolocated to Japan, differs from the page's totals. Previdian's page lists the flaw as not in CISA's catalog (Previdian, 2026-11-05).

Alpine's advisory adds that updating the package does not restart a running sshd, so sshd must be restarted, and that on exposed machines the administrator should review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys, treating the machine as compromised if a login cannot be ruled out (Alpine Linux, 2026-11-05). No vendor or authority source reports attacks on production systems.

Improvement09 Nov 2026 03:25 UTCrun 2026-11-09T0255Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_notesummarybody

SANS Internet Storm Center's Cowrie SSH honeypots independently record the attempts: ISC dates the first genuine sshole attempt to 2026-11-05, with an all-"A" password, from scanners it lists on commercial hosting and telecom networks, and counts long-password attempts at 232 on 2026-11-05, 713 on 11-06, 246 on 11-07 and 51 on 11-08 (the day the page was published) (SANS ISC, 2026-11-08). The honeypots collect only the first 255 characters of a password, which limits what ISC sees; after listing the first scanners, its author expects that quite a few of those login attempts succeeded on its honeypots and promises a follow-up (SANS ISC, 2026-11-08). Two sensor sets, ISC's from 2026-11-05 and Previdian's from 2026-11-06, now record exploitation attempts; Previdian's page, read again on 2026-11-09, shows 20 attempts from 13 addresses in 9 countries, the last on 2026-11-08 (Previdian, 2026-11-05). No source reports a compromised production host.

Update10 Nov 2026 03:36 UTCrun 2026-11-10T0255Z-intelheadlinesummarytagstechniquescvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

CISA added CVE-2026-123158 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-09 on evidence of active exploitation, without describing a victim or the behavior (CISA, 2026-11-09); the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security repeats the listing (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-11-09). NCSC Switzerland's advisory, last edited on 2026-11-06, still rates the exploitation status unknown (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-11-05). GreyNoise, which holds the telemetry, says its first successful exploitation came on 2026-11-07 at 00:46 UTC against one of its vulnerable gridpoints, and the sessions it records there show reconnaissance, attempts to read root's SSH keys and /etc/shadow through doas, a new key written into authorized_keys, and in some sessions a Python runtime installed with apk and an init-script service for a Python agent that polls an HTTPS server every 150 seconds; on the host it describes, the agent never enrolled and never received a task (GreyNoise, 2026-11-10). GreyNoise's confirmed successes are on its own gridpoints, and no source reports a compromised production host.

03Research, reports & policy1 item

NOTABLENATOB2

Microsoft Email Threat Landscape Q3 2026: tenant and user overrides delivered spoofed business-service mail that failed authentication, SVG attachments return as CAPTCHA-phishing carriers, and Teams impersonators move to ordinary personal names

Microsoft Threat Intelligence's report on Q3 2026 draws four points that matter to a Microsoft 365 defender (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). First, malicious messages that spoof the sender domains of business services, such as document-signing and survey platforms, were often delivered because tenant- or user-level overrides applied, even after the messages failed email authentication and were identified as malicious: in September overrides applied to 63% of messages with a recorded security outcome, most of them tenant-level (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). Microsoft says the figures do not show that recipients opened the messages and that an overly broad exception made for a legitimate workflow can weaken protection against messages impersonating it (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Second, CAPTCHA-gated phishing recovered while QR-code phishing kept falling, with SVG attachments central to the recovery: they carried 65% of CAPTCHA-gated attacks in August and 49% in September (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). Third, in Teams, ordinary personal-name display names rose from 46% of the observed July sample to 88% in September while explicit help-desk identities fell from 17% to 2%; Microsoft notes a personal name can accompany a help-desk claim while the account address keeps technical wording, and that more targeted attempts used domains resembling the victim organisation's (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05). Fourth, an August campaign against legal organisations sent a Word document with a personalised QR code that led to a device-code phishing page and the genuine Microsoft device sign-in portal; completing the sign-in would have transferred a valid session token that gave persistent access without exposing the password or re-triggering MFA (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Exposure
A Microsoft 365 tenant that has tenant- or user-level allow or override entries covering the sender domains of widely used business services, since a message that fails authentication and is detected as malicious can still be delivered when such an override applies.
Detection
In mail-flow and message-trace telemetry, delivered messages that claim a business service's domain but fail SPF, DKIM and DMARC, together with the override that applied; in mail-gateway logs, SVG attachments that lead to a CAPTCHA page; in Teams audit, first-contact chats and calls from external tenants whose display name is a personal name but whose account address carries help-desk or service wording; in sign-in logs, device-code flow sign-ins.
Defender takeaway
Review the tenant and user overrides in your mail protection for entries that cover well-known service sender domains, because the override, not the detection, decided delivery; Microsoft's own advice is to check its recommended settings for Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365 (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-11-05).

Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controllers compromised in France, six more European countries and Switzerland, with France blaming the IRGC unit Shahid Kaveh for the October campaign; Midnight Blue reports six unpatched pre-authentication flaws in AK-SM 800A firmware up to 5.3.2

First published 2026-10-13 · open finding →

Update06 Nov 2026 03:44 UTCrun 2026-11-06T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

SRF reported on 2026-11-05 the first publicly known cases of the refrigeration attacks in Switzerland, a butcher in Köniz whose freezer reached 50 to 70 degrees and three Volg stores with changed cooling parameters; BACS has received one reportable notification about an attack on commercial refrigeration, and CISA, FBI, HHS, USDA and DOT published a joint fact sheet on refrigeration and cold-chain controllers that names no vendor, CVE or actor. No source names the controller make or the access route in the Swiss cases.

SRF reported on 2026-11-05 the first publicly known attack of this kind in Switzerland: the butcher Lüthis Fleischwaren in Köniz, canton Bern, told customers that manipulation of the electronic control of its cooling and freezer systems caused considerable temperature deviations, the owner told SRF he found 50 to 70 degrees in the freezer, and the firm disconnected the installation from the network and closed the branch (translated from German) (SRF, 2026-11-05). Keystone-SDA adds that the shop can probably only reopen on 20 November and that the Bern cantonal police were briefly informed on Monday and had received no complaint yet (Keystone-SDA via swissinfo.ch, 2026-11-05). Volg says three of its stores noticed that parameters in the cooling shelves had been changed (SRF, 2026-11-05). No source names the controller make, the access route or a maintenance provider in the Swiss cases; Keystone-SDA notes that operators can supervise cooling plants centrally over the internet and that the butcher apparently has such an installation, which is the agency's inference and not the owner's statement (Keystone-SDA via swissinfo.ch, 2026-11-05). BACS told Keystone-SDA that it does not comment on specific incidents and has received one reportable notification about a cyberattack on commercial refrigeration so far, and it stressed that voluntary reports are welcome at any time (Keystone-SDA via swissinfo.ch, 2026-11-05). Blutspende SRK Schweiz told Keystone-SDA that no attacks on Swiss blood-donation services are known to date (SRF, 2026-11-05).

On the same day CISA, the FBI, HHS, USDA and DOT published a joint fact sheet on malicious cyber activity against industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide: the actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, through authentication bypass, arbitrary code injection or weak configurations, with loss of visibility into current temperatures as a further effect (CISA, 2026-11-05). It names no vendor, CVE, victim or actor; its mitigations include keeping controller panels off the internet, allowlisting the devices and IP addresses that may change settings, defining reasonable setpoint limits for downstream devices with alerting on deviations, and collecting network traffic between OT assets where logs are not available (CISA, 2026-11-05).

HIGHCVE-2026-116606 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-116606 / CVE-2026-111560, Barracuda Email Security Gateway: an unauthenticated configuration-import bypass chained with a root command injection, with watchTowr's detection tool public since 2026-11-03 and its full chain since 2026-11-05; patches are out, Barracuda reports exploitation against a small number of organizations and CISA lists both flaws as exploited (CVSS 9.3 and 8.6)

First published 2026-11-04 · open finding →

Update06 Nov 2026 03:41 UTCrun 2026-11-06T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryprioritytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

watchTowr Labs published the full chain on 2026-11-05 and a detection tool: one unauthenticated request to the Email Security Gateway's login handler reaches the backup-restore function, a secret that is hard-coded in the product lets an attacker build a valid archive, and the restored timezone value reaches the root command injection, so exploitation needs no account; Barracuda changed its own advisory the same day to say authentication is not required for CVE-2026-116606. No source reports attacks.

watchTowr Labs published the full chain on 2026-11-05 after comparing firmware 9.4.0.027 with 9.4.0.029 (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). In the login handler a failed password-change attempt returns the login-screen role instead of ending the request, so one unauthenticated POST to /cgi-mod/index.cgi that submits mismatching new and retyped passwords with a backup upload reaches the backup-restore function (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). The restore accepts a backup whose checksum matches, and the checksum is built from the file bytes and a secret that is hard-coded in the product, so an attacker can build a valid archive (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). A restored system_timezone value then reaches an unescaped shell call that runs as root (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). watchTowr shares a Detection Artefact Generator so that owners can test their own appliances, and its post does not claim exploitation in the wild (watchTowr Labs, 2026-11-05). Its README describes a tool that takes a target URL and a command, builds a backup, uploads it to the target and attempts to check whether the target is vulnerable (watchTowr Labs README, 2026-11-03).

Barracuda changed its advisory the same day, 2026-11-05 at 2:30pm EST: the Authentication Required field for CVE-2026-116606 now reads No (Administrative UI Access Required), and the advisory says authentication is not required to exploit it but the administrative user interface must be accessible to the attacker (Barracuda, 2026-11-05). The advisory's entry for CVE-2026-111560 still reads Yes (Administrative Access) (Barracuda, 2026-11-05).

Sources: Barracuda Trust Center · Barracuda Campus · Mandiant (CVE-2026-116606 disclosure) · Mandiant (CVE-2026-111560 disclosure) · NCSC Switzerland (Security Hub post 13144) · watchTowr Labs · watchTowr Labs (GitHub README) · Barracuda Trust Center (advisory update of 2026-11-09) · Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (AV26-1112, Update 1) · CISA · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog

05Action items6 items

  • In every Entra tenant you run or manage for others, list the app registrations that hold client secrets, starting with multitenant, delegated-admin (GDAP) and Partner Center apps, security-tool integration apps and Azure DevOps service connections, and search the service-principal and non-interactive sign-in logs for the invalid-secret or expired-secret errors AADSTS7000215 and AADSTS7000222 followed by a success for the same app; on any hit remove all client secrets, certificates and federated credentials on that app, including ones you did not add, disable its service principal if needed and rotate everything stored in any Key Vault it could read, because issued tokens stay valid until they expire.
    FindingEntra app-credential abuse: agents hunt GitHub for…→
  • Restrict the administrative interface of every Barracuda Email Security Gateway, Load Balancer ADC, Message Archiver, WAF Control Center, Web Application Firewall and Web Security Gateway to trusted internal networks now, update every Email Security Gateway to firmware 9.4.0.029 or later, the build Barracuda names (the CVE record lists builds before 9.4.0.030 as affected), and apply Barracuda's patch to each of the other products (BNADC-16586 for the Load Balancer ADC and the Web Application Firewall, BNMA-32468, BNWF-60060, BNYF-24789), confirming that automatic patching is on.
    FindingCVE-2026-116606 +1→
  • On every Email Security Gateway whose interface was reachable before the patch, check its configuration for a restore nobody made and its timezone setting for anything other than a timezone name, because watchTowr's single unauthenticated request can reach both and CISA lists both flaws as exploited and requires forensic triage.
    FindingCVE-2026-116606 +1→
  • Upgrade every FreeSWITCH to 1.11.3, or until then set enable-chat=false on every SIP profile that does not need inbound SIP chat and remove directory users that have no password; on an instance that SIP peers could reach, rotate the SIP trunk and directory credentials stored in its configuration, because the advisory lists disclosure of configuration and credentials as an impact, the vendor says exploitation has been observed and CISA lists the flaw as exploited.
    FindingCVE-2026-116779→
  • On every musl-based Linux host that runs sshd (Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto), install OpenSSH 10.6p2 or the distribution's fixed openssh package and restart sshd, because updating the package does not replace the running server, and rebuild container and cloud images from a fixed base; until then set PasswordAuthentication no in sshd_config and restart sshd.
    FindingCVE-2026-123158→
  • On each such host that allowed password logins while reachable, search the sshd log for an accepted password on an account whose password field is *, and check root's and the default alpine user's authorized_keys for keys nobody added and the init scripts for a service nobody installed, because CISA lists the flaw as exploited and GreyNoise saw both persistence steps.
    FindingCVE-2026-123158→

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-11-05
item.description:
• Vaud: device-code phishing against Microsoft 365 is running in Romandie; several organisations already affected. The canton of Vaud said on 2026-11-04 that a Microsoft 365 device-code phishing campaign is running in French-speaking Switzerland and that several organisations are already affected: mail that appears to come from a company or a known contact leads the reader to type a code on a genuine Microsoft sign-in page, which gives the attacker access to the account. Microsoft documents a Conditional Access policy that blocks the device code flow for tenants that do not need it. →
  • APT29-linked watering hole uses n-day iOS and Chrome chains; CISA lists CVE-2024-27834; updated devices resist. Sekoia reports a watering-hole campaign it assesses with moderate to high confidence to be APT29 or a subgroup, serving platform-specific exploit chains for iOS 16.7, a DarkSword-based iOS chain and Chrome 139 to 145 on Android through injected sites, clone domains and a one-week compromise of the Plerdy analytics script; Sekoia says none of the chains works against fully updated devices. CISA added the Apple WebKit pointer-authentication bypass CVE-2024-27834, the second step of the iOS 16.7 chain and fixed in May 2024, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-04; no Swiss victim is named. →
  • SEPPmail gateway: unauthenticated sender reaches root RCE or file access; fixed in 15.1.1, 15.0.x has no fix. SEPPmail's patch release 15.1.1 of 2026-11-03 fixes five flaws in the Secure Email Gateway, with NCSC.ch as the CNA: CVE-2026-114424 lets an unauthenticated remote sender run operating-system commands as root through an active address-replacement rule that uses message-derived data, and CVE-2026-114425 lets one disclose, move or delete files as root when Large File Transfer is enabled (both CVSS 4.0 9.2). The vendor says 15.0.7 was the last 15.0 release, so 15.0.x gateways must move to the 15.1 branch; no source reports exploitation. →

Active threats, incidents & disclosures 3Trending vulnerabilities 2Research, reports & policy 1Updates to prior coverage 5Action items 12

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures3 items

HIGHNATOA2

Canton Vaud warns of a device-code phishing campaign against Microsoft 365 accounts running in French-speaking Switzerland, with several organisations already affected

The canton of Vaud said on 2026-11-04 that a phishing campaign is currently running in French-speaking Switzerland and that several organisations have already been affected (translated from French) (Canton of Vaud, 2026-11-04). The messages can appear to come from a company or a known contact and invite the reader to view an invoice, open a document or verify information through a link; the campaign uses device-code phishing, which gets the victim to type a code on a genuine Microsoft authentication page and so gives the attackers fraudulent access to the Microsoft 365 account (Canton of Vaud, 2026-11-04). The links printed in the notice combine a company-style name and a portal word on a workers.dev subdomain whose second label starts with a cloud-storage word and an identifier, and the canton says other addresses can be used too (Canton of Vaud, 2026-11-04); workers.dev is the route assigned to every Cloudflare Worker (Cloudflare Docs, 2026-09-22). The notice names no actor, kit, count of organisations, sector or start date.

Exposure
Any Microsoft 365 tenant whose users can complete the device code flow, which Microsoft describes as meant for devices without local input such as shared devices or digital signage and as a high-risk method that phishing can use (Microsoft Learn, 2026-03-24).
Detection
Mail, web proxy and DNS telemetry for links to workers.dev subdomains of the structure above; in the Entra sign-in logs, device code events found with the authentication protocol filter (Microsoft Learn, 2026-03-24). Microsoft says protocol tracking persists through token refreshes, so later sign-ins in the same session can fall under an authentication-flows policy, and it records an original transfer method property in the activity details of the Conditional Access sign-in logs (Microsoft Learn, 2026-03-24).

Triage: Microsoft documents device code sign-in for shared devices and signage; a device-code sign-in by a user who has no such device, soon after that user received a mailed link, falls outside that use (Microsoft Learn, 2026-03-24).

Defender takeaway
Where the tenant has no documented need for device code flow, Microsoft recommends blocking it with a Conditional Access policy, testing in report-only mode and auditing existing use first (Microsoft Learn, 2026-04-07). Tell users never to enter a Microsoft login code at a third party's request, and that anyone who has entered a code or validated an authentication request must call IT support at once, which is the canton's own instruction (Canton of Vaud, 2026-11-04).

Sekoia: an APT29-linked watering hole serves n-day iOS and Android exploit chains through compromised sites, clone domains and a one-week compromise of the Plerdy tracker; CISA lists the Apple WebKit pointer-authentication bypass CVE-2024-27834 as exploited on 2026-11-04

CISA added CVE-2024-27834, a WebKit flaw that lets an attacker with arbitrary read and write capability bypass Pointer Authentication and that Apple fixed on 2024-05-13, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-11-04, and names no victim or method (CISA KEV, 2026-11-04; Apple, 2024-05-13; Apple, 2024-05-13). The same day Sekoia reported a watering-hole campaign that it assesses with moderate to high confidence to be APT29 or one of its subgroups and in which that flaw is the pointer-authentication bypass of an iOS chain (Sekoia, 2026-11-04); the link between the listing and the campaign is the date alone. Sekoia retrieved three chains from the delivery host, which profiles the visitor and serves a platform-specific exploit without user interaction: an iOS 16.7 chain (CVE-2025-43529, then CVE-2024-27834) that steals the cookies of running apps; a DarkSword-based iOS chain that Sekoia's table labels iOS 18.5 (CVE-2025-43529 with CVE-2026-20700, then CVE-2025-14174 with CVE-2025-43510, then CVE-2025-43520) that harvests the phone; and an Android chain for Chrome 139 to 145 except 143 (CVE-2026-3910, then the Adreno driver flaw CVE-2025-27038) that takes Chrome cookies, saved logins, history and Wi-Fi configuration (Sekoia, 2026-11-04). The payloads exfiltrate data without establishing persistence, and Sekoia says none of the chains contains a zero-day or works against fully updated devices (Sekoia, 2026-11-04).

Delivery used JavaScript injected into legitimate sites, among them a Ukrainian gas producer, a US chemical-industry trade association, a Bulgarian military-related site and an Australian clinic; reverse-proxy clones of high-profile sites; and a one-week compromise, 27 August to 3 September 2026, of the Plerdy SEO tracker script, which Sekoia says exposed hundreds or thousands of sites, mostly Ukrainian (Sekoia, 2026-11-04). Sekoia names no Swiss victim, counts no infected devices and says it is working with national CERTs on victim identification.

Exposure
IPhones and iPads below the builds that fix the six iOS flaws, and Android phones on Chrome before the fix of CVE-2026-3910 or an unpatched Adreno driver. Sekoia's iOS 16.7 chain filters for iOS 16.7 and 16.7.10, and the sources do not establish whether the later 16.7.x builds Apple lists for iPhone 8, 8 Plus, X, iPad 5th generation and the first-generation iPad Pro models, up to 16.7.16 of 2026-05-11, are exploitable (Sekoia, 2026-11-04; Apple, 2026-05-11).

Fixes: iOS 26.2 and 18.7.3 close CVE-2025-43529 and CVE-2025-14174, iOS 26.1 and 18.7.2 close CVE-2025-43510 and CVE-2025-43520, iOS 26.3 closes CVE-2026-20700, and Chrome 146 closes CVE-2026-3910 (Apple, 2025-12-12; Google Threat Intelligence Group, 2026-03-18; Chrome Releases, 2026-03-12).

Detection
Sekoia names one on-device trace, a marker cookie that the iOS 16.7 chain's script sets as a replay guard so the exploit does not fire twice on a victim; it publishes some indicators and withholds several delivery and exfiltration hosts, so a visit to an injected site shows in web proxy and DNS telemetry from managed phones only against indicators obtained from Sekoia or a national CERT; the dependable check is the OS and Chrome version inventory (Sekoia, 2026-11-04).
Defender takeaway
Bring managed iOS devices to the newest release for each model and Android phones to current Chrome and the OEM patch level, because Sekoia says updated devices resist these chains and CISA lists every flaw they deliver as exploited (Sekoia, 2026-11-04; CISA KEV, 2026-11-04); the devices that cannot go past iOS 16.7.x are the open question.

Sophos's own root-cause analysis of a developer-targeted intrusion: a fake job-interview repository's VS Code workspace settings ran BeaverTail and InvisibleFerret on a Mac whose endpoint agent had not reported since 11 June, and a third-party OAuth authorization outlived the session revocation

On 2026-09-14 a Sophos employee cloned a public repository presented as a job-interview coding assignment and opened it as a workspace in VS Code; a weaponized workspace settings file replaced the editor's integrated terminal profile with a command that downloads and runs a remote script in a loop, delivery relied on the user opening the workspace as trusted, and no exploit or vulnerability was involved (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20). Opening a terminal was enough: a shell script fetched a JavaScript component and a package manifest into a hidden directory in the user profile, a package-manager install ran, the JavaScript ran under Node.js and the final-stage backdoor lived in memory only, with no persistence found (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20). SophosLabs identified the BeaverTail loader followed by the InvisibleFerret backdoor, able to steal browser-stored credentials, keychain data and SSH keys, and the JavaScript stage sent the process environment to an attacker web endpoint on a cloud application-hosting service (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20).

Two gaps lengthened the exposure. The Sophos Endpoint agent was installed but its core services were not running, so it enforced nothing and reported nothing; the device was last seen in Sophos Central on 2026-06-11, the cause is still under investigation, and SophosLabs says a working agent would have blocked the chain at the first dropped file (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20). A third-party application authorization on the employee's source-code platform account survived the session revocation and password reset of 2026-09-15 and made 27 read requests against two internal repositories from an address new to the user until it was revoked on 2026-09-16; Sophos found no other host, no cloud activity and no customer impact (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20). The analysis names no group; Sophos CTU says the technique matches the tradecraft of NICKEL ALLEY, which it describes as running the Contagious Interview campaign of fake companies, fake recruiters and malicious code repositories (Sophos blog, 2026-11-04).

Exposure
Developer workstations whose users clone and open repositories from outside parties, recruitment pretexts included, in an editor that trusts the workspace; and any managed device that is compliant in identity and device management but does not report to the endpoint console, as Sophos's fleet review found (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20).
Detection
In macOS process lineage, the code editor's integrated terminal launching a download-and-run command that a cloned workspace's settings define, followed by a hidden directory in the user profile and a package-manager install run from it (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20). In identity telemetry, a device that still signs in but does not report to the endpoint console is a coverage gap; a third-party authorization reading repositories from an address new to the user is the second signal (Sophos blog, 2026-11-04; Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20).

Triage: a terminal profile normally launches a shell executable; this one launched a command that downloads and runs a remote script in a loop; it came from the settings of a freshly cloned repository (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20).

Defender takeaway
Treat a coding assignment or repository from a recruiter or interviewer as untrusted code, because here the compromise needed only a trusted workspace and an opened terminal. Sophos's lasting controls are to require the endpoint agent for device compliance, to monitor for managed devices that stop reporting, and to revoke application authorizations as part of credential containment, not only sessions and passwords (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20).

Sophos's root-cause analysis INC-2026-002 carries the dateline 20 October 2026 (Sophos RCA, 2026-10-20); 4 November 2026 is the date of the Sophos blog post that links to it. The facts drawn from the analysis are unchanged.

CVE-2026-114424 and CVE-2026-114425, SEPPmail Secure Email Gateway before 15.1.1: an unauthenticated mail sender can reach root command execution through a replacement rule and root file access through Large File Transfer, with three more flaws fixed in the same release and no fix for the 15.0 branch (CVSS 4.0 9.2)

SEPPmail's revision history lists patch release 15.1.1 of 2026-11-03 with five security fixes in the Secure Email Gateway, all for versions before 15.1.1 (SEPPmail, 2026-11-03). Two are unauthenticated and rated 9.2: in CVE-2026-114424 attacker-influenced replacement text in sender or recipient address-replacement rules is evaluated as Perl code, so a remote sender can run operating-system commands in the mail-processing worker when an active rule uses message-derived replacement data and its search condition matches, and the validated worker context was root (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04); in CVE-2026-114425 a file path supplied in the attachment metadata of an incoming message lets the worker disclose, move or delete an accessible file when Large File Transfer is enabled, also as root (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04). CVE-2026-114426 lets an unauthenticated attacker exhaust workers and disk because the upload interface processed data before checking authentication (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04), and two flaws in the GINA webmail let an unauthenticated attacker take over a created but unregistered account with an empty initial password (CVE-2026-114421) and enumerate email addresses through an unescaped LDAP filter (CVE-2026-114420) (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04; ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04). The vendor says 15.0.7 of 2026-09-02 is the last release of the 15.0 branch, so the fix for a 15.0.x gateway is the move to 15.1 (SEPPmail, 2026-11-03). None of the sources read reports exploitation.

Exposure
A SEPPmail Secure Email Gateway before 15.1.1; the Home page of the administration interface shows the running version in the System section as "Firmware version" (SEPPmail, retrieved 2026-11-05). CVE-2026-114424 applies where an active rule uses message-derived replacement data, and CVE-2026-114425 where Large File Transfer is enabled (ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04; ENISA EUVD, 2026-11-04).
Detection
No source publishes an indicator. What the mechanism implies, not stated by a source: a child process or shell started by the mail-processing worker after inbound mail whose sender or recipient strings reach a replacement rule, and file operations by the Large File Transfer worker outside its storage area, both running as root.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade to 15.1.1, moving 15.0.x gateways to the 15.1 branch because 15.0 gets no fix, and until then review which active replacement rules use values taken from the message and whether Large File Transfer is enabled, the two conditions the CNA names (SEPPmail, 2026-11-03). Because the worker runs as root, a gateway that was exposed with such a rule or with Large File Transfer enabled warrants a compromise check.

NOTABLENATOB2

SpecterOps: a Windows iSCSI Target Server set up without CHAP lets any host that knows the target and an authorised initiator name read the shared disks below file permissions, a Hyper-V domain controller's among them

SpecterOps shows that the Windows iSCSI Target Server role, set up as a community cluster guide describes it with the optional CHAP step skipped, accepts a login from any host that knows the target host, the target name and an authorised initiator name (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04). The post says the role registers a service principal name on its computer account, so a directory query lists the target hosts, that initiator names are built from the host's DNS name and are therefore predictable, and that in the author's experience the service has no rate limiting or brute-force protection (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04). Access is below the file system, so NTFS permissions do not apply, and volume encryption such as BitLocker defeats it (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04). The worst case the post shows is a volume that holds a Hyper-V domain controller's virtual disk, from which the local credential stores and the directory database can be taken (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04). The author has not tested the technique in production and warns that it can cause outages, and the post cites no Microsoft response.

Exposure
Windows Server hosts that run the iSCSI Target Server role without CHAP, found by the service principal name the role registers and by a listener on TCP 3260 (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04; Pen Test Partners, 2016-05-18). The author's own research puts the common uses with clustered resources such as Hyper-V, SQL Server and Exchange database availability groups, followed by third-party backup products (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04).
Detection
The post names no telemetry. What the mechanism implies, not stated by the post: iSCSI traffic to TCP 3260 on a target host from a source that is not one of its cluster nodes, and a login that presents a listed initiator name from another source address, because the access list keys on initiator names that an impersonator can present (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04).
Defender takeaway
Enable CHAP on every iSCSI target, and isolate iSCSI traffic with segmentation and host-based firewalling, which the post calls arguably the most effective step; the post says IPsec mitigates network sniffing, and BitLocker or similar volume encryption makes the stolen disk unreadable (SpecterOps, 2026-11-04). Treat the disks of any domain controller that sat on an unprotected target as exposed.
