LiteLLM 1.107.0: the PyPI wheels and the official Docker images carried a credential stealer and a dormant remote-code loader that Python starts at every launch, published through the maintainers' own release workflow with stolen developer tokens

Socket reports that LiteLLM 1.107.0, an open-source LLM gateway, carries malicious Python startup files in all seven wheels, and that Upwind found the same payload in the published images (Socket, 2026-10-21). A startup hook and a second startup module in the Python library directory run at every Python start without the application importing LiteLLM: the first collects cloud, Kubernetes, CI, registry and database credentials, SSH, GPG and TLS private keys, browser stores, AI-tool credential files, environment variables and, where configured, the credentials saved in a LiteLLM proxy database; the second forks a detached loader that polls a file in a GitHub repository for a domain and would execute Python downloaded from it with no signature or hash check, though at 13:01 UTC the pointer returned an empty body, which stops the loader before its download stage (Socket, 2026-10-21).

The payload is not in the git tag: a packaging setting in an untagged commit pulls it into the wheel, and the container build provenance records a source repository named Berri-AI/litellm, one hyphen away from BerriAI/litellm (Socket, 2026-10-21). The maintainers' root-cause post of 2026-10-23 traces the chain to a configuration file committed on 2026-05-27 to a public repository with the administrative key of an experimental internal agent service; a follow-up commit deleted the file about three hours later, but the original commit stayed in the repository's public history until 2026-10-22 and the key was never revoked (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). On 2026-10-10 the attacker used that key against the service's API, which returned the GitHub CLI OAuth token of an organization owner, not a service account and not scoped down, and from then on the attacker held owner-level access to every repository; such CLI tokens are post-2FA and exempt from GitHub's re-authentication for sensitive actions (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). With it the attacker pushed throwaway branches whose workflows posted CI secrets to an external capture endpoint, yielding the CLI tokens of two maintainers, and deleted the workflow runs minutes later (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). Socket found secret-exfiltration workflows running in the repository on 2026-10-10 from its Actions performance metrics, eleven days before the release attack, says it has not established how the attacker first obtained access and does not claim that the 2026-10-10 theft produced the access used on 2026-10-21, while LiteLLM says its audit logs tie the token stolen on 2026-10-10 to the approval of the release (Socket, 2026-10-23). On 2026-10-21 a push to the private release-orchestration repository with a maintainer's token was rejected by branch protection, and the owner's token then overrode it so that the build could be pointed at the look-alike repository; the owner's token dispatched the staging build, a second maintainer's token approved the production gate, a third maintainer's token deleted the run records, and the owner's token force-pushed the history clean, after the maintainers had relaxed the release rule earlier that week so that any two engineers could trigger and approve a release (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). PyPI quarantined 1.107.0 and the images were pulled the same day (Aikido, 2026-10-21; LiteLLM, 2026-10-21).

Exposure
An environment that installed litellm 1.107.0 from PyPI between 11:39 and 13:23 UTC on 2026-10-21, or pulled the v1.107.0, latest, main-latest or main-stable tag of the official images from GHCR (until about 13:51 UTC) or Docker Hub (until 14:20 UTC); lockfiles, caches, build logs and running image digests show which (Socket, 2026-10-21; LiteLLM, 2026-10-21).
Detection
In the cloud audit logs of every account the host could reach, a caller-identity check followed by a Bedrock model listing and IAM enumeration, made with an instance-role credential harvested from CI runners or Kubernetes nodes from an address outside your estate, which Wiz saw from 16:20 UTC on 2026-10-21 (Wiz, 2026-10-21); on hosts, startup hooks and sitecustomize modules in a Python library directory that your tooling did not install, a detached Python process holding a lock file, and an encrypted archive posted to a path labelled as a health check (Socket, 2026-10-21). In the GitHub organization audit log, short-lived throwaway branches that add a single workflow file, workflow runs deleted minutes after they ran, and branch-protection and force-push-block overrides made with an owner's token; the log records a hash of the token behind each action, which tied the stolen maintainer token to the release approval (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). Starting Python or pip in an affected environment can run the payload again, and removing the package directory does not remove the startup files or stop a running loader (Socket, 2026-10-21).
Defender takeaway
Rotate every credential the host could reach (LiteLLM, 2026-10-21), because removing the package does not remove the startup files (Socket, 2026-10-21) and stolen cloud credentials were in use within hours (Wiz, 2026-10-21); rebuild from a reviewed release and pin container digests (Socket, 2026-10-21), and move to 1.106.2 or an explicit earlier version as the maintainers advise (LiteLLM, 2026-10-21). For your own pipelines, the root cause was a key whose file was deleted from a public repository while the commit stayed in its history and the key was never revoked, and an organization owner's CLI token held by an automation service; the maintainers call it an illustration of the risk of failing to rotate a potentially exposed key (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23).

The maintainers published a root-cause post on 2026-10-23 that supersedes the earlier hypothesis that the tokens were read from the logs of an internet-exposed internal deployment: their request logs show the first token came from a different service, an experimental agent platform whose administrative key had been committed to a public repository on 2026-05-27 and never revoked (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). The attacker used the key on 2026-10-10 to obtain an organization owner's GitHub CLI token, so access began eleven days before the release, and the same day throwaway branches in two repositories ran workflows that posted CI secrets to an external capture endpoint and were deleted minutes later, yielding the tokens of two further maintainers (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23).

Socket found the same activity independently from the repository's Actions performance metrics, including a second run on 2026-10-12 that took 14 further secrets, and says it has not established how the attacker first obtained access (Socket, 2026-10-23). On 2026-10-21 three credentials did different jobs: the owner's token overrode branch protection and later force-pushed the history clean, a second maintainer's token approved the production gate and a third maintainer's token deleted the run records, after the maintainers had relaxed the release rule earlier that week so that any two engineers could trigger and approve a release (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23). The maintainers say they are revoking every token tied to every internal system and vendor platform, and that the attacker's activity on other systems focused on upstream inference API tokens (LiteLLM, 2026-10-23).

Microsoft Threat Intelligence's analysis of 2026-10-23 adds that endpoint observations on Windows and macOS matched the collector's discovery, encryption and outbound-connection behaviour, and that in one Windows case a routine Python invocation to install an unrelated dependency activated it, so developer workstations on Windows and macOS are in scope as well, not only gateways, CI runners and containers (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-23). Microsoft advises isolating affected hosts and investigating them from a known-clean system without running python, pip or other commands that invoke the affected interpreter, confirming that the malicious startup files are gone from the library path rather than assuming that deleting the litellm directory removed them, and it treats Python-launched OpenSSL public-key encryption of files staged in a temporary directory as a behavioural lead (Microsoft Threat Intelligence, 2026-10-23).

CVE-2026-109618 / CVE-2026-109619, Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS and Panorama: the PHP2Shell flaws affect every release below its train's hotfix through the management web interface, and Palo Alto reports active exploitation against internet-exposed management interfaces; all twenty hotfixes are out

Palo Alto Networks' advisory of 2026-10-21 lists PAN-OS 12.2, 12.1, 11.2, 11.1 and 10.2 and Panorama as affected by CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the unauthenticated PHP remote-code-execution flaws (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21) (PHP, 2026-10-21). Only the management web interface is affected; the GlobalProtect portal and gateway and the captive portal are not (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21).

The advisory says active exploitation has been observed against the management interface exposed to the internet (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-28). Dream Research reports that a custom PHP2Shell build for the PAN-OS management web server, chained with the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-46300 to turn the web server's unprivileged context into root in one unauthenticated HTTPS request, rooted 25 PAN-OS firewall and management servers in the United States, Japan, Taiwan and South Korea (Dream Research, 2026-10-29). On the second of two firewalls of a US government-affiliated organization (the first crashed) it added a reboot-persistent reverse SSH tunnel and, through it, ran the same chain against the organization's internal firewall management server, decrypted the directory service account's password from the device configuration, enumerated the Active Directory and attempted a password spray and backdoor accounts, which Dream cannot say succeeded (Dream Research, 2026-10-29). Unit 42 says it independently verified the attacker's tooling and results and that customers who applied the available patches are not affected (Unit 42, 2026-10-29); Dream relays that Unit 42 tracks it as CL-UNK-1280, a Chinese-speaking attacker in UTC+8, while Dream names none (Dream Research, 2026-10-29).

All twenty hotfixes are released (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-30); its Threat Prevention coverage (Threat IDs 543004, 97622 to 97625 and twenty further IDs between 97643 and 97678) applies only where inbound management traffic is decrypted on a dataplane interface with the certificate replaced and threat prevention enabled (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-27).

Exposure
Every PAN-OS firewall and Panorama appliance below its train's hotfix through its management web interface; it is reachable from the internet where the management port, or a dataplane interface with a management profile, answers from outside the administrator range, which Palo Alto says is what is being attacked (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-28); Dream found attacker profiles for PAN-OS 12.1, 12.2 and 11.1 only and says the web server also fronts the GlobalProtect portal, which Palo Alto's advisory says is not affected (Dream Research, 2026-10-29; Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-30).
Detection
In management-plane web access logs, very large multipart POST requests from outside the administrator range (Dream Research, 2026-10-29). A hotfix does not remove an attacker already in: on an interface that was internet-reachable and unpatched, look for a PHP file nobody deployed in a web-reachable directory of the management web server, a systemd service or rc.local entry that starts scripts from a hidden directory under /usr/local/lib, and outbound SSH from the management plane; in directory logs, bulk LDAP enumeration and password-spray bursts against all users, launched from the firewall management server (Dream Research, 2026-10-29).
Defender takeaway
Move management access behind a jump box or trusted internal addresses, as Palo Alto recommends (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-27), and install the hotfix for your maintenance line. An interface that was internet-reachable and unpatched is a possible root compromise until those checks are clean; where a web shell or tunnel turns up, rotate what the device held: the directory bind account, HA replication keys, certificate private keys and device authentication keys (Dream Research, 2026-10-29).

CVE-2026-76466, Cisco Expressway-C and Expressway-E: unauthenticated root command execution on clustered devices, fixed in X15.5.20 with no workaround (CVSS 9.8), alongside same-day hardening releases for Unified CM, Unity Connection and Snort 3

Cisco's advisory of 2026-10-21 fixes CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS 3.1 9.8, network, no privileges, no user interaction) in the database service of Expressway-C and Expressway-E, virtual and appliance: an unauthenticated remote attacker with network access can run operating-system commands as root (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). The cause is the use of persistent cookies together with insufficient validation of client certificates for clustering, even when TLS Verify Mode is enabled; an attacker who possesses the cookies connects to the database service and invokes remote procedure call commands, and Cisco does not say how an attacker obtains the cookies (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). Only devices configured in a cluster are affected; X15.5.3 and earlier are fixed in X15.5.20, X14 and earlier must migrate to a fixed release, there is no workaround, and Cisco's PSIRT is not aware of any public announcement or malicious use (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). The X15.5.20 release also carries Expressway's own hardening fixes, whose worst class scores 8.6 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).

The same day Cisco ships two further hardening releases whose worst classes are exploitable over the network without authentication. For Emergency Responder, Prime Collaboration Deployment, Unified CM, Unified CM IM&P, Unified CM SME and Unity Connection, regardless of device configuration, the worst classes score 9.8 (CVE-2026-76473, improper control of a resource through its lifetime, and CVE-2026-76474, improper authentication); release 15 is fixed in 15SU5 and release 14 must migrate (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). For Snort 3 in Secure Firewall Threat Defense, Cyber Vision, Unified Threat Defense (UTD) on IOS XE and other Snort-based products, the worst classes score 9.0 with high attack complexity (CVE-2026-20043, an out-of-bounds write, and CVE-2026-20236, an incorrect calculation); FTD is fixed in 7.0.10, 7.2.12, 7.4.8, 7.6.6, 7.7.13, 10.0.2 and 10.1.0, Snort in 3.12.4.0, Cyber Vision in 5.6.0 and UTD on IOS XE in 17.12.8, 17.15.6, 17.18.5, 26.1.2 and 26.2.1, while Meraki MX devices that are online and connected to the Dashboard and Cisco's cloud firewall services were updated automatically on 2026-10-21 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). Cisco says the flaws were found during internal security testing using existing processes as well as frontier AI models, and are not known to be actively exploited (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21; Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).

Exposure
Expressway-C and Expressway-E in a cluster on X15.5.3 or earlier, or on X14 or earlier; the affected component is the database service, and Cisco does not say on which network it listens, so an Expressway-E in a cluster is the case to check first (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21). A standalone Expressway is outside the vulnerable-product statement for CVE-2026-76466 (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21), but it still needs X15.5.20 for the hardening fixes, which Cisco lists for every Expressway-C and Expressway-E regardless of configuration (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).
Detection
Connections to the database service from hosts that are not cluster peers, and new root-owned processes started by that service; Cisco publishes no flaw-specific indicator and states no exploitation, so no post-compromise check is defined (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).
Defender takeaway
Upgrade Expressways to X15.5.20, clustered ones first, and schedule the move of X14 and earlier, Unified CM family and Unity Connection to 15SU5 (release 14 migrates), and FTD to the fixed build of its train; Cisco reports no exploitation of any of them and lists no workaround for the Expressway flaw (Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21; Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21; Cisco PSIRT, 2026-10-21).

CVE-2026-110264, GitLab CE/EE: an unauthenticated code-execution flaw in the Org-mode renderer's regular-expression handling, fixed in 19.5.1, 19.4.3 and 19.3.6 and backported to four older lines (CVSS 10.0)

GitLab's ad-hoc critical patch release of 2026-10-21 fixes CVE-2026-110264 (CVSS 3.1 10.0), an integer overflow while compiling a specially crafted regular expression that could let an unauthenticated user execute code on the GitLab server (GitLab, 2026-10-21). GitLab's detection write-ups place the flaw in the rendering of Org-mode files: the org-ruby gem builds a regular expression from a custom TODO keyword in a .org file, a keyword with more than 32,767 repeats makes the Onigmo engine write out of bounds when it matches, and with heap grooming that becomes command execution as the git user (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). The attack needs no authentication, only one public project that can hold the .org payload (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). Affected are all versions from 7.0 before 18.11.13, 19.0 before 19.0.10, 19.1 before 19.1.9, 19.2 before 19.2.9, 19.3 before 19.3.6, 19.4 before 19.4.3 and 19.5 before 19.5.1; GitLab.com is already patched, and GitLab Dedicated tenants on 19.3.5-internal0, 19.4.2-internal0 or later need no action (GitLab, 2026-10-21). The builds 19.4.2, 19.3.5 and 19.2.8 from GitLab's earlier regular-expression fixes do not contain this fix (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). GitLab does not state that the flaw is exploited, and its patch notes and detection pages mention no public proof of concept (GitLab, 2026-10-21). The bug is in Ruby's Onigmo regular-expression engine: the Ruby project released 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 on 2026-10-23 with the fix, the release of 4.0.8 lacks the fix for this flaw, and GitLab fixed its own servers by patching the Ruby it ships (Ruby, 2026-10-23).

Exposure
Self-managed GitLab CE and EE on the versions above; the vulnerable path is reached when GitLab renders a .org file, so an instance with public projects, or one where untrusted users can create them, is the exposed shape, and until patching GitLab advises reducing public visibility (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). A Ruby application outside GitLab is exposed to the same bug when it compiles a regular expression from a string an attacker controls, through Regexp.new, Regexp.union, Regexp.compile or interpolation into a regexp literal; applications that only use patterns written by their own developers are not affected (Ruby, 2026-10-23).
Detection
GitLab's two detections key on, first, five or more render timeouts from the Org-mode renderer on .org files from one client within 30 minutes in the Rails exceptions log, with the request that actually crashes a worker visible only as a 502 on the .org blob route in the Workhorse log, and second, a native Ruby crash report in the Puma error log whose backtrace runs through org-ruby or Onigmo frames (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). In repository content, scan each suspect checkout for .org files with an oversized TODO-keyword line, and in the Rails request log look for editor preview requests whose file_path ends in .org while the URL names another file type, which forces the Org renderer (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). A successful exploit is quiet and does not reliably crash, so the absence of a hit never clears an instance (GitLab security, 2026-10-21). On an exposed, unpatched instance, hunt for unexpected child processes of Puma, new files owned by git in the temporary directory, outbound connections and changed crontabs or SSH keys for the git user, and treat the secrets, CI/CD variables, runner tokens and access tokens the git user can read as at risk (GitLab security, 2026-10-21).

Triage: a reader of documentation .org files renders each file once and quickly, while an attack produces a burst of timeouts from one client over a few minutes (GitLab security, 2026-10-21); a worker crash with no accompanying render burst from one client is more likely a benign parser bug than an attack (GitLab security, 2026-10-21).

Defender takeaway
Upgrade to the fixed build of the instance's line now, internet-reachable instances and those with public projects first; an instance that moved to 19.4.2, 19.3.5 or 19.2.8 for the earlier flaws is not yet fixed for this one (GitLab, 2026-10-21). For other Ruby applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns, Ruby recommends upgrading to 4.0.9, 3.4.12 or 3.3.13 or later, or avoiding compiling such patterns, and says neither Regexp.timeout nor a pattern-length limit reliably protects; Ruby has not requested CVE identifiers of its own for now and tells operators to track the issues under GitLab's identifiers (Ruby, 2026-10-23).
Update24 Oct 2026 03:42 UTCrun 2026-10-24T0255Z-intelaffected_productsbodycvesevidencesourcessourcing_notesummaryentities

The Ruby project published an advisory on 2026-10-23 and released Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 with fixes for the bugs in its Onigmo regular-expression engine behind four GitLab flaws: CVE-2026-89078 (a double free when parsing a pattern fails after an alternation), CVE-2026-93577 and CVE-2026-97229 (an integer overflow in the size of a compiled pattern) and CVE-2026-110264 (an overflow of internal IDs in a pattern with many repeats) (Ruby, 2026-10-23). Ruby's table gives the first release of each series that carries each fix: the fix for CVE-2026-110264 first appears in 4.0.9, so 4.0.8 is not enough, and 3.4.12 and 3.3.13 carry all of them; GitLab fixed its own servers by patching the Ruby it ships (Ruby, 2026-10-23).

The advisory widens the exposure beyond GitLab to any Ruby application that compiles a regular expression from a string an attacker controls, says Regexp.timeout does not protect against these bugs and that limiting pattern length does not reliably protect, and says Ruby has not requested CVE identifiers of its own and that operators should track the issues under GitLab's identifiers (Ruby, 2026-10-23).

Update22 Oct 2026 03:47 UTCrun 2026-10-22T0256Z-intelbodyevidencesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniques

OVHcloud's postmortem traces the account compromise to a poisoned editor extension installed on a developer's personal MacBook on 2025-10-20, ties it to the GlassWorm actor through a Solana wallet, describes a stealer that reads AI-agent data stores and cloud and developer credentials and exfiltrates through Solana RPC calls, and names a missing release-immutability setting as the main issue; the malicious assets were online for 1h33 and downloaded about 250 times.

OVHcloud published its advisory and postmortem. It says the compromised account belongs to a developer who installed the editor extension color-picker-universal 2.8.91 on a personal MacBook on 2025-10-20; the extension queries a Solana wallet that OVHcloud says belongs to the GlassWorm actor, a persistent Node.js service was registered on the laptop, and several personal repositories of the account were compromised in March 2026. The release replacement was made with stolen keys, not from that laptop, and OVHcloud says neither the developer's OVHcloud laptop nor its internal CI/CD was compromised as far as it knows (OVHcloud, 2026-10-20). OpenSourceMalware reads the same account as already compromised for seven months, which is its assessment, and says that the same actor made both steps is its inference (OpenSourceMalware, 2026-10-19).

OVHcloud describes the payload as the original CLI recompiled with embedded stealer code that copies a list of credential files and AI-agent data stores into a temporary folder named envchecker, archives them and exfiltrates through Solana RPC calls and an upload endpoint; the malicious assets were online for 1h33 and downloaded about 250 times (OVHcloud, 2026-10-20). It names the missing release-immutability setting as the main issue, says it allows developers to attach personal GitHub accounts to the organisation, and reports that it enabled immutable releases on every repository, suspended the account, reviewed write access and repository logs without finding another compromise, and published v0.16.0 with a signed tag as the clean release (OVHcloud, 2026-10-20).

Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor, was responsible for the compromise, using the ARTEX agentic-AI framework to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants after an automated password spray from the same network range, and warns that credential changes planted in tenants can persist after the vendor application is remediated. Microsoft Threat Intelligence assesses that Storm-0940, a China-state aligned actor active since 2021, was responsible for the compromise. It says AI agents running the ARTEX framework kept signing in to customer tenants as the ConnectWise applications, without an interactive user sign-in, and in multiple tenants went on to Microsoft Graph reconnaissance, application credential changes and attempts to change privileges (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). It counts attempted sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants and links the activity to an automated cross-tenant password spray between 2026-10-10 and 2026-10-14 against 327 accounts at eight organizations, from the same network range and including an address that ConnectWise's advisory later listed among its indicators; the spray peaked on 2026-10-11 at 2,900 failed logons a minute and produced no successful authentication (Microsoft, 2026-10-21).

Microsoft warns that the application credential changes can remain active as a backdoor after the vendor application is remediated, and asks tenants to review service-principal sign-ins from at least 2026-10-15, and from 2026-10-01 where records exist, together with the Entra audit trail for credential additions, role assignments, consents and owner changes (Microsoft, 2026-10-21). Expel, which analysed the activity separately, relays the attribution, notes that ConnectWise's fix leaves secrets planted on other applications in place and that Graph directory reads leave no Entra audit record, and says Huntress has not tied its Global Administrator observation to the same operator (Expel, 2026-10-21). ConnectWise itself says that, based on the evidence available to it, including threat intelligence shared by Microsoft, it appears a China state-aligned group was responsible and used an openly available agentic AI framework (ConnectWise, 2026-10-21). It began restoring services in controlled phases on 2026-10-21, expects it to take several days, says the start of restoration does not mean all capabilities are available, and tells partners to keep affected connections disabled until formal instructions apply to their service, while noting that its actions do not remove unauthorized access already established in individual customer tenants (ConnectWise, 2026-10-21; heise online, 2026-10-21).

First published 2026-10-21 · open finding →

Update22 Oct 2026 03:45 UTCrun 2026-10-22T0256Z-intelactionsbodyclassificationconfidencecvesevidenceheadlineimmediate_actionpriorityregionssourcessourcing_notesummarytagstechniquestitle

The fixed releases (PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35) shipped on 2026-10-21, so the earlier no-fix status ends; Cloudflare, watchTowr and VulnCheck report attack traffic and at least one unsuccessful web-shell attempt, proofs of concept are circulating, VulnCheck holds an exploit that succeeds with ASLR enabled and no source reports a confirmed compromise, so priority moves to critical. Swiss cantons, universities, the Lodur fire-brigade platform and Publica took sites offline as a precaution, and BACS, CERT-EU and ENISA tell operators to update the runtime, check embedded installations and look for compromise.

The fixed releases shipped on 2026-10-21 between 13:30 and 14:00 UTC, depending on the source, together with the technical advisories, so the earlier statement that no fix existed no longer holds (CERT-EU, 2026-10-21; ENISA, 2026-10-21; Sansec, 2026-10-21). ENISA, the European Commission, CERT-EU, Europol EC3 and the CSIRTs network advise organisations to identify their PHP-based applications, coordinate with hosting and service providers, apply the update to internet-facing systems first, and isolate exposed applications from public networks where that is not possible (ENISA, 2026-10-21). BACS published its warning the same day, telling operators to check embedded and internal PHP installations as well as public sites, to restart long-running PHP processes and rebuild containers, to verify the running version, and, where an immediate update is impossible, to consider disconnecting critical applications from the internet (BACS, 2026-10-21). BACS told RTS it knows of no reliable, confirmed substitute for the updates and that the interim measures give no guaranteed full protection (RTS, 2026-10-21).

Attack traffic was reported on the day: Cloudflare saw it against its customers while the flaws were still leaked, watchTowr's honeypots recorded exploitation, and VulnCheck's canary hosts logged scanning from 08:37 UTC and at least one unsuccessful web-shell attempt through a session file, while VulnCheck says it holds a working exploit for CVE-2026-109618 that succeeds on x86-64 with ASLR enabled; no source reports a confirmed compromise (Cloudflare, 2026-10-21; watchTowr, 2026-10-21; VulnCheck, 2026-10-21). Palo Alto Networks confirmed that every PAN-OS and Panorama release is affected through the management web interface, with no fixed release yet (Palo Alto Networks, 2026-10-21).

Public-sector sites went offline as a precaution, mostly on the evening of 2026-10-21. The canton of Basel-Stadt activated its crisis staff and shut down every PHP-run cantonal website with no restoration time given, while stating that no security-relevant incident had been registered (Canton of Basel-Stadt, 2026-10-21). The Ticino cantonal administration temporarily disabled some online services, the website of the University of Geneva was unreachable, and the EPFL site displayed a notice that its pages were currently unreachable, although nau.ch says it still worked (nau.ch, 2026-10-21); RTS lists the EPFL and University of Geneva sites as temporarily suspended (RTS, 2026-10-21). Several Neuchâtel canton and city sites were unreachable without an official statement; Arcinfo presumes a link to the PHP flaw, which the state had not confirmed (RTS, 2026-10-21). Lodur, the platform many Swiss fire brigades use to manage their fire brigades and alarm groups, was out of service because its provider took its servers offline as a precaution: users could neither read stored data nor edit alarm groups, though the Valais cantonal fire office said this does not necessarily mean the alarm-triggering systems are down (nau.ch, 2026-10-21; RTS, 2026-10-21). Publica took its website offline on the afternoon of 2026-10-21 as a precaution, says it has closed the vulnerabilities with security updates and was back online that evening, and states the outage is unrelated to the cyberattack on its software supplier (Publica, 2026-10-21). Dutch authorities took DigiD, MijnOverheid, Overheid.nl, TweedeKamer.nl and the tax authority offline for a time, and most were back by that evening (Security.nl, 2026-10-21); RTS reports that the site of the Paris police prefecture was also suspended (RTS, 2026-10-21). Basel-Stadt said it would report on progress on the morning of 2026-10-22, and no restoration status had been published as of the early morning of 2026-10-22 UTC.

Verification & coverage notes

Window: gap 24.0 h from 2026-10-21T0256Z-intel, window 26 h, developing-story window 72 h. The container clock agreed with the network date (skew 0 s) and the first fetch of origin/main was current. A Thursday-morning fire dominated by one story: the PHP release that the previous fire had published at 11 h before it landed as "no fix yet" shipped at about 13:30 UTC on 2026-10-21, with technical advisories, attack traffic from three telemetry owners, and Swiss cantons, universities, a fire-brigade platform and Publica taking sites offline. The rest of the window is one vendor bulletin that matters (GitLab), a no-fix vendor advisory that follows from PHP (PAN-OS), Cisco's scheduled run, a supply-chain compromise (LiteLLM), two threat-research items on identity and edge-device tradecraft, and three root-cause or scope developments on covered incidents.

KEV sweep (work/2026-10-22T0256Z-intel/kev-window.txt, catalogue 2026.10.21): no KEV addition inside the window; S1 read the catalogue twice and confirmed it, and nothing carried a RANSOMWARE row. Neither PHP CVE is KEV-listed; CVE-2025-64446, CVE-2019-6693 and CVE-2026-0257 are, which the k0t entry cites.

Backlog (state/coverage_backlog.md): no open row, nothing carried or added.

Published (6 new): pan-os-panorama-php2shell-mgmt-interface-no-fixed-release (notable: no fixed release on any train, a firewall management plane, Palo Alto scores the PAN-OS impact as availability only and knows of no exploitation against its products, no action item because the management-interface restriction already stands on the CVE-2026-0322 entry; declares the PHP entry and the two earlier PAN-OS entries in references[]), cve-2026-110264-gitlab-org-mode-renderer-unauth-rce (notable: unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 path to code execution on self-managed GitLab, clears PD-11(b) through its own mechanics, GitLab ships detections and its pages state neither exploitation nor a public proof of concept), cve-2026-76466-cisco-expressway-cluster-unauth-root-rce (notable: the scheduled-release row of Cisco's 2026-10-21 run, with the Unified CM family and Snort 3 hardening releases that reach the 9.0 bar, none reported exploited), litellm-1-107-0-pypi-docker-credential-stealer-lookalike (notable: S1 and S3 returned it, merged), artex-storm-0940-agentic-llm-pentest-spraying-oauth-abuse (notable: Microsoft's attribution plus Expel's Okta self-registration observation; CrowdStrike and Recorded Future corroborate other users of the tool) and k0t-fortiweb-fortigate-globalprotect-edge-device-campaign (notable: single vendor source, declares the CVE-2026-0257 and FortiBleed entries in references[]). Updated (4): the PHP entry (moved to critical: unauthenticated runtime RCE, fixed builds out, attack traffic observed by Cloudflare, watchTowr and VulnCheck, public proofs of concept circulating, authorities telling operators to patch today; nothing confirmed as compromised and neither CVE KEV-listed, so exploitation is written as attempts), the ConnectWise entry (Microsoft's Storm-0940 attribution, the 2,250-tenant attempt count and the restoration start), the OVHcloud CLI entry (root cause, payload and exfiltration from OVHcloud's postmortem) and the Publica entry (the assumed scope of practically all federal and federally affiliated staff, one chain of reporting).

Deep dive: none. PHP2Shell already has its entry and the exploitation evidence is attempts only; no other candidate clears the bar.

borderline-drop lines:

  • borderline-drop: Fortinet FortiSIEM CVE-2026-106173 (9.4, unauthenticated, public Horizon3 proof of concept) (S1) - only 7.5.0 is affected, the gRPC port is normally an internal management plane and no source reports exploitation; reopen on an exploitation report. S1 offered it as borderline.
  • borderline-drop: CrowdStrike's four agentic-AI actors (S3) - gated report, vendor summary only, no detection specifics and no Swiss victim; the ARTEX entry carries the transferable lesson.
  • borderline-drop: Symantec's Skynet LLMjacking agent (S3) - hijacks exposed LLM endpoints and AI gateways, no constituency exposure.
  • borderline-drop: Tor exit-relay SSH interception with Ebury 1.8.3 (S3) - SSH over Tor is not a constituency practice.
  • borderline-drop: Cisco Talos trusted-platform message abuse, Huntress finger.exe ClickFix and Abnormal AI Athena StealthRoute (S3) - delivery and phishing-as-a-service variants with no new detection decision.
  • borderline-drop: NorForge exposed Cairn panels, Pillar Security opencode flaw patched without a CVE, and two Wiz CIRT posts (S3) - lookback items below the bar; the Wiz feed is added to the next rotation.
  • borderline-drop: EFK audit of federal Microsoft 365 (S2) - oversight findings with no patch, hunt, block or detect decision; the audit report is accepted by the BIT and binds no other body.
  • borderline-drop: CERT-FR CTI-008 report on web-application data breaches (S2) - statistics and generic principles, dated 2026-10-20.
  • borderline-drop: BACS week-42 review (TWINT relay phishing) and the Swiss Government Cloud tender (S2) - consumer fraud and procurement.
  • borderline-drop: Zeabur and Railway environment-variable breaches, Onamae.com Desktop Cloud, UK ICO reprimands of Ogi Networks and Data Cymru, Kreisverwaltung Oberspreewald-Lausitz (S4) - no constituency nexus, a two-year-old incident, or a precautionary shutdown with no attack confirmed (incident floor).
  • borderline-drop: Plex and SiteGuard KEV rows, Chrome 156, the Mozilla dot releases, Laravel, Roundcube, the WordPress plugin batch, MikroTik token replay, Splunk, Apache Traffic Server and Pulsar, the lesser Cisco advisories, the rest of the Fortinet October batch and the ICS advisories (S1) - already dropped by the previous fire, routine, out of window, authenticated, or without constituency exposure. The October Patch Tuesday CVRF still shows Windows Shell CVE-2026-96951 as the only exploited flaw.

Single-source and carve-outs: the PAN-OS, GitLab and Cisco entries rest on the vendors' own advisories (reliability A, single-source); the k0t entry rests on Group-IB with NyxLab alone (B2), with the three CVEs independently KEV-listed; the Storm-0940 attribution is Microsoft's alone and Expel relays it; the Publica scope claim rests on Tamedia's paywalled article relayed by Netzwoche (the ICTjournal copy returned an empty body and is not cited). Contradictions: EPFL's site displayed a not-reachable notice while nau.ch says it still worked, and RTS lists it as suspended; the PHP entry reports both.

Verification: eight iterations of the single cold verifier, none CLEAN. Iteration 1 returned 24 findings (truth 5, editorial 10, advisory 9), among them a real error on LiteLLM: the build authorisation was in the maintainers' own status updates, which the run had not read. Each later pass checked the previous fixes first and then walked the ledger. Truth plus editorial counts ran 15, 8, 6, 6, 3, 3, 4 and 5; the later findings were mostly low-confidence one-clause attribution items, a few caused by an earlier fix (the PHP CVE-mapping sentence, a stray parenthesis) and two by cited pages that changed after the run read them (VulnCheck's weaponized exploit that succeeds with ASLR enabled, ConnectWise's archived advisory updates), both now in the entries. Iteration 8 was the cap, so the run publishes fail-open. The five iteration-8 truth findings were fixed by the main agent afterwards (the ConnectWise indicator date, the Lodur description, the Meraki qualifier, 'at least one' web-shell attempt, the run-record GitLab sentence) and are not re-verified, which is why the residual count is 5, not 0. Declined across passes: the OVHcloud staging-folder and extension names, the PHP exploited status, the watchTowr date label and the PAN-OS reference to the CVE-2026-0257 entry. For the audit: the CVE-2026-97229 GitLab entry still says to upgrade to 19.4.2, 19.3.5 or 19.2.8 now, which the CVE-2026-110264 entry says stay affected; the ConnectWise Trust Center is walled live and its 2026-10-21 updates were read from an archived copy through the metered jina reader; and the PHP entry's VulnCheck exploit wording deserves an independent read.

Source health (tools/source_health.py, 259 probed): nine fresh flags, four cleared in this run. efk-ch and bs-ch-medienmitteilungen got content_scope: general-news (general press and audit listings, mostly non-security by design), cyberattaque-org read again minutes after the sweep (transient), and fox-it-blog is demoted with one reliability-tier drop because blog.fox-it.com now serves a coming-soon placeholder with no posts (the publisher is covered by ncc-research). Five flags are origin-side outages no recipe can repair and stay in rotation with a note: cnil-fr (503 maintenance page), dcod-ch (503), zimbra-security-advisories (502), ec-digital-strategy-newsroom (403 on every transport, which never demotes) and lab52 (TLS reset).

Coverage: all 21 essential sources were attempted and every slice record was attempted (S1 18, S2 27, S3 14, S4 10 plus ransomware-live, databreaches-net and sec-disclosures-edgar). The previous two fires' attempts excluded 10 sources from the rotational ranking, and S4's slice was topped back up with all 10 recently attempted records because the exclusion would have emptied it. Entities added: four, plus two product records from sync_products.py. Promoted: swissinfo-ger. New candidates: php-net-news (first-party PHP security announcements), efk-ch (federal audit reports) and nau-ch (fast Swiss relay of cantonal communiqués); the sub-agents also proposed thephp-foundation-blog, watchtowr-intelligence, tio-ch, norforge, pillar-security-blog, safedep-blog and abnormal-ai-threat-intel, which are left for the audit's source pass. The extract transport fell to the metered reader for Wordfence, ICTjournal, Dark Reading and the CNIL maintenance page; the notes on those records say so.

Next-fire watch: Basel-Stadt's promised status update of 2026-10-22 and any compromise report from a PHP-running public body, PAN-OS fixed releases and a KEV listing for either PHP CVE, whether the Confederation, Publica or the Federal Prosecutor confirms the actor or the scope for PK Softech, Basel-Stadt and other cantonal restoration, ConnectWise's restoration instructions, the LiteLLM maintainers' next incident updates and the vulnerability they scheduled for disclosure on 2026-10-27 (a changelog record on the LiteLLM entry when it lands). For the audit: trendmicro-research recipe check (feed stale since 2026-09-25) and including wiz-blog in the next rotation.

Coverage gaps: zimbra-security-advisories (HTTP 502 on every transport), dcod-ch (HTTP 503 on feed and homepage), cnil-fr (503 maintenance page), connectwise-trust-center (403 on every transport), prodaft (no dated listing), news-admin-ch (only the 12 newest cards reachable), tagesanzeiger.ch (paywalled body, lead read), trendmicro-research (feed stale, no in-window post confirmable), citizen-lab (feed lags, listing used).

item.title: CTI Daily Brief · 2026-10-21
item.description:
• PHP2Shell: CISA lists both flaws as exploited after honeypot code execution; update the runtime, not the CMS. The PHP project released 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 on 2026-10-21 to fix CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (CVSS 4.0 9.2), two flaws in the runtime that allow unauthenticated remote code execution as the web worker account, most directly on Apache mod_php, with no upstream release for PHP 8.1 and older and a third path, CVE-2026-115560, left unfixed (keep session.upload_progress.enabled=0). CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-26, after a honeypot operator documented 35 successful code executions on PHP 8.4.26 under single-worker mod_php and VulnCheck extended its working exploit across builds of PHP 8.2 to 8.5; GreyNoise's sensors have recorded shell sessions since 2026-10-28, Palo Alto Networks' advisory now reports active exploitation against internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces, Dream Research recovered a custom build chained with the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-46300 that rooted 25 Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS firewall and management servers and attacked a US government-affiliated network, SRF links a data theft at TCS Camping's booking-system supplier to the flaws without naming a CVE, and Unit 42 retracted on 2026-10-25 its update that linked an attack on a European government agency to them. As of 2026-10-22 BACS knew of no attack in Switzerland but said federal PHP applications were affected and that it had no complete overview of the update status, and Swiss cantons, universities, Cyon, the Lodur platform and Publica took sites offline as a precaution. →
  • Stolen UpdraftCentral keys install backdoor plugins on WordPress sites; the plugin update alone does not evict them. TeamUpdraft, the vendor of the UpdraftPlus backup plugin, says unauthorised access to teamupdraft.com on 17 and 18 October probably exposed its customer database, including UpdraftCentral connection keys, and Patchstack and Nethemba report an attacker using those keys to install backdoor plugins on connected WordPress sites, which Patchstack's telemetry dates from 2026-10-18 15:32 (it gives no time zone), and that create hidden administrators. It is not a flaw in UpdraftPlus: the plugin obeys commands signed with a valid key, a key exists on many sites that never used the service because connecting a teamupdraft.com account ticks the option by default, and the update disconnects only connections made before 13:07 BST (12:07 UTC) on 18 October, so keys created later that day have to be deleted by hand. TeamUpdraft says the attacker used a compromised key to enter its own site, and Nethemba saw the stolen keys used again on 2026-10-21, after 1.26.13 shipped. →
  • Symantec: APT28's hidden-Edge backdoor hit law-enforcement and defence targets; at a shipbuilder it added an SSH tunnel. Symantec reports that APT28, which it tracks as Swallowtail, used the HOOKEDGE backdoor against a law-enforcement agency, a naval shipbuilder and a military aircraft-engine manufacturer in two NATO member states, none named. A macro-enabled Word document started a script chain that uses a hidden, off-screen Microsoft Edge window as its HTTP client against a public webhook service; at the shipbuilder the operators then pushed an SSH private key for a persistent tunnel, captured NTLM handshakes from the host itself and ran a previously undocumented in-memory loader, in an intrusion that lasted at least two months. Recorded Future had documented HOOKEDGE against government and diplomatic targets in Romania, Spain and Turkiye in August. →

TL;DR · the day in one read
  1. 01PHP2Shell: CISA lists both flaws as exploited after honeypot code execution; update the runtime, not the CMS. CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 2026-10-26, after a honeypot operator documented 35 successful code executions on PHP 8.4.26 under single-worker mod_php and VulnCheck extended its working exploit across builds of PHP 8.2 to 8.5; GreyNoise's sensors have recorded shell sessions since 2026-10-28, Palo Alto Networks' advisory now reports active exploitation against internet-exposed PAN-OS management interfaces, Dream Research recovered a custom build chained with the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-46300 that rooted 25 Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS firewall and management servers and attacked a US government-affiliated network, SRF links a data theft at TCS Camping's booking-system supplier to the flaws without naming a CVE, and Unit 42 retracted on 2026-10-25 its update that linked an attack on a European government agency to them. As of 2026-10-22 BACS knew of no attack in Switzerland but said federal PHP applications were affected and that it had no complete overview of the update status, and Swiss cantons, universities, Cyon, the Lodur platform and Publica took sites offline as a precaution. →
  2. 02Stolen UpdraftCentral keys install backdoor plugins on WordPress sites; the plugin update alone does not evict them. TeamUpdraft, the vendor of the UpdraftPlus backup plugin, says unauthorised access to teamupdraft.com on 17 and 18 October probably exposed its customer database, including UpdraftCentral connection keys, and Patchstack and Nethemba report an attacker using those keys to install backdoor plugins on connected WordPress sites, which Patchstack's telemetry dates from 2026-10-18 15:32 (it gives no time zone), and that create hidden administrators. It is not a flaw in UpdraftPlus: the plugin obeys commands signed with a valid key, a key exists on many sites that never used the service because connecting a teamupdraft.com account ticks the option by default, and the update disconnects only connections made before 13:07 BST (12:07 UTC) on 18 October, so keys created later that day have to be deleted by hand. TeamUpdraft says the attacker used a compromised key to enter its own site, and Nethemba saw the stolen keys used again on 2026-10-21, after 1.26.13 shipped. →
  3. 03Symantec: APT28's hidden-Edge backdoor hit law-enforcement and defence targets; at a shipbuilder it added an SSH tunnel. Symantec reports that APT28, which it tracks as Swallowtail, used the HOOKEDGE backdoor against a law-enforcement agency, a naval shipbuilder and a military aircraft-engine manufacturer in two NATO member states, none named. A macro-enabled Word document started a script chain that uses a hidden, off-screen Microsoft Edge window as its HTTP client against a public webhook service; at the shipbuilder the operators then pushed an SSH private key for a persistent tunnel, captured NTLM handshakes from the host itself and ran a previously undocumented in-memory loader, in an intrusion that lasted at least two months. Recorded Future had documented HOOKEDGE against government and diplomatic targets in Romania, Spain and Turkiye in August. →
Active threats, incidents & disclosures 4Trending vulnerabilities 2Updates to prior coverage 152Action items 33

01Active threats, incidents & disclosures4 items

NOTABLENATOB2

APT28 (Swallowtail) used the HOOKEDGE backdoor against a law-enforcement agency, a naval shipbuilder and an aircraft-engine maker in two NATO states; at the shipbuilder it then pushed an SSH key for a persistent tunnel, captured NTLM handshakes and ran a reflective loader

Symantec's Threat Hunter Team reports that Swallowtail, which it equates with APT28, Fancy Bear and Forest Blizzard, targeted organizations in two NATO member states: a law-enforcement agency, a naval shipbuilder and a manufacturer of military aircraft engines, none named (Symantec, 2026-10-20). Recorded Future had documented the HOOKEDGE backdoor in August, from campaigns between late September 2025 and early April 2026 against government and diplomatic organizations in Romania, Spain and Turkiye, and assesses with moderate confidence that BlueDelta, which overlaps APT28, is behind it (Recorded Future, 2026-08-27).

At the shipbuilder the vector was a macro-enabled Word document opened from the Outlook attachment cache on 2026-07-24, so it arrived by email; its macro dropped a VBScript launcher, an HTML pair that auto-submits a hidden form to a webhook endpoint and a batch script (Symantec, 2026-10-20). The batch script kills any running Microsoft Edge and restarts it as a one-pixel, off-screen window carrying an inline script instead of a URL, so the browser fetches the next task from the public webhook.site service, and the batch script then runs the task and uploads its output to the same endpoint (Symantec, 2026-10-20). A second stage then took its tasks from a dedicated address, and seven tasks arrived in about 30 seconds, a cadence Symantec reads as interactive (Symantec, 2026-10-20).

The operators then pushed an SSH private key onto the host and at once opened an outbound SSH session to their own server with host-key checking disabled, legacy RSA algorithms enabled and a background remote port forward, a persistent route into the internal network; separately a short PowerShell script ran an HTTP listener on loopback and net use against it, forcing the host to authenticate to itself so the NTLM handshake could be captured (Symantec, 2026-10-20). On 2026-07-31 they ran a previously undocumented reflective loader, which decrypts an encrypted file in memory; the payload was not recovered, and the launcher was last seen on 2026-09-24 (Symantec, 2026-10-20).

Exposure
Windows endpoints where users can open Office documents from mail and macros from internet-originated documents are allowed, and hosts with outbound access to webhook services. Symantec names no victim or country.
Detection
Process-creation telemetry with parent lineage for Word spawning script hosts or the command shell, then msedge.exe killed and restarted with a one-pixel window, an off-screen position and a data: URL argument; network and proxy telemetry for msedge.exe or curl reaching a webhook service; ssh.exe started with an identity file, a remote forward and host-key checking disabled; a PowerShell HTTP listener on loopback followed by net use to localhost; and scheduled-task creation by the launcher or installer, since Symantec says the second-stage installer has a scheduled task and Recorded Future advises detecting scheduled-task abuse (Recorded Future, 2026-08-27) (Symantec, 2026-10-20).

Triage: the distinctive sequence is an Office document's script host, then Edge killed and relaunched as a one-pixel off-screen window carrying an inline script instead of a URL; the Edge launch alone is not the signal.

Defender takeaway
Block macro execution from internet-originated documents and, on any host where a HOOKEDGE launcher is found, hunt for the credential theft and the SSH tunnel described above and reset the credentials the host used, because the shipbuilder intrusion continued long after the dropper ran (Symantec, 2026-10-20).

Sources: Symantec Threat Hunter Team · Recorded Future Insikt Group
NOTABLECVE-2020-3259 +4exploitedNATOA2

AA26-293A: FBI, CISA and German and UK law enforcement describe SafePay ransomware, which enters through VPN credentials and five edge-device and backup-server flaws and factory-resets backup NAS devices before encrypting

CISA, the FBI, the US Secret Service, Germany's Landeskriminalamt Rheinland-Pfalz and UK law enforcement published advisory AA26-293A on 2026-10-20, drawing on investigations as recently as August 2026; they say SafePay has affected businesses and critical infrastructure in North America, South America, Europe and Australia since August 2024, was among the most active ransomware groups in 2026 and has impacted at least 600 separate victims (CISA et al., 2026-10-20). Initial access is exposed credentials, brute force password attacks and VPN access, with the actors using Mullvad VPN addresses and phished account profiles to reach victim networks and exploit CVE-2020-3259 and CVE-2023-20269 on edge devices, and automated scripts exploiting CVE-2023-27532, CVE-2024-40711 and CVE-2024-40766 on internet-exposed systems (CISA et al., 2026-10-20). CISA's catalog names them as Cisco ASA and Firepower Threat Defense (the first two), Veeam Backup & Replication (the next two) and SonicWall SonicOS flaws (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-20).

Once inside, the actors take administrative rights on existing accounts or create new ones, run commands remotely with PsExec and WinRM, enumerate network shares with ShareFinder.ps1 and SharpShares.exe, disable security software, bypass User Account Control, then move over RDP and remote-management tools (CISA et al., 2026-10-20). They compress data with 7-Zip or WinRAR and exfiltrate it with WinSCP, RClone, FileZilla or OneDrive, and sometimes install AnyDesk or TeamViewer (CISA et al., 2026-10-20). Before encrypting they halt the Volume Shadow Copy Service and reset network-attached storage that holds backup data to factory settings; encryption then appends .SafePay (CISA et al., 2026-10-20).

Exposure
An internet-facing Cisco ASA or Firepower Threat Defense, Veeam Backup & Replication or SonicWall SonicOS system that one of the five flaws affects, and any VPN or remote-access account protected by a password alone; the advisory states neither affected versions nor fixes, so they come from each vendor's advisory for the CVE. Cisco calls CVE-2020-3259 reachable by an unauthenticated, remote attacker and SonicWall's CVSS vector for CVE-2024-40766 needs no privileges and no user interaction (Cisco, 2024-02-21; SonicWall, 2024-11-20). CISA's catalog says CVE-2020-3259 affects only specific AnyConnect and WebVPN configurations, and describes CVE-2023-27532 as a Cloud Connect flaw for an unauthenticated user within the backup infrastructure network perimeter (CISA KEV catalog, 2026-10-20).
Detection
VPN and firewall authentication logs for repeated failures then a success, Mullvad exit addresses and new accounts; directory audit logs for administrator-group changes; process-creation events for PsExec, WinRM and remote-management tools installed outside a change window; archive and file-transfer tools run by non-administrative workflows; and backup and NAS audit logs for a shadow-copy service stop or a factory reset.

Triage: 7-Zip, WinRAR, RClone, FileZilla, AnyDesk, TeamViewer, PsExec and WinRM are everyday administrative tools, and the advisory warns against calling them malicious without evidence of actor use (CISA et al., 2026-10-20); a shadow-copy service stop or a factory reset of backup storage that follows them is the discriminating step.

Defender takeaway
Confirm that every Cisco ASA or Firepower Threat Defense, Veeam Backup & Replication and SonicWall SonicOS system has the vendor's fix or mitigation for the five flaws, require multi-factor authentication on VPN and administrator accounts, and keep offline backups that are encrypted and immutable so that a factory reset of the NAS does not remove the restore path; the advisory recommends offline, encrypted and immutable backups (CISA et al., 2026-10-20).

Builds on: 2026-09-30/manno-ti-commune-ransomware-safepay-claim · 2026-06-23/sonicwall-cve-2024-40766-why-patched-firewalls-keep-falling

threat21 Oct 03:42Zsingle-source · national CERTOpen finding →
Sources: CISA, FBI, USSS, LKA Rheinland-Pfalz, UK NCA (AA26-293A) · CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog · Cisco (advisory cisco-sa-asaftd-info-disclose, last updated 2024-02-21) · SonicWall (advisory SNWLID-2024-0015, last updated 2024-11-20)
HIGHupdatedNATOB1

TeamUpdraft breach: stolen UpdraftCentral connection keys are used to push backdoor plugins to connected WordPress sites, with no flaw in UpdraftPlus and no CVE; deleting the keys is the fix

TeamUpdraft says unauthorised access to teamupdraft.com on 17 and 18 October and that it believes its customer database was accessed, which holds connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault and UpdraftClone; it says UpdraftPlus plugin files and downloads were not affected, that the attacker used a compromised key to access its site, and that there is no evidence the attacker still has access, and it suspects, from exploit speed and faulty first plugins, that AI accelerated the attack (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19). Patchstack reports that an attacker holding valid UpdraftCentral dashboard keys has been installing backdoor plugins on connected WordPress sites since 2026-10-18 at 15:32 (the page gives no time zone), and that this is not a vulnerability in UpdraftPlus: the UpdraftCentral client ships inside every copy of the plugin and executes any command signed with the dashboard's private key once the site holds a key (Patchstack, 2026-10-19; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-20).

The attacker sends a signed plugin.upload_plugin command as an ordinary POST to the site root and WordPress installs and activates the plugin; each delivered plugin wakes on a secret URL parameter carrying a 32-character token, creates an account with a hardcoded password, gives it the Editor role and then the manage_options and install_plugins capabilities, and logs the visitor in with a cookie, which bypasses the login form, two-factor authentication and login-protection plugins (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). The account stays after the plugin is removed, and early samples crash the site with an HTTP 500 and must not be repaired, because fixing the error switches the backdoor on (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). Nethemba adds a variant that logs the attacker in as an existing administrator without a database trace (Nethemba, 2026-10-19).

A site holds a key if it was connected to UpdraftCentral or if a teamupdraft.com account was logged in from the plugin, where the option to add the site to UpdraftCentral is ticked by default, and keys do not expire (Patchstack, 2026-10-19); on UpdraftPlus 1.26.4 or 2.26.4 and earlier an attacker needs no key at all, through CVE-2026-10795, fixed in 1.26.5 and 2.26.5 (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). BleepingComputer reports an estimate of up to about 400,000 sites (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-20; Nethemba, 2026-10-19). TeamUpdraft says UpdraftPlus 1.26.13 and 2.26.13 disconnect every UpdraftCentral connection made before 13:07 BST (12:07 UTC) on 18 October; Nethemba says 1.26.12 and 2.26.12 deleted none and that 1.26.13 does not delete keys created on 18 October between 12:07 and 21:00 UTC, which have to be deleted by hand (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19; Nethemba, 2026-10-19). Nethemba saw the attacker send UpdraftCentral commands to two of its sites on the morning of 2026-10-21, after 1.26.13 had shipped, blocked by Nethemba's own blocking plugin, with the keys already deleted, and says sites that neither run 1.26.13 or 2.26.13 nor have deleted the key by hand remain at risk (Nethemba, 2026-10-19).

Exposure
A WordPress site running UpdraftPlus, free or premium, that holds an UpdraftCentral key; wp option get updraft_central_localkeys prints it, including on sites whose owners never used UpdraftCentral (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). Self-hosted UpdraftCentral is not affected (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19).
Detection
Web server access logs for POST requests to the site root carrying an UpdraftCentral command whose user agent lacks the library version and URL that genuine dashboard traffic carries, and for GET requests with a short underscore-prefixed parameter and a 32-character token, which mean a backdoor was used; the UpdraftCentral log on the site for plugin.upload_plugin and plugin.delete_plugin commands without a matching administrator action; the user table for an Editor that also holds manage_options (Patchstack, 2026-10-19; Nethemba, 2026-10-19); and the plugin and must-use plugin directories (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19). TeamUpdraft asks users to look at the sites listed under their UpdraftCentral account for any they did not knowingly connect since 2026-10-19 and says it is seeing a pattern of unexpected Editor roles (TeamUpdraft, 2026-10-19). The backdoor account stays after the plugin is removed (Patchstack, 2026-10-19).
Defender takeaway
Delete the UpdraftCentral key on every site first, then update; if a backdoor is found, delete the key before removing it or the attacker pushes a replacement, and treat the site as compromised (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). IP blocking is not a control, since Patchstack saw the source addresses rotate within a day (Patchstack, 2026-10-19). NOTABLECVE-2026-91403 +3updatedNATOA1

eMudhra: the private keys of eight ECDSA intermediate CA certificates were trivially recoverable, so anyone could forge trusted HTTPS certificates, and eight RSA intermediates were revoked on 2026-11-07 for key handling eMudhra cannot show compliant; browsers block them, clients with their own trust store or no revocation checking need an update (CVE-2026-111943 in Go)

On 2026-10-17 a researcher reported to the Chrome Root Program, and Mozilla received a report the same day, that the private keys of eight eMudhra subordinate CA certificates were compromised: the keys were so weak that anyone could forge trusted HTTPS certificates to impersonate any website against clients that have not removed trust in those CAs; Google describes the cause as insufficient randomness (Google, 2026-10-20; Mozilla, 2026-10-20). BleepingComputer, citing Mozilla's incident report, says all eight were P-384 keys generated in April 2025 with values below 256, so testing 256 numbers recovers a key (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-20). eMudhra's incident report of 2026-11-10 says the keys were generated correctly on its hardware module at a ceremony on 2025-04-30 and then passed through a custom Python wrap/unwrap script that truncated the eight ECDSA private values; the keys of eight RSA-4096 issuers (G2B and G2C) stayed intact but were handled in that script's process memory, so eMudhra cannot show compliance with its certification practice statement, and it revoked them on 2026-11-07 with the reason cessationOfOperation after having said on 2026-10-19 that they were not impacted; its G2C issuers had issued end-entity certificates, the last on 2026-11-03, and no source says any RSA key leaked (eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-11-10; eMudhra, Mozilla bug 2083449, 2026-10-19; BleepingComputer, 2026-11-11). The tracker says it is not known whether attackers used the flaw against other clients (Dennis Jackson, 2026-10-20).

Chrome blocked the intermediates on 2026-10-17, Firefox through OneCRL the same day, Microsoft platforms on 2026-10-20 and Apple products on 2026-10-22, and eMudhra revoked all eight (Dennis Jackson, 2026-10-20; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-20). Microsoft went further: an out-of-band Windows update of 2026-10-26 removes seven certificates, six eMudhra G3 roots and an AAA Certificate Services cross-sign, from the Windows trust list, and the same seven left the Edge trust list on 2026-10-27 (Microsoft, 2026-10-26). Google removed the root that signed them, emSign ECC Root CA - G3, from the Chrome Root Store, with the removal expected to reach devices on 2026-10-27 (Google, 2026-10-20). Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 filter chains that contain the intermediates in crypto/x509, tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (Go team, 2026-10-20), and GitLab's release of 2026-10-29 removes trust for the eight intermediates in self-managed CE and EE, with Runner 19.5.1 and the AI Gateway updated separately (GitLab, 2026-10-29).

Oracle's Security Alert of 2026-10-21 for CVE-2026-91403 (CVSS 3.1 9.1, JSSE) provided Java updates that distrust the impacted eMudhra intermediate CA certificates (Oracle, 2026-10-21), and a second Security Alert of 2026-10-24, CVE-2026-114820, removes the impacted root CA certificates and also covers the Java component of Oracle Database Server, Autonomous Health Framework and OPatch (Oracle, 2026-10-30). OpenJDK's guidance tells users of a standalone runtime to act immediately even if they updated in the past few days (OpenJDK, 2026-10-24).

Exposure
Any software that keeps its own CA bundle or does not check revocation keeps trusting the intermediates until updated; Python 3.15.2, 3.14.10, 3.13.18, 3.12.16 and 3.11.18 carry a built-in denylist (Python Insider, 2026-10-26); Apple says the curl, git, python3, ruby, perl and openssl that ship with macOS or the Xcode command-line tools read /etc/ssl/cert.pem, check neither Apple's block nor revocation and keep trusting them until macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 or 15.8.3 (Apple, 2026-11-10). SonicOS firewalls with Client DPI-SSL enabled re-signed the chains with their own DPI-SSL CA, so client browsers could not reject a forged one, until SonicOS 7.3.4-7015 (Gen7) and 8.2.3-8015 (Gen8) (SonicWall, 2026-11-10; SonicWall advisory data, 2026-11-10).
Detection
EMudhra says it found no evidence that the intermediates were used to issue end-user certificates (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-20), so a server certificate chain seen in TLS session metadata, proxy or EDR network telemetry that contains one of the eight intermediates or their Sectigo cross-signs, which the tracker lists, is worth treating as a possible forged certificate (Dennis Jackson, 2026-10-20). CT monitoring will not show one, because Google found no certificate chaining to the six TLS intermediates logged before it blocked them (Google, 2026-10-20).

Triage: a site that still chains to emSign ECC Root CA - G3 failing in Chrome after 2026-10-27, or a certificate that chains to one of the seven certificates Microsoft removed failing in Windows or Edge once the change reaches the device, is the announced root removal, not an attack (Google, 2026-10-20; Microsoft, 2026-10-26).

Defender takeaway
Update trust bundles and toolchains on every non-browser client, rebuild container images that embed an old bundle, and do not rely on revocation or CT for those clients; website operators with certificates chaining to emSign ECC Root CA - G3 need one from another hierarchy now (Google, 2026-10-20), and so does anything issued under emSign Root CA - G1 after 2026-11-16, because Chrome 153 and higher will not trust such a certificate by default when its earliest SCT is later (Google, 2026-11-04). On Macs, update to macOS 27.2.1, 26.7.3 or 15.8.3, which block them in the command-line tools; where that is not possible, remove emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from that file as Apple describes (removing AAA Certificate Services as well is optional and can stop tools that read only that file from verifying some unaffected sites) (Apple, 2026-11-10). From 2026-11-16 Microsoft removes the remaining eMudhra roots from Windows, Edge and WebView2, so a certificate under emSign Root CA - G1 stops validating there too (Microsoft, 2026-11-10). Certificates from the eight revoked RSA G2B and G2C issuers are revoked and eMudhra says its subscribers were migrated, so check inventories for any holder still on them.
